**The disclosure, and what it would have cost them.**

In order to assure the Muslims of their sincerity and to win their favour, these hypocrites would now and then disclose to them that the Torah itself had given out the good tidings of the coming of the Holy Prophet and mentioned the Holy Qur'an. Muhammad and his Companions (of that which Allah hath disclosed to you) about that which Allah has shown you regarding the description and traits of Muhammad in your Book (so that they may contend with you) argue against you (before your Lord concerning it? Have ye then no sense?) do you not have any common sense? Do you speak to them of what God has disclosed to you so that they may thereby dispute with you before your Lordḍ Have you no understandingḍ Do they not know that God knows what they keep secret and what they proclaimḍ They encouraged one another among themselves to reject the Real and to hide the situation from the Muslims. Have you no understanding?’ of the fact that they will contend with you if you speak to them in this way? (And what they reveal?) meaning, when they said to the Companions of Muhammad ,. But they did not know that God was informing His Messenger of their secrets and that a light the Real makes manifest cannot be extinguished by the efforts of anyone other than Him. When the tongue agrees but the mind162 objects it only increases separation.

77.text:
The verse is a single question and it is about knowledge. "Do they not know that Allah is aware of what they conceal and what they reveal" is put as a question whose answer is given in its own form, since the interrogative is affirmative and the not in it is not a doubt but a way of putting the knowledge as something they cannot miss. The two things named are the concealed and the revealed, and the pair covers the whole of what a person does, so the awareness of Allah is not put as reaching one of them and not the other but as reaching both at once, which is what makes the concealment of the last verse pointless. The concealment and the revealing are named in that order, and the order matters, since the hidden comes first in the sentence and the open second, so the awareness is turned first on the thing no one else can see and only then on the thing everyone can, which is the reverse of the order a person would take them in. The question is asked of people who have just been described as speaking one way in public and another in private, and it is asked in a form that expects the answer, so the verse is not opening a doubt about their knowledge but closing a way out of it. The verse does not threaten and does not promise, and the whole of its weight is in the word aware, since an awareness that covers the hidden and the open leaves nothing that can be kept from it.

**Do they not know.**

God says Know they not the interrogative is affirmative the inserted wāw of a-wa-lā is to indicate the supplement that God knows what they keep secret and what they proclaim? that is what they hide and what they reveal in this matter and all other matters so that they may desist from these things. Do they not know that God knows what they keep secret and what they announce? He presents His lordhood and kingship to him and says, "Do they not know that God knows what they keep secret and what they announce? (Are they) i.e. these leaders (then unaware that Allah knoweth that which they keep hidden) amongst themselves (and that which they proclaim?) to Muhammad and his Companions. They behave in this pathetic manner as if they are unaware that Allah knows what they hide, in terms of what they say and do, and what they reveal; but He will reveal it and expose them. With every hope of a positive response, it was with sublime feelings that they called on the Jews to join them in their belief in the Prophet.

**The secret and the hidden, and the apparent.**

When the Lord of the Worlds says that He knows the secret cores and is aware of the hidden things, they sweep the dust of the others from their secret cores and give scatteredness no way into their hearts. When He says that He knows the apparent, they bring truthfulness to bear in their outward interaction with God's creatures. This is why the folk of allusion have said that He knows what they keep secret is a command to watchfulness between servant and Lord, and what they announce is a command to truthfulness in interactions and settling accounts with the creatures. In one of God's books has come, "If you do not know that I see you, that is a defect in your faith. If you do know that I see you, why do you make Me the lowliest of gazers upon you?

**The treachery of the eyes, and what the breasts conceal.**

Allah reminds the Jews that He is omniscient, and knows what they try to keep concealed as well as what they say or do openly. "He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal" [40:19]. There are diverse treacheries in the eyes of the lookers, because the travelers are diverse. The treachery of the eyes of the worshipers is that in the dark night, when it is time for whis pering to God, they fall asleep and the intimacy of seclusion is lost to them. The prophet David received the revelation, "O David, he who claims to love Me is a liar if night comes, and he goes to sleep on Me. Does not every lover love to be secluded with his beloved? " God praised Abraham for this attribute when He said, "When night darkened over him" [6:76].

78.text:
The verse divides the people of the last verses into two, and this is the second of them. "And among them are the illiterate who know nothing about the Scripture except lies" sets a group apart by what it does not know, and the not knowing is of the Scripture itself, so the group named is not outside the book but inside it without it, and the one thing it has in place of the book is a lie. The exception is the hinge of the sentence, since except lies turns a statement about ignorance into a statement about what fills the ignorance, and what fills it is not nothing but something taken for the Scripture. "and so they wishfully speculate" is the consequence, and the speculation is named as wishful, so the guessing is not a shortfall of information but a direction of the will, and the two halves of the verse answer each other, the lie being what is taken for the book and the speculation being the taking of it. The word used for this speculation carries a range of meanings in the Qur'an, and the sense it has here is the weakest of them, an opinion with nothing under it.

**The illiterate among them, who know nothing of the Scripture.**

And there are some of them the Jews that are illiterate unlettered not knowing the Scripture the Torah but only desires lies which were handed down to them by their leaders and which they relied upon; and in their rejection of the prophethood of the Prophet and fabrications of other matters they have mere conjectures and no firm knowledge. And there are among them (Jews) 'Ummyyun (unlettered) people, who know not the Book, but they trust upon Amani (false desires) and they but guess Then woe to those who write the book with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," to purchase with it a little price! (Among them are unlettered folk who know not the scripture) they do not know how to read or write it (except from hearsay) except the unfounded things they hear. A group of them do not know how to read or write and do not know what is in the Torah or what it says. In this verse the attribute of unletteredness is a censure of the estranged and a mark of their short coming. In the verse where He says, "Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet" [7:157], it is a praise of MuṣṬafā and a mark of his perfection. (Who know not the Book) meaning, are they not aware of what is in it.

**The tales taught to the masses, and what they guess.**

The scholars who taught these tales, attributing them to past saints, became highly regarded for the theories they expounded were designed to win popular support. Such sacred recipes for cheap salvation are very attractive to the masses, for they give credence to the popular notion based on wishful thinking that there is no need to discipline oneself—no need to lead a responsible life; superstitious charms and magical remedies are enough to cure one’s spiritual ills and have one admitted to heaven. (They but guess) their talk is all surmise based on what they heard from their leaders. They have only lies which they heard from some of their leaders, and think it is the Torah revealed by Allah. (But they trust upon Amani) means, "It is just a false statement that they utter with their tongues. " Qatadah, Abu Al-'Aliyah and Ar-Rabi' said that it means, "They have evil false ideas about Allah." Then, the Jewish scholars did not give them correct or proper information about their religion.

**The word they were given, and the context it was used in.**

Some people do not pay any attention to the context in which the word has been used here, and come to the erroneous conclusion that it is not legitimate to accept or follow any view or injunction based on Zann which they always translate as "a fanciful supposition. Let us explain that the Holy Qur'an uses the word Zann in three ways: " This, no doubt, is one of the lexical meanings of the word, but only one. This verse condemns the Jews for having followed this kind of Zann which consists in a fanciful opinion that is not supported by a respectable argument or goes against a valid one. When someone fancies that having the same meaning is to be of the same kind, that is to go by the road of the road less, and it is nothing but rebellion.

**Cheap salvation, and the dream world.**

Facilitation of eternal salvation became for them a lucrative source of worldly income. They were showered with offerings, for they ushered others along the path to a paradise that did not have to be earned; in return they received worldly wealth that they did not have to labour for. They wanted to live in a dream world, thinking that they had no obligations save the perfunctory performance of certain empty rituals, and deluding themselves into believing that they had certain inalienable rights given by God. Such people cannot accept the call of true religion, for truth demolishes all their wishful thinking, and makes them face the stark realities of life. According to Ibn ‘Abbas, Fara’ and Mujahid—some of the most reliable of the Quranic commentators—the word refers to the mythical tales invented by Jewish scholars. So, it would make no difference at all, if the hypocrites tried to conceal their infidelity from the Muslims, or the other group, not to disclose the verses of the Torah which speak of the Holy Prophet . The position of the Folk of the Sunnah in affirming the attributes of the Real was established according to this rule: the agreement of one name with another does not bring about the agreement of meanings. What God said about Himself should be accepted from the eyeteeth and assented to from the depth of the spirit.

79.text:
The verse turns from what the last verses described to what is now put over it, and the word it turns on is woe. "So woe to those who distort the Scripture with their own hands then say, This is from Allah" names the act in three parts, and the parts are ordered as an act is ordered, since the distorting comes first, the writing of it second and the naming of it third, and each part is qualified: the distorting is of the Scripture, so the thing altered is a book that was given and not a book being composed; it is with their own hands, so the altering is not a slip in transmission but a thing done by the people doing it; and what they then say is that this is from Allah, which puts a source on the altered text and makes the alteration a claim about where the text came from. The distortion is therefore not of a wording only but of an attribution, and the verse treats the attribution as the heavier of the two, since the words put in are given a divine origin and the people who read them afterwards are not reading an opinion of men but what they have been told is from Allah. "seeking a fleeting gain" gives the reason, and the reason is a gain, so the act is not done for a doctrine or for a party but for something taken, and the gain is qualified as fleeting, which puts the trade in terms of what is got now against what the getting is worth later. "So woe to them for what their hands have written" repeats the woe and attaches it to the writing rather than to the distorting, so the second woe is on the thing that remains, the written text, and not only on the act that produced it. "and woe to them for what they have earned" repeats it a third time and attaches it to the earning, which is the gain named a moment earlier, so the three woes cover the altering, the writing and the taking, and each is put with the same word and the same preposition, which is what makes the verse read as a reckoning and not as a description. The hands appear twice, once in the doing and once in the accounting, and the second appearance is what ties the gain to the writing, since what is earned is earned by the same hands that wrote. Neither qualification is incidental: the hands remove any defence that the text came down altered or that the altering was done by others, and the gain removes any defence that the altering was done for the religion, since a thing done for a gain is done for the gain. The saying is put in the present and the writing in the past, and the sequence in the verse is that the writing happened and the saying goes on, so what is condemned is not a single forgery but a standing practice of putting a divine name on a human text. The people the woe falls on are the same people the last verses described, the ones who heard the word of Allah and corrupted it after understanding it, and the ones who kept one speech for the believers and another for themselves, so this verse closes that description with a reckoning and states the price of it.

**Woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands.**

(Therefore woe) severe punishment, and it is said this means: a valley in hell (be unto those who write the Scripture with their hands) change the description and traits of Muhammad ﷺ in the Book (and then say, �This is) in the Book that has come (from Allah�, that they may purchase) through changing and altering it (a small gain therewith) a small gain in terms of means of subsistence and surplus of property. So woe a severe chastisement to those who write the Scripture with their hands that is fabricating it themselves then say ‘This is from God’ that they may sell it for a small price of this world these are the Jews the ones that altered the description of the Prophet in the Torah as well as the ‘stoning’ verse and other details and rewrote them in a way different from that in which they were revealed. Misery and great suffering awaits those who write the scripture with their own hands, and then say, falsely, that it comes from Allah, exchanging the truth and guidance for a small gain in this world, such as money or leadership. (Woe to them), "Means the torment will be theirs because of the lies that they wrote with their own hands,. (Neither did you (O Muhammad) read any book before it (this Qur'an) nor did you write any book (whatsoever) with your right hand. In that case, indeed, the followers of falsehood might have doubted)(29:48). Ummyyun, is plural for Ummi, that is, a person who does not write, as Abu Al-'Aliyah, Ar-Rabi', Qatadah, Ibrahim An-Nakha'i and others said. Then, the Jewish scholars did not give them correct or proper information about their religion.

**What their hands have written, and the woe on it.**

So woe to them for what their hands have written of fabrications and woe to them for their earnings by way of bribery rishan plural of rishwa. (Woe unto them) theirs is a severe punishment (for what their hands have written) have altered (and woe unto them) and theirs is a severe punishment (for what they earn thereby) of unlawful earnings and bribes. They will experience misery and suffering because of what their hands have written, through which they told lies about Allah, and for whatever wealth or leadership they may gain through these lies. (Woe to them for what their hands have written and woe to them for that they earn thereby) means, "Woe to them because of what they have written with their own hands, the lies, falsehood and alterations. It means they have lost in the present and in the end. He related that they differed in the shortcomings of their disbelief. It was not that doubt seized them but rather that they were misled by conjecture and speculation.

**The worldly gain, and the money under it.**

They were greedy and self-seeking, and in order to please the people for receiving money and respect from them, they used to misrepresent divine injunctions, going so far as to change the words of the Torah or distort the sense, pretending all the while that this was just what Allah had said or meant. The Verse 79 announces a grievous punishment for these two sins - distorting the Word of Allah and earning money by doing so. The Jewish rabbis and doctors used to gain some worldly benefits from the Jewish people and so they were afraid of losing this gain if they were ever to show the real description. It is for this reason that they had changed it . Whenever the clamor of worldly fortunes call they rush to respond will ingly but when the demands of the Real direct them to some endeavor their situation is a bad one since they are not sincere. Among this group are those who are mostly concerned with what they desire for themselves. They have no share in their scriptures other than to recite them without knowledge of their meanings.

**The description they changed, and why they changed it.**

This was revealed about those who had changed the description of the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, and altered his traits. They had changed the description of Allah's Messenger, Allah bless him and give him peace, in their Scripture. They made him white and tall while the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, was brown and of medium height. Look at the description of the prophet who will be sent at the end of time; his description does not match that of this [man] . Ummi was one of the descriptions of the Prophet because he was unlettered. Added to this, statements in support of the theory that the Jews were God’s ‘chosen people’ were attributed to venerated Jewish saints. It was made out that certain magical properties were inherent in their religion, ensuring salvation by virtue of mere adherence to the run-of-the-mill rites of Judaism. This has been a failing in the people of the Book in every age.

80.text:
The verse puts a claim and then answers it with two questions. "Some of the Jews claim" opens it, and the claim is put as a claim rather than as a report of what a people believed, so the verse is already marking the distance between the thing asserted and the thing known. What is asserted, and then answered, runs in one breath in the verse itself: "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days. Say, O Prophet, have you taken a pledge from Allah—for Allah never breaks His word—or are you just saying about Allah what you do not know?" The number is left uncounted in the verse itself, which is why the commentators go looking for it and find it in two different places, forty days with the calf and seven days with the length of the world. The touching named here is a touching and not an entering, and the exception is the whole of the claim, since the Fire is not denied but limited, and the limit is what the verse takes up. The turn to the one addressed comes at once, and the answer is not a denial of the Fire but a demand for the ground of the limit. The first of the two questions asks whether that limit rests on something given by Allah, a pledge taken from Him, so that the number of days would be a term of a contract rather than an estimate. The clause on Allah never breaking His word is put inside the question and not after it, and it concedes the whole force of the pledge, since if there were a pledge it would stand, Allah not breaking His word; so the question is not about whether Allah keeps promises but about whether one was ever given. The second question closes the alternative, and the alternative is exhaustive, since a limit on the Fire either comes from a pledge or comes from speech about Allah without knowledge, and the just marks the second as the one that is happening.

**The claim, and the days behind it.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar takes the claim at its word and marks it false: they say that the fire of Hell will not touch them and that they will not be in it except for a few days. Ibn Kathīr gives the same shape to it and puts the weight on the hoping, that the Jews hope they will only remain in the Fire for a few days and then be saved from it, so the claim is not a doctrine about the Fire but an expectation about a term. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān takes it apart differently, as an argument resting on another argument. The principle common to all the Sharīʿahs is that a believer who commits sins is punished in Hell for a time, in measure with the degree and nature of his sins, and that because he possesses faith he is not assigned to Hell forever but released after he has served his term. On that principle the claim would be sound if the premise under it were sound, and the point Maʿārif al-Qurʾān makes is that the premise is the false one: the Jews took the Sharīʿah of Mūsā not to have been abrogated, and so took themselves to be believers rather than infidels in denying the prophethood of ʿĪsā and of Muḥammad, and so took a few days of punishment to end the matter. The Torah nowhere gives that Sharīʿah perpetuity, and to claim perpetuity for it is an unfounded assertion, which leaves a false assertion resting on a false one.

**Forty days, and the calf.**

The forty days are not chosen at random, and both of the sources that give them tie them to the same event. Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives forty days as the number of days in which their forefathers worshipped the calf. Al-Jalālayn gives the same measure for the same reason and adds the ending, a short time of forty days, the length of time their forefathers worshipped the calf, after which the Fire will cease. Ibn Kathīr carries the forty days as well, and puts beside it the report that the Jews said the Fire would only touch them for forty days. So the limit is measured against an event in their own history, and the punishment is sized to the sin, forty days of the calf answered by forty days of the Fire. What makes the reading sharp is that the sin it is measured against is one this surah has already gone over at length, so the number is not arbitrary but has a history behind it, and the history is theirs. Tazkirul Qurʾān puts the claim in the same family as the other false notions of these verses, the word for them being amānī, and gives it a source: on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, Faraʾ and Mujāhid, the word refers to the mythical tales invented by Jewish scholars, whose overall aim was to prove that Paradise was reserved for the Jews, with statements supporting the theory of a chosen people attributed to venerated saints of theirs and a salvation made out to follow from mere adherence to the run-of-the-mill rites.

**Seven days, and the arithmetic of the world.**

Al-Wāḥidī gives the occasion and a second arithmetic. The Messenger came to Madīnah and found the Jews holding that this worldly life would last seven thousand years, and that for every one thousand years of its days people would be tormented in the Fire for one day, so that the torment would last seven days only. Al-Wāḥidī then carries the report further, into the Fire itself: the people of the Book found that a journey of forty years was needed from one end of the Fire to the other, and so they proceeded in their torment until they reached Saqar, wherein is the tree of Zaqqūm, until the certain number of days; and the denizens of the Fire then put it to them that they had claimed not to be tormented except for a certain number of days, and that those days had now elapsed while eternity remains. Two different numbers therefore sit behind one claim in these sources, forty days measured against the calf and seven days measured against the length of the world, and the verse itself commits to neither, which is why the answer it gives is not about the number at all.

**Have you taken a pledge from Allah.**

The first of the two questions is about the ground of the claim. Al-Jalālayn reads it as a question put to them: have you taken with God a covenant, a pledge from Him to this, and God will not fail in His covenant in this matter, or nay, say you against God what you do not know. Al-Jalālayn also gives the grammar of its first word, that in aʾttakhadhtum the conjunctive hamza has been omitted on account of the interrogative hamza sufficing, which is why the sentence reads as a question and not as a statement about a taking. Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts the same two halves in the same order and ties the covenant to the saying: have you received a covenant from Allah for what you are saying, and truly Allah will not break His covenant if indeed you have a covenant with Allah. Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the conditional explicit, that they are to be asked whether they have had a promise from Allah that this will be the case, and that if they have had a promise then Allah will not break His contract. Ibn Kathīr puts the same point as a proclamation of the verse, that if you had a promise from Allah for that then Allah will never break His promise. The force of the question is therefore not in doubting the keeping of a promise but in asking whether one exists, and every one of these readings leaves the pledge unproduced.

**Saying about Allah what you do not know.**

The second question is the one the claim actually answers. Tanwīr al-Miqbās narrows it to a book: or do you tell concerning Allah that which you know not, that which you know does not exist in your Book, so the knowledge asked for is a knowledge they would have had to receive, and the Torah is where it would have to be. Ibn Kathīr puts it as a lie, that what they say about Allah they have no knowledge of and so utter a lie about Him, and he carries it from al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Qushayrī takes the question inward and reads the claim as a state of the one making it: such a person abides with the murmurings of his lower desires, and he judges the unseen by what he has himself neglected, having forgotten the ugliness of what he has done; he is a servant of his lower self whose good opinion of himself has gotten the better of him, and in reality the results of his neglect and deceit possess him. Al-Qushayrī brings the Qurʾān's own word on such a supposition, that the supposition they supposed of their Lord had ruined them. On this reading the second question is not a challenge to produce a text but a diagnosis, and a limit on the Fire is what a good opinion of oneself looks like when it is turned into a number. The two questions cover the claim from both sides, then: either there is a pledge, in which case Allah keeps it, or there is speech about Allah without knowledge, in which case the number is not a term but a wish, and the verse leaves them with the second.

81.text:
The verse answers the claim of the last two verses, and it answers it with a rule. "But no! Those who commit evil and are engrossed in sin will be the residents of the Fire" begins with a refusal, and the refusal is not of a person but of a claim, so the but no is closing the previous verse's question about a number of days before the rule is given. The rule has two conditions in it and they are joined, since the committing of evil is one thing and being engrossed in sin is another, and the second is a state rather than an act, a being taken over by the sin rather than a doing of it. The engrossing is what makes the case, and without it the evil committed is an act that ends, whereas the sin that has taken hold does not end, and it is the not ending that the punishment answers. The residents of the Fire are named as residents and not as visitors, and the word is one used for a dwelling, so the verse is not describing a punishment that is passed through but a place that is lived in. "They will be there forever" states the term, and the term is the point at issue with the last verse, since the number of days claimed there is answered here by a forever with no number in it. The forever is therefore not an intensifying of the punishment but a change of kind, and the change is what the two conditions produce, the evil committed and the sin that has closed over the one committing it.

**Whoever earns evil, and is encompassed by his sin.**

Not so it will touch you and you will abide therein; whoever earns evil through associating another with God and is encompassed by his transgression in the singular and the plural that is to say it overcomes him and encircles him totally for he has died an idolater — those are the inhabitants of the Fire therein abiding khālidūn this plural noun takes account of the plural import of man ‘whoever’. here Allah answers the Jews, (but whoever hath done evil) ascribes partners to Allah (and his sins surround him) and dies ascribing partners to Allah; (such are) those who have these attributes (rightful owners of the Fire) the dwellers of hell; (they will abide therein forever) perpetually, they will neither die nor leave it. Allah repays those who reach the evil of disbelief, and whose disobedience dominates them, with suffering in the fire of Hell, where they will live eternally. Not so; whoever earns evil and is encompassed by his transgression those are the inhabitants of the fire therein abiding khālidūn. In the language of scholars168 the one who is encompassed by his trans gression is the disbeliever. Those who commit evil deeds knowingly and deliberately so that evil takes hold of them completely, leaving no trace of goodness - such men shall go to the Hell, and live there forever, without any intermission or release.

**The sin that surrounds, and the small sins that gather.**

Whosoever earns evil and his sin has surrounded him, they are dwellers of the Fire (i.e. Hell); they will dwell therein forever And those who believe and do righteous good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise, they will dwell therein forever. Rather, whoever does an evil deed and abides purposefully in his error, coming on the Day of Resurrection with no good deeds, only evil deeds, then he will be among the people of the Fire. (And his sin has surrounded him) means, "His Shirk (polytheism) has surrounded him. When Small Sins gather, They bring about Destruction. (Beware of the belittled sins, because they gather on a person until they destroy him.) (This is the example of people who set up camp on a flat land, and then their servants came. One of them collected some wood and another man collected some wood until they collected a great deal. They then started a fire and cooked what they put on it.) (It will not be in accordance with your desires (Muslims), nor those of the People of the Scripture (Jews and Christians), whosoever works evil, will have the recompense thereof, and he will not find any protector or helper besides Allah. And whoever does righteous good deeds, male or female, and is a (true) believer [in the Oneness of Allah (Muslim)], such will enter Paradise and not the least injustice, even the size of a Naqira (speck on the back of a date stone), will be done to them)(4:123-124).

**Evil taking hold completely, and the faith that leaves a trace of good.**

Let us explain how evil can take hold of a man so completely that no trace of goodness is left. This kind of thing happens only to infidels (Kafirs), and not to Muslims, even when they are sinners. That is why on the Day of Judgment, infidels will have to show nothing but evil, in punishment of which they shall live in Hell for ever. On the contrary, men of faith will, to begin with, have the greatest and highest good deed to their credit - namely, faith ('Iman) itself. So, they cannot be devoid of all goodness, and evil cannot be said to have taken hold of them completely. In short, the infidel, according to this divine law, must always live in Hell. So, in accordance with this law, they too will be assigned to Hell for ever like other infidels, and their claim that they would be released from Hell after few days can now be seen to be totally false and baseless.

**The heart, the realities possessed, the majesty, and obedience.**

But the allusion in it is to one whose heart has ceased its perpetual calling for help. The possessors of realities are like grain in the frying pan in their moments of wakefulness ṣaḥw. Those [of them] who have become still are thus because of His excessive majesty not because they are listless. Whoever relies on obedience seeks favor from it and thinks that he [can] draw near by means of it but he should keep his distance from this [idea]. Whoever comes to know the truth of God's unity knows that there is no means to Him except through Him.

82.text:
The verse is the second half of a pair, and it is the half that is not about the Fire. "And those who believe and do good will be the residents of Paradise" answers the last verse clause for clause, and the answering is exact: the committing of evil and the being engrossed in sin are matched by believing and doing good, and the residents of the Fire by the residents of Paradise, so the two verses are one rule put from both of its ends. The two conditions here are joined as they were there, and the second is again the active one, since doing good is a doing and not a state, and the belief it follows is what makes the doing count. The residents are named with the same word as before, a word for people who dwell somewhere, so the Paradise is a place lived in and not a reward handed over, and the reward is the living in it. "They will be there forever" repeats the forever of the last verse without changing it, and the repetition is the point, since the same term is given to both of the two groups and neither of them is released from it, so the forever is not a quality of the reward but of the residence. The good named is not specified, and the belief is not specified either, so the verse gives the rule and its two conditions and leaves the filling in of both to what comes with it, which takes up what the belief is a belief in and whether the doing has to be complete for the residence to follow.

**Those who believe and do good.**

And those who believe and perform righteous deeds — those are the inhabitants of Paradise therein abiding. (And those who believe) in Muhammad and the Qur'an (and do good works) acts of obedience that are between them and their Lord, (such are rightful owners of Paradise. They will abide therein forever) perpetually, they will never die or come out of it. So those who have faith in Allah and His Prophet, and do good, will be rewarded with entry into the Garden, where they will live eternally. (And those who believe and do righteous good deeds) meaning, "They believe in Allah and His Messenger and perform the good deeds that conform with the Islamic Law. But those who believe in Allah and the Holy Prophet - whose Shari ah has now abrogated all the earlier Shari'ahs and who do good deeds in conformity with the Islamic Shari'ah, - it is these men who shall go to Paradise, and will live there forever. Having refuted the claim of the Jews as baseless, the Holy Qur'an lays down the divine law in this regard. Those who have faith and do wholesome deeds-those are the companions of the Garden, and they shall be there forever. Allah says, the matter is not as you have wished and hoped it to be.

**The residents of Paradise, and forever.**

(And those who believe and do righteous good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise, they will dwell therein forever) "Whoever believes in what you (Jews) did not believe in and implements what you refrained from implementing of Muhammad's religion, shall acquire Paradise for eternity. Allah stated that the recompense for good or evil works shall remain with its people for eternity. Those are the companions of the Garden is an allusion to the produce of the tree and the ripening of its fruit. Today in the house of service on the carpet of obedience they have the paradise of recognition, neither turned aside from them nor veiled. Tomorrow in the house of union on the carpet of friendship they will have the paradise of approval, neither cut off nor withheld, and upraised carpets [56:33-34]. Since Sayyidna Musa (Moses) was not the last prophet, but was followed by two other prophets, Sayyidna Isa (Jesus) and Sayyidna Muhammad the Jews turned into infidels by denying these two prophets. For, no good deed on the part of an infidel is acceptable to Allah on account of his infidelity; even the good deeds he has done before his apostasy and infidelity are lost, and rendered null and void. Then, their secondary good deeds too are recorded in their account.

**The tree of faith, and its fruit.**

It has been said that those who have faith is an allusion to the tree of faith and its being planted in the heart of the faithful. Do wholesome deeds is an allusion to the branches of that tree and its nurturing and growing. This is the tree about which the Lord of the Worlds speaks and reports in another place: "Its roots fixed, and its branches in heaven. It gives its fruit every season by the leave of its Lord" [14:24-25]. The fruit of this tree is not like the fruit of other trees, which bring forth fruit once year after year. Rather, this tree brings forth new fruit every hour, or rather every moment. Each has another color, another taste, and another fragrance. The sweetness of worshipers is a fruit of this tree, the feast of the desirers' heart is a fruit of this tree, the limpid ness of the recognizers' present moment is a fruit of this tree.

83.text:
The verse is a list of what was taken from a people, and then a statement of what they did with it. "And remember when We took a covenant from the children of Israel stating" sets it as a remembrance and not as a new command, and the covenant is one taken from them, so the obligation named in what follows is an obligation they accepted, and the stating introduces the terms in their own order. The first term is "Worship none but Allah", and it stands alone at the head of the list, which puts the worship first and makes everything after it a consequence of it rather than a parallel to it. The second is "be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy", and the four are named in a descending order of closeness, from the parents to the relatives to those with no relation at all and then to those with no means, so the kindness is not limited to the people a person would be kind to anyway, and the last two named are the two with nothing to offer in return. The third, the fourth and the fifth run together in the verse without a break: "speak kindly to people; establish prayer; and pay alms-tax", and the order puts a duty of speech between the kindness owed to the four groups and the prayer and the alms owed to Allah, so the list moves from what is owed to Him to what is owed to people and back to what is owed to Him. The turning comes at once: "But you Israelites turned away", and the turning is from the covenant just listed, so the verse does not accuse them of ignorance of the terms but of leaving terms they had taken. "except for a few of you" limits the accusation, and the few are named inside the same sentence as the turning, so the exception is part of the charge and not a qualification added to it afterwards. "and were indifferent" is the last word of the verse and the lightest of its terms, and it describes a state rather than an act, an indifference that goes with the turning and accounts for how a covenant taken in words could be left without a struggle.

**Worship none but Allah.**

Worship none but Allah (alone) and be dutiful and good to parents, and to kindred, and to orphans and (the poor), and speak good to people and perform As-Salah and give Zakah. Allah reminded the Children of Israel of the commandments that He gave them, and the covenants that He took from them to abide by those commands, and how they intentionally and knowingly turned away from all of that. Allah commanded them to worship Him and to associate none with Him in worship, just as He has commanded all of His creatures, for this is why Allah created them. (And We did not send any Messenger before you (O Muhammad) but We revealed to him (saying): La ilaha illa Ana [none has the right to be worshipped but I (Allah)], so worship Me (alone and none else)(21:25), and,. (And when We made a covenant with the Children of Israel: Worship none save Allah) declare Him as the only true God and do not ascribe any partner to Him, (and be good to parents) be dutiful to them (and to kindred) and keep contact with relatives (and to orphans) and be kind to orphans (and the needy) and generous to the needy, (and speak kindly to mankind) say the Truth regarding Muhammad ﷺ; (and establish prayer) perfect the five daily prayers (and pay the poor-due) and give from your wealth what is due to the poor. Man’s first duty to God is to become His worshipper without ascribing any partners to Him. Remember the promise made between Allah and the Israelites: to worship Him alone; to be kind to parents, relatives, orphans and the poor; to say good words to people, telling them to do what is right and not what is wrong, without harshness or severity; to perform the prayer as instructed; and to give Zakat to those who have a right to it.

**Kind to parents, and the rights named with His.**

Allah usually mentions the rights of the parents along with His rights. (Give thanks to Me and to your parents. Unto Me is the final destination)(31:14). (And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him. And that you be dutiful to your parents)(17:23), until,. (And give to the kinsman his due and to the Miskin (poor) and to the wayfarer)(17:26). (Worship Allah and join none with Him (in worship); and do good to parents, kinsfolk, orphans, Al-Masakin (the poor), the neighbor who is near of kin, the neighbor who is a stranger, the companion by your side, the wayfarer (you meet), and those (servants) whom your right hands possess. Verily, Allah does not like such as are proud and boastful)(4:36). (and to orphans) meaning, the young who have no fathers to fend for them. (and Al-Masakin (the poor), plural for Miskin, the one who does not find what he needs to spend on himself and his family. Kindness starts at home, with one’s parents and family, extends to one’s neighbours and relatives, and finally reaches out to everyone with whom one comes into contact.

**The weaker members of society, and the deference the benefactor looks for.**

Where one is really tested is in one’s dealings with ‘orphans and the needy’, that is, with the weaker members of society. As for the strong, their strength itself guarantees that they will be given deferential treatment. But so far as the weak are concerned there is no such incentive to deal with them justly. People who are good to those who wield no worldly power and possess scant resources, do so for God’s sake alone, for they have no other incentive. There are various reasons for having little inclination to show kindness when dealing with the weak. Benefactors frequently regard themselves as ‘superior’ persons and, when they are not shown what they consider to be due deference, they tend to treat people less fortunate than themselves with disdain. When the benefactor is not shown what he considers to be due deference, he regards the beneficiary as unworthy and incompetent.

**Good words to people, then prayer and the alms-tax.**

(and speak good to people) meaning, say good words to them and be lenient with them, this includes commanding good and forbidding evil. (and speak good to people), "The good saying' means commanding good and forbidding evil, and being patient and forgiving. The 'good words to people', as Allah commanded, also includes every good type of behavior that Allah is pleased with. (Do not belittle any form of righteousness, and even if you did not find any good deed except meeting your brother with a smiling face, then do so.) Allah commands the servants to say good words to people, after He commanded them to be kind to them, thereby mentioning two categories of manners: good speech and good actions. He then emphasized the command to worship Him and the command to do good, ordaining the prayer and the Zakah,. (I said, 'O Messenger of Allah! What is the best deed?' He said, 'Performing the prayer on time.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'Being kind to one's parents.' I said, 'Then what?' He said, 'Jihad in the cause of Allah.') Of these orders, this Ummah has practiced what no other nation before it has, and all praise is due to Allah.

**A gentle tone, and the address to Pharaoh.**

This verse brings out the basic elements common to Islam and all the earlier Shari ah: Tauhid (the doctrine of Unity or Oneness); service to one's parents, relations, orphans and the needy; being gentle in speaking to all human beings; Salah and Zakah . The verse asks us to adopt a gentle tone and an open-hearted manner in speaking to others, whether they are good or evil, pious or impious, orthodox or aberrant, followers of Sunnah or adherents to partitive innovations in it. In religious matter, however, one should not try to hide the truth for the sake of pleasing people or of winning their approval. The Holy Qur'an tells us that when Allah sent Sayyidna Musa and Sayyidna Harun (Moses and Aaron) to the Pharaoh He instructed them to use gentle and soft words (20:42). None of us who addresses another today can be superior to Sayyidna Musa nor can the man addressed be viler than the Pharaoh . Talha ibn Umar recounts that once he said to the great master of the Sciences of Exegesis and Hadith, 'At-a' "One can see around you people who are not quite orthodox in their beliefs. If such people come to me, I deal with them harshly." Ata' replied, "Do not behave like this," and, reciting the present verse, he added, Allah has commanded us to speak to people politely. When Jews and Christians all are to be treated like this, would this commandment not apply to a Muslim, no matter what kind of a man he is?

**You turned away from the orders, and the few who did not.**

This verse speaks of the pledge which Allah had made the Israelites take, and the few people it refers to as having been true to the pledge were those who acted upon the Shari'ah of Sayyidna Musa (Moses) as long as it was in force, and when it was abrogated, followed the Shari ah of Sayyidna Muhammad . (Then, after that, ye slid back) you turned back on this covenant, (save a few of you) from amongst your forefathers; as it is said that this refers to 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and his companions, (being averse) denying and leaving it aside. But all they did after making this promise was to turn away, rejecting the promise they had made. Allah informed us that the People of the Book, except for a few among them, ignored these orders, that is, they knowingly and intentionally abandoned them.

84.text:
The verse is the second half of a covenant, and the half it gives is the one between the people themselves. "And remember when We took your covenant that you would neither shed each other's blood nor expel each other from their homes" is put as a remembrance, as the covenant of the last verse was, and it is taken from them and not merely given to them, so what follows is a thing they accepted. The two things forbidden are joined by neither and nor, and both are about what one of them does to another, so the covenant here is not between the people and Allah in the first place but between the people and each other, with Allah as the one taking it. The blood named is each other's blood and the homes are each other's homes, and the possessive in both cases does the work, since the prohibition is not on killing or on expulsion in general but on killing and expelling one's own, which is the form the two things actually took in the history the verse is read against. "you gave your pledge and bore witness" is the second half of the verse and it is about their own part in the taking, so the covenant is not something told to them but something they ratified, and the bearing of witness puts them in the position of witnesses against themselves, since a witness is one who can be asked what he saw.

**Shed not the blood of your people, nor turn them out of their dwellings.**

And when We made a covenant with you and We said ‘You shall not shed your own blood spilling it by slaying one another; neither expel your own from your habitations’ let no one of you expel the other from his house; then you confirmed it that is you accepted this covenant and you bore witness upon your own souls. " Allah mentioned the word 'your own' here, just as He said in another Ayah. (shed not the blood of your people) do not kill one another (nor turn your people) i.e. one another (out of your dwellings) from your homes, meaning: the Banu Qurayzah and Banu'l-Nadir. Remember the contract Allah made with you in the Torah: forbidding you from killing each other and forcing people to leave their homes. This verse is a supplement to the previous verse, and speaks of the other articles of the pledge taken by the Israelites. They had agreed not to kill one another by engaging themselves in an internecine war, and also not to send their men into exile - that is to say, not to harass a man so as to force him to migrate.

**You gave your pledge, and bore witness.**

Then, (this) you ratified and (to this) you bore witness After this, it is you who kill one another and drive out a party of you from their homes, assist (their enemies) against them, in sin and transgression. (Then, (this) you ratified and (to this) you bore witness.) means, "You testified that you know of the covenant and that you were witnesses to it." (Then ye ratified (Our covenant) you agreed to it (and ye were witnesses (thereto) while knowing what you were doing. You admitted the contract, and you witnessed its validity. Now, it may sometimes happen that one does not express one's willingness in so many words, but the manner of his speech suggests it. The agreement of the Israelites was not of this order, but as clear and explicit as the statement of a witness usually is.

**The tribes of Madinah, and the camps they divided into.**

Before the advent of Islam, three Jewish tribes inhabited the area around Madīnah: the Banu Nadir, the Banu Qurayzah, and the Banu Qaynuqa‘. Despite the fact that all of them adhered to Mosaic law, ignorant prejudices had divided them into two groups. They had become enmeshed, along with the polytheist tribes of Madīnah—al-Aws and the Khazraj—in political manoeuvering. The Banu Nadir and the Banu Qurayzah had aligned themselves with the Aws tribe, and the Banu Qaynuqa‘ with the Khazraj. Divided into two camps in this manner, the three Jewish tribes were constantly at war with one another. When war erupted between Aws and Khazraj, their Jewish allies would assist them. When fighting erupted between Aws and Khazraj, Banu Qaynuqa' would fight along with the Khazraj, while Banu An-Nadir and Qurayzah would fight along with the Aws. Each Jewish camp would fight against their Jewish brethren from the other camp.

**Fighting the brethren, and ransoming the prisoners.**

The Jew would kill his Arab enemy, and sometimes they also killed Jews who were the allies of the other Arab tribe, although the Jews were prohibited from killing each other according to clear religious texts in their Books. They would also drive each other from their homes and loot whatever furniture and money they could. When the war ended, the victorious Jews would release the prisoners from the defeated party, according to the rulings of the Tawrah. They would shed each other's blood, although they had the Tawrah with them, and they knew their rights and dues. When the war would end, the Jews would ransom their prisoners and implement the Tawrah. Consequently, Banu Qaynuqa' would ransom their prisoners who were captured by the Aws, while Banu An-Nadir and Qurayzah would ransom their prisoners who were captured by the Khazraj. During these wars, they would kill whomever (Jews or Arabs) they could, while helping the polytheists against their brethren. (So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves, that will be better for you with your Creator)(2:54) because the followers of one religion are just like one soul.

**The renunciation the law demands, and the pretence of piety.**

The basic teachings of Islamic law demand the total renunciation of pagan ways, the suppressing of one’s selfish desires and the controlling of one’s worldly needs— that is why the commands of Islamic law are ignored in politics. Obedience to them would bring about true piety, but people do not like to involve themselves in such arduous practices. They prefer to put on a pretence of piety by conducting certain superficial rituals. This is tantamount to issuing a self-made edition of divine religion; it is to disregard the Hereafter and attach importance to the worldly aspect of religion in the hope that zeal in performing actions which promise worldly fame and honour will qualify them for the reward reserved for true piety. But such brazen distortion of religion can only earn one God’s wrath; it does not merit any reward from God. (The example of the believers in their kindness, mercy and sympathy to each other is the example of one body, when an organ of it falls ill, the rest of the body rushes to its aid in fever and sleeplessness.) 85.text:
The verse turns the covenant of the last verse back on the people who took it, and it does it in the second person. "But here you are, killing each other and expelling some of your people from their homes, aiding one another in sin and aggression" is not a story about a people far off but an address to people present, and the here you are puts the two things side by side at once, the covenant and the conduct, with nothing between them. Three acts are named in the clause and they are graded: the killing, the expelling from homes, and the aiding of one another in the doing of it, and the third is the one that makes the first two a common matter rather than a series of crimes, since the aiding puts the acts in a society that cooperates in them. The sin and the aggression are named as two things, and the pair covers what is done against the law and what is done against the person, so the cooperation is in both at once. "and when those expelled come to you as captives, you still ransom them" turns to the second half of the conduct, and the turning is sharp, since the same people who expelled are the people who ransom, and the ransoming is put as something done still, that is, done in spite of the expelling. "though expelling them was unlawful for you" is the clause that keeps the two halves together, and it is put as a statement about the law rather than about the case, so the expulsion is unlawful whether or not the captive is afterwards ransomed, and the ransoming does not cancel it. "Do you believe in some of the Scripture and reject the rest?" is the question the two halves produce, and it is a question about belief and not about consistency, since the belief named is a belief in parts of a book, with some of it taken and some of it left. "Is there any reward for those who do so among you other than disgrace in this worldly life and being subjected to the harshest punishment on the Day of Judgment?" answers that question in the form of a question, and the reward named is not a reward but its opposite, one part of it in this world and the other on the Day of Judgment, so the two halves of the conduct are matched by two halves of the recompense. "For Allah is never unaware of what you do" closes the verse, and the closing is not a threat added to the rest but the ground of it, since a recompense measured out in two worlds has to be measured by one who sees both.

**Here you are, killing one another and expelling a party of you.**

Then there you are killing one another and expelling a party of you from their habitations conspiring tazzāharūna the original ta’ has been assimilated with the zā’; a variant reading has it without the assimilation that is tazāharūna assisting one another against them in sin in disobedience and enmity injustice and if they come to you as captives a variant reading for usārā has asrā you ransom them a variant reading for tafdūhum has tufādūhum that is to say you deliver them from captivity with money etc. and this ransoming was one of the things to which they were pledged; yet their expulsion was forbidden you muharramun ‘alaykum ikhrājuhum is semantically connected to wa-tukhrijūna ‘and expelling’ and the statement that comes in between is parenthetical that is expulsion was forbidden you in the same way that non-ransoming was forbidden you. Qurayza had allied themselves with the Aws and the Nadīr with the Khazraj but every member of an alliance would fight against a fellow ally thus destroying each other’s homes and expelling one another taking prisoners and then ransoming them. (Yet ye it is who slay each other and drive out a party of your people from their homes, supporting one another against them by sin) contravention (and transgression) offence-(and if they came to you as captives) captives who belong to your religion (ye would ransom them) free them by paying a ransom to the enemy (-whereas their expulsion was itself unlawful for you) whereas their expulsion and killing were unlawful in the first place. Then you broke the contract: some of you killing others, and forcing a group of them to leave their homes, assisted by their enemies, unjustly and with aggression. "Allah mentioned what they were doing, and that in the Tawrah He had prohibited them from shedding each other's blood, and required them to free their prisoners. There lived in Madīnah two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj who were hostile to each other, and would often go to war.

**And when they come to you as captives, you ransom them.**

When they were asked ‘Why do you fight them and then pay their ransom?’ they would reply ‘Because we have been commanded to ransom’; and they would be asked ‘So why do you fight them then?’ to which they would say ‘For fear that our allies be humiliated’; God exalted says What do you believe in part of the Book that is the part about ransom and disbelieve in part? namely the part about renouncing fighting expulsion and assistance against one another; What shall be the requital of those of you who do that but degradation disgrace and ignominy in the life of this world they were disgraced when Qurayza were slewn and the Nadīr were expelled to Syria and ordered to pay the jizya; and on the Day of Resurrection to be returned to the most terrible of chastisement? If they found a man from amongst them a prisoner of war, they should pay a ransom, and get him released. However, when some of the Jews became prisoners of war, each of the two Jewish groups would persuade their respective friends among the non-Jews to accept a ransom and to release the prisoners. When they were asked why they showed such a solicitude for the prisoners, they would say that it was obligatory for them to get prisoners released. But when someone objected to their helping the non-Jews in slaughtering the Jews, they used to reply that it would be a real disgrace if they did not go to the aid of their friends, even if they were not Jews. Then if prisoners came to you in the hands of enemies, you pay their ransom and rescue them from their captivity, even though making them leave their homes was forbidden to you. This Ayah means, 'Do you ransom them according to the rulings of the Tawrah, yet kill them while the Tawrah forbade you from killing them and from expelling them from their homes? You do all this to acquire the life of this world.' I was informed that the behavior of the Jews regarding the Aws and Khazraj was the reason behind revealing these Ayat."

**Believing part of the Scripture, and rejecting part.**

(Believe ye in part of the Scripture) the part that stipulates freeing your captives from the enemy (and disbelieve ye in part thereof?) and leave the captives of your friends without ransoming them. It is also said that this verse means: do you believe in those parts of the scripture that suit your whim and disbelieve in those parts that do not? What do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in partḍ And if they come to you as captives you ransom them that is Just as you protect their rights by ransoming them so must you restrain your hands from them and forswear expelling them from their homelands. When you uphold some of what has been made obligatory for you what keeps you from doing the rest of what you have been commanded to doḍ Do you not know that whoever picks and chooses in what he has been commanded so that he believes in some parts and disbelieves in others has the reward for his deeds nullified because of what he has neglectedḍ What shall be the requital of those of you who do that but degrada tion in the life of this world; and on the Day of Resurrection to be returned to the most terrible of chastisementḍ And God is not heedless of what you do. But instead of referring to this aspect of their infidelity, the verse points out another aspect. If we take the words of the present verse literally, it means that the Jews had become infidels by not having faith in some parts (that is to say, some injunctions) of the Torah. The Jews, may they suffer the curse of Allah, hid all of these facts among themselves, and this is why Allah said,.

**The disgrace in this world, and the One not heedless of what you do.**

Then what is the recompense of those who do so among you, except disgrace in the life of this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they shall be consigned to the most grievous torment. (Then what is the recompense of those who do so among you, except disgrace in the life of this world), because they defied Allah's Law and commandments,. (And what is the reward of those who do so save ignominy in the life of the world) by being killed or captured as slaves, (and on the Day of Resurrection they will be consigned to the most grievous doom. For Allah is not unaware) He is not reducing your punishment because (of what ye do) in terms of transgression; and it is also said: because of what they concealed. For those of you who do that, there is only humiliation in this life and the most severe torment in the Afterlife. The verse announces that the Jews will have to bear a punishment not only in the other world, but in this world too - in the shape of humiliation and disgrace. And God is not heedless of what you do ta‘malūna or read ya‘malūna ‘they do’. Allah knows what you do; in fact, He is fully aware, and He will hold you to account. The rescue of the captive drowning in the sea of whim hawā is to be directed to guidance. The ransom of the captive who remains in the hands of whisperings wasāwis is to show him the way to certainty by the glimmers of proofs.

**The direst punishment, and the degrees in it.**

One may very well ask here why the direst punishment should be reserved for the Jews, and not for atheists, for the Jews at least believe in Allah. So, what the verse implies is not that the punishment given to the Jews will be more severe than the one given to all the other infidels, but that they will be given the kind of punishment which is "the direst" in the sense of having no end or limit. In other words, the verse suggests that the punishment given to the infidels will be more severe than the one given to Muslim sinners. But if there are going to be different degrees in the punishment meted out to different kinds of infidels, it does not in any way go against the implications of this verse. That is they thought that what they did would benefit them but in the hereafter it will be disclosed to them that everything that they did when it was combined with what was damaging and stripped of sincerity and devotion was not accepted from them.

86.text:
The verse is a verdict on the conduct set out in the last verse, and it states the trade that conduct amounts to. "These are the ones who trade the Hereafter for the life of this world" names the two things traded and the direction of the trade, and the direction is what makes it a loss, since the thing given up is the one that does not end and the thing taken is the one that does. The word trade is the verse's own, and it puts the conduct of the last verse in the language of a market: the killing and the expelling and the ransoming were not acts of passion in this reading but transactions, each of them a taking of something now in exchange for something later, and the rate of exchange is what the verse is about. The ones named are the same ones addressed in the last verse, so the trade is not a general description of the world but an accounting of a particular conduct, and the accounting is put in the plural and in the present, which makes it a standing description of people who go on doing the thing. "So their punishment will not be reduced" follows from the trade, and the so makes the connection a consequence rather than an addition, since the price having been paid in full in this world leaves nothing to be deducted from what comes after it. The reduction named is a reduction of the punishment and not an end to it, so the verse is not putting the punishment in doubt but fixing its measure, and the fixing of it is the answer to a trade already completed. "nor will they be helped" is the second half of the consequence, and the help excluded is help from another, so the two negatives cover the two ways a punishment can be escaped, by its being lessened and by its being lifted by someone else, and both are closed. What the verse puts beside the last one is therefore not a new charge but a valuation, and the valuation is given in three clauses, the trade, the punishment not reduced, and the help not coming, so that the whole of the sentence is one reckoning of what the conduct was worth and what it will cost.

**The ones who have bought this world at the price of the Hereafter.**

Those are the ones who have purchased the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter by preferring the former to the latter — for them the punishment shall not be lightened neither shall they be helped neither shall they be protected against it. Those are the ones who have purchased the life of this world at the price of the hereafter-for them the punishment shall not be lightened neither shall they be helped. (Such are those who buy the life of the world at the price of the Hereafter) they choose this lower world instead of the Hereafter, and disbelief instead of belief: They are the people who exchange the Afterlife for this life, preferring what is temporary to what is eternal. And Allah is not unaware of what you do Those are they who have bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter. This verse explains why the Jews will have to undergo such a severe punishment.

**The punishment will not be reduced, and they will not be helped.**

Their sin being so great, Allah will not reduce or mollify their punishment, nor will He allow anyone to intercede on their behalf. (Their punishment will not be lightened) will not be reduced; as it is said: it will not be lifted, (neither will they have support) be precluded from Allah's chastisement. Their suffering will not be lightened, and they will have no one to help them. Their torment shall not be lightened nor shall they be helped. (Nor shall they be helped), and they shall find no helper who will save them from the eternal torment they will suffer, nor shall they find any to grant them refuge from it.

**Desires obeyed, the Tawrah defied at times, and anything preferred over God.**

They have been disobeying Allah in order to satisfy their desires and to enjoy worldly pleasures; they have also sacrificed for these things their salvation in the other world. These noble Ayat criticized the Jews for implementing the Tawrah sometimes and defying it at other times, although they believed in the Tawrah and knew what they were doing was wrong. This is why they should not be trusted to preserve or convey the Tawrah. Those who have preferred anything over [God] have lost in this world and the hereafter. People turned away from us without cause or sense. If they have no need of us we have even less need of them.

87.text:
The verse sets out what was given to a people and then asks them a question about what they did with it. "Indeed, We gave Moses the Book and sent after him successive messengers" names two gifts and puts them in order, the book first and the messengers after, and the after is not a single sending but a succession, so the gift is a continuing one, a line of messengers following the first of them rather than one messenger replacing him. The book given to Moses is the thing the messengers after him come with, and the succession is what keeps it in force, since a book given once and then left would need no succession, and a succession of messengers with no book behind them would have nothing to carry. "And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and supported him with the holy spirit" is the last name in the succession and the one given most, and the two things given him are of different kinds: the clear proofs are what he came with and could be seen, and the support with the holy spirit is what was with him in the coming of it, so the verse distinguishes the evidence of a messenger from the aid given to him. The naming of him by his mother is part of the description of the gift and not an addition to it, since the son of Mary is a messenger whose beginning was itself a sign. "Why is it that every time a messenger comes to you Israelites with something you do not like, you become arrogant, rejecting some and killing others" turns the verse from the giving to the receiving, and the question is put as a question about a habit rather than about an event, since every time makes the coming of the messenger a repeated thing and the answer to it a repeated thing as well. The not liking named here is of something in what the messenger comes with, so the ground of the rejection is not that the messenger lacked proofs but that what he brought was not to their liking, and the arrogance is the posture taken towards it. The two acts that follow are graded as they were graded in the verses before, rejecting some and killing others, and the grading is in the order, since the rejection is of the message and the killing is of the one who brought it, and the verse puts them together as the two ends of one habit. What the verse leaves unasked is which messengers were rejected and which were killed, and the naming is left to what comes with it, so the charge is put in a form that covers the whole of the succession rather than a part of it. The question is also put to the people addressed and not about a people long dead, since the messenger coming with something not liked is in the present, and the arrogance and the rejecting and the killing are answers to a coming that is still going on, which is what makes the question a question about the people being asked it.

**We gave Moses the Book, and sent after him successive messengers.**

And We gave Moses the scripture and after him We sent successive mes sengers and We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs and We confirmed him with the holy spirit and whenever there came to you a messenger with what your souls did not desire you became arrogant; and some you called liars and some you slayḍ The allusion is that We [God] delivered the address to them and made one messenger follow after another all calling to the same thing. First of all, He gave them a Divine Book, the Torah, through Sayyidna Musa (Moses); then, sent them a number of prophets; and, at the end of this line, sent down Sayyidna Isa (Jesus) along with clear and irrefutable evidences of his prophethood, like the Evangel and miracles, and appointed the Archangel Jibra'il (Gabriel) to give him support. The Qur'an again reminds the Israelites how Allah in His mercy forgave them their transgressions again and again, and provided them with all the means of guidance. Allah mentioned that He gave Musa the Book, the Tawrah, and that the Jews changed, distorted, and defied its commands, as well as altered its meanings. Allah sent Messengers and Prophets after Musa who followed his law, as Allah stated,. Allah gave Moses the Torah, and followed him with other messengers. After Moses, several prophets arose among the Jewish people—Joshua, David, Zachariah, John the Baptist and finally Jesus, to name but a few—all of whom pointed out to the Jews that it was not enough just to revere the Torah as a holy book. Gradually, however, they ceased to treat it as a source of divine guidance and came to regard it as a sacred relic of their national heritage, a symbol of ethnic superiority; it became more a guarantee of salvation than a guide as to how salvation could be earned. (And surely, We gave unto Moses the Scripture) the Torah (and We caused a train of messengers to follow after him) to come after him in succession, (and We gave unto Jesus son of Mary clear proofs) commands, prohibitions, wondrous things and signs, (and We supported him) strengthened and helped him (with the holy Spirit) with Gabriel, the purified.

**Jesus, son of Mary, and the clear signs given to him.**

He gave Jesus, the son of Mary, clear signs of the truth of what he came with, such as bringing the dead back to life and healing the blind and the lepers, and He strengthened him with the angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit ﷺ. Thereafter, Allah sent the last Prophet among the Children of Israel, 'Isa the son of Mary, who was sent with some laws that differed with some in the Tawrah. These included bringing the dead back to life, forming the shape of birds from clay and blowing into them, afterwhich they became living birds by Allah's leave, healing the sick and foretelling the Unseen, as Ibn 'Abbas stated. All of these signs testified to the truthfulness of 'Isa and what he was sent with. Yet, the Children of Israel became more defiant and envious of him and did not want to differ with even one part of the Tawrah, as Allah said about 'Isa,. (And to make lawful to you part of what was forbidden to you, and I have come to you with a proof from your Lord)(3:50).

**Supported with the holy spirit.**

The Archangel Jibra'il has often been called "Ruh al-Qudus" (the Holy Spirit) in the Noble Qur'an and the Hadith. For example, in Verse 16:102 - ‌ ‌ ‌ 102 - "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it (the Noble Qur'an) down;" or in a couplet of the poet and blessed Companion Hassan ibn Thabit reported in the Hadith: Allah helped and supported Sayyidna Isa through Jibra'il in several ways. He was conceived through the breath of the Archangel. Jibra'il protected him against being touched by Satan at the time of his birth. The Archangel always accompanied him in order to defend him against the hostility of the Jews. It was through him that Sayyidna Isa was raised to the heavens. Allah also aided him with Ruh Al-Qudus, and that refers to Jibril. The proof that Jibril is the Ruh Al-Qudus is the statement of Ibn Mas'ud in explanation of this Ayah.

**The trustworthy spirit, the heart it was brought down on, and Hassan aided.**

(Which the trustworthy Ruh (Jibril) has brought down. Upon your heart (O Muhammad) that you may be of the warners)(26:193-194). Al-Bukhari recorded 'A'ishah saying that the Messenger of Allah erected a Minbar in the Masjid on which Hassan bin Thabit (the renowned poet) used to defend the Messenger of Allah (with his poems). (O Allah! Aid Hassan with Ruh Al-Qudus, for he defended Your Prophet.) (Ruh Al-Qudus informed me that no soul shall die until it finishes its set provisions and term limit. Therefore, have Taqwa of Allah and seek your sustenance in the most suitable way.)

**Every time a messenger comes with what you do not like.**

(Is it ever so, that, when there cometh unto you) O group of Jews (a messenger with that which ye yourselves desire not) which does not agree with your hearts and religion, (ye grow arrogant) you disdain believing in him. Is it that whenever there came to you a Messenger with what you yourselves desired not, you grew arrogant? (Is it that whenever there came to you a Messenger with what you yourselves desired not,you grew arrogant? Some you disbelieved and some you kill). Yet is it, O Israelites, that whenever a messenger comes to you from Allah with what does not agree with your whims, you become full of pride towards the truth, looking down on the messengers of Allah? They were characterized by this self-serving desire and moreover became servants ʿabadū to it. The [human] attributes of the worshiper ʿābid became the object of worship maʿbūd. All of this occurred because the Prophets used to command the Jews with what differed from their desires and opinions. The reason for such a reaction on their part was that they had allowed self-interest and worldly ambitions to rule their lives, while passing themselves off as bearers and upholders of the true faith. As long as religion served to consolidate their worldly status, they welcomed it, but were loath to accept the message of truth—presented to them in all its purity—which they saw as a threat to the hegemony they had secured for themselves on the basis of religion. It was their egoism which came in the way of true religiosity. It is futile to believe in the sacredness of the holy scriptures if one does not implement their message in one’s everyday life.

**Rejecting some, and killing others.**

Hence, the Children of Israel treated the Prophets in the worst manner, rejecting some of them and killing some of them. Therefore, they rejected the Prophets and killed some of them. (Some you disbelieved and some you kill), "Allah did not say 'killed' here, because the Jews would still try to kill the Prophet in the future, using poison and magic. (I kept feeling the effect of what I ate (from the poisoned sheep) during the day of Khaybar, until now, when it is the time that the aorta will be cut off (meaning when death is near).) (And some ye disbelieve) you disbelieve in a group of them, namely Muhammad and Jesus, Allah bless them and give them peace (and some ye slay?) and some you killed, namely, John the Baptist and Zachariah. Do you reject a group of them and kill a group of them? Instead of being the first to believe in it, they rejected the message as well as the messenger, subjecting God’s prophets to scorn and victimisation. They called them impostors and even went to the extent of killing them. But the Jews, the very people who held the Torah in such high esteem, were extremely intolerant of the Prophet’s exhortations. In. spite of all these divine favours, the Jews persisted in their rebellion.
