They were so stubborn in the worship of their desires, that whenever the prophets brought to them certain divine injunctions which did not please them, the Jews would deny the prophets – they denied even Sayyidna Isa or would kill them outright -- for example, they dealt in this vile manner with Sayyidna Zakariyya (Zachariah) and Sayyidna Yahya (John the Baptist).

88.text:
The verse gives a people's own words and then takes them back, and it does both in one breath: "They say, Our hearts are unreceptive! In fact, Allah has condemned them for their disbelief". The first half is put as their speech and not as a description of them, and the thing they say about themselves is a state of their hearts, so the claim is not that they have not understood but that they cannot, and the cannot is offered as an excuse lying outside their own control. The word translated as unreceptive is a word for a thing wrapped or covered, and the covering is put on their side of the exchange, which makes the failure to receive a property of the receiver rather than of what was sent. The in fact that follows is not a contradiction of the first clause but a re-reading of it, since the covering they describe as their condition is named as a thing done to them, and done for a reason, and the reason given is their disbelief, so the state they appeal to is itself the consequence of the thing they are charged with: the heart is closed, and the closing has a cause that is theirs. "They have but little faith" is the last clause and the smallest of the three, and it measures what is left after the condemnation, a little rather than nothing, which leaves the verse with a quantity to account for and not only with a refusal. The three clauses therefore run from an excuse to its cause to its remainder, and what follows takes up the word for the covered heart, the readings of the curse, and what the little faith was a faith in.

**Our hearts are unreceptive, and what they meant by it.**

And they say to the Prophet mockingly ‘Our hearts are encased’ ghulf is the plural of aghlaf that is to say wrapped up in covers and cannot comprehend what you say; God exalted be He says Nay bal introduces the rebuttal but God has cursed them removed them far from His mercy and degraded them when they rejected the messengers for their unbelief which is not the result of anything defective in their hearts; and little will they believe fa-qalīlan mā yu’minūn the mā here is extra emphasising the ‘littleness’ involved that is their belief is minimal. The Jews used to say sarcastically that their hearts were "veiled", by which they meant that their hearts were so well protected against Islam that it could never touch them. This was their way of congratulating themselves on being staunch in their belief. (And they say, "Our hearts are Ghulf."), means, "Our hearts are screened. (And they say, "Our hearts are Ghulf."), means, "They are covered. " Mujahid and Qatadah said that Ibn 'Abbas read the Ayah in a way that means, "Our hearts contain every type of knowledge and do not need the knowledge that you (O Muhammad) have. The Israelites argued that their stubbornness was because their hearts were wrapped in a cover, so that none of what was said to them could reach them, or make sense to them. (And of their saying: "Our hearts are wrapped (with coverings, i.e. we do not understand what the Messengers say) nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief, so they believe not but a little.)

**Allah has cursed them for their disbelief.**

(Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief) meaning, "Allah expelled them and deprived them of every type of righteousness. (Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is that which they believe.) meaning, "It is not as they claim. Rather, their hearts are cursed and stamped," just as Allah said in Surat An-Nisa' (4:155),. this is a reply to them, (but Allah hath cursed them) sealed their hearts (for their disbelief) as a punishment for their disbelief. Nay but God has cursed them for their unbelief; and little will they believe.

**They have but little faith, and what the little was.**

The Holy Qur'an points out that this is not the firmness of faith, but a damnation, for they deny Islam which now is the true religion, and stick to a religion which has been abrogated. They, consequently, possess only "a little" faith ('Iman). Since a little faith is not acceptable, they turn out to be infidels. The little “ faith" which they possessed pertained to the doctrines which are common to Islam and Judaism - for example, belief in Allah, or belief in the Day of Judgment. But they did not accept Sayyidna Muhammad as a prophet, and the Holy Qur'an as the Word of Allah. (So little is that which they believe.) means, "Only a few of them believe. Some scholars said that the Ayat indicate that a few of them would believe, or that their faith is minute, because they believe in Resurrection and in Allah's reward and punishment that Musa foretold. Yet, this faith will not benefit them since it is overshadowed by their disbelief in what Muhammad brought them. (So little is that which they believe), meaning, they do not believe. (Little is that which they believe) they believe neither much nor a little; it is also said that this means: they do not believe in what you say at all.

**The faith that is not faith, and the pretension under it.**

If the Verse describes 'the little faith' as 'Iman it does so only in the lexical sense, for 'Iman signifies total certitude, even if it pertains to certain things, and not to others. But from the point of view of the Shari'ah, such a partial faith cannot be described as 'Iman . The Shari ah would accept as valid only that 'Iman which affirms with certitude each and everything that the Shari ah requires one to affirm. Some scholars said that the Jews did not actually believe in anything and that Allah said,. This meaning is similar to the Arabic expression, "Hardly have I seen anything like this," meaning, "I have never seen anything like this." If there had been anything in them free of pretension it would have become easy to find meanings [from God's signs and scripture]. But when [they must] recognize the truth the fangs of pretenders are bared... When tears flow down cheeks The one who is crying is distinguished from the one who is only pretending.

89.text:
The verse sets a prayer and its answer against each other, and the answer is not the one that was prayed for. "Although they used to pray for victory by means of the Prophet over the polytheists" is the first half, and it is put as a habit rather than an event, a praying they used to do, so the prayer was a standing practice and not a single appeal made in a single need. The victory asked for is over the polytheists, and the means of it is named in the verse as the Prophet, so the prayer already carries a recognition in it, since a means named in a prayer is a means whose coming is expected and whose truth is not in question. "when there came to them a Book from Allah which they recognized" is the second half, and the coming is of a book and not of a victory, which is the first of the two things the verse sets side by side: what was prayed for was a triumph, and what came was a text. The recognition named here is a recognition of the book, so the verse does not put the coming of it as a surprise to them, and the recognition is what makes what follows a rejection rather than an ignorance. "confirming the Scripture they had in their hands" is the clause that ties the two books together, and the confirming is of a Scripture they already had and still had, in their hands, so the book that came did not replace what was in their possession but bore witness to it, and the recognition of the second book is therefore a recognition that passes through the first. "they rejected it" is the shortest clause in the verse and the one everything turns on, and it is put without a reason, so the reason is what the rest of the verse and what comes under it supply. "So may Allah's condemnation be upon the disbelievers" closes the verse with a supplication of its own, and the supplication is the reverse of the one that opened it, since the prayer for victory was a prayer for a thing to be given to them and this is a word against them, and the people it is against are named not by their book or their race but by the rejection just described. The verse therefore runs from a prayer to a book to a rejection to a curse, and each of the four is given in a single clause, so the shape of the sentence is the shape of the case: what was asked for, what was sent, what was done with it, and what follows from that. The disbelievers named at the end are the same people who prayed at the beginning, and the distance between the two is the whole of the verse.

**They used to pray for victory over the polytheists.**

(although aforetime they had invoked Allah (for coming of Muhammad) in order to gain victory over those who disbelieved) meaning, before this Messenger came to them, they used to ask Allah to aid them by his arrival, against their polytheistic enemies in war. They used to say to the polytheists, "A Prophet shall be sent just before the end of this world and we, along with him, shall exterminate you, just as the nations of 'Ad and Iram were exterminated. Before it was revealed, they used to say that they would be helped against the idolaters, who worship others alongside Allah, and would have success over them when a prophet was sent, since they would have faith in him and follow him. The Jews of Khaybar were at war with Ghatafan, and whenever the two parties used to meet, Khaybar ended up in defeat. We beseech You by the truth of the unlettered Prophet whom You promised to send forth to us at the end of time to give us victory over them'. And so whenever they said this supplication, Ghatafan was defeated. It is due to this that Allah, exalted is He, revealed ( though before that they were asking for a signal triumph over those who disbelieved) i.e. by means of you, O Muhammad, up to His saying (The curse of Allah is on disbelievers) . The Jews knew the description of Muhammad in the Torah and used to ask Allah to send him so that they could fight with him against the Arabs. \ When there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them-and they formerly prayed for victory over the disbelievers; but when there came to them what they recognized they disbelieved in it; and the curse of God is on the disbelievers. The Jews were awaiting the Prophet's coming, but They disbelieved in Him when He was sent.

**A Book from Allah came to them, confirming what was with them.**

When there came to them a Book from God confirming what was with them in the Torah that is the Qur’ān — and they formerly before it came prayed for victory for assistance over the disbelievers saying ‘God give us assistance against them through the Prophet that shall be sent at the end of time’; but when there came to them what they recognised as the truth that is the mission of the Prophet they disbelieved in it out of envy and for fear of losing leadership the response to the first lammā particle is indicated by the response to the second one; and the curse of God is on the disbelievers. (And when there cometh unto them a Scripture from Allah, confirming that in their possession) which accords with that which is in their possession (though before that) before Muhammad ﷺ (they were asking for a signal triumph) through Muhammad and the Qur'an (over those who disbelieved) of their enemies: the tribes of Asad, Ghatafan, Muzaynah, and Juhaynah (and when there cometh unto them that which they knew) of his traits and description in their Book (they disbelieved therein) they denied it was him. (confirming what is with them) meaning, the Tawrah. (a Book from Allah) meaning, the Qur'an that Allah sent down to Muhammad,. The verse says that the Holy Qur'an confirms the Torah it means that the Holy Qur'an is a concrete evidence of the truth of the prophecies made in the Torah with regard to the coming of the Holy Prophet and of the Holy Qur'an. The Torah had in several places foretold the coming of the Holy Prophet . In fact, the Jews themselves used to tell the Arabs that a new prophet and a new Divine Book was soon to come. The Qur’ān came to them from Allah, agreeing with the universal true principles of the Torah and the Gospel. They had seen prophecies of the coming of a final prophet in their scriptures, and had eagerly anticipated his arrival.

**The truth they recognized, and what followed from recognizing it.**

But when the Holy Qur'an came down from Allah, and even when they had recognized its authenticity, the Jews denied it out of sheer spite. One may want to know why the Holy Qur'an calls the Jews Kafirin (infidels), when they did recognize the truth as truth, which should qualify them to be called "believers. " Let us explain that 'Iman (faith) does not merely mean "knowing the truth", but really signifies "accepting the truth and affirming it deed-wise. " Otherwise, Satan too will have to be called a believer, for he knows fully well what the truth is. In fact, this knowledge of the truth on the part of Satan intensifies the gravity of his Kufr (infidelity) all the more. But when the Qur’ān and Muhammad ﷺ came to them, according to the description they recognised and the truth they knew, they disbelieved him. They could not dispute the authentic indications presented by the Quran in support of his prophethood; all they could say was, ‘It all sounds very impressive, but our ancestral religion is good enough for us. Our hearts are sealed and we will not accept anything besides the faith we have inherited from our forefathers.’

**Malice, envy, and the race of the prophet.**

However, the next verse attributes the infidelity of the Jews to their malice. When Muhammad, Allah bless him and give him peace, came to them, they disbelieved in him out of resentful envy. They said: 'all the messengers were from the descendents of Jacob, how is it that this one is a descendent of Ishmael?'. But when the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, was sent forth, they disbelieved in him. They were shown to be steeped in bigotry, reluctant to believe in a prophet who did not come from the Jewish race. But these proved to be empty words on their part, a pretence aimed at consolidating their status as undisputed guardians of divine faith. When he comes, they used to say, we will join with him in a grand alliance against the pagans and idolators. The Jews of Arabia behaved similarly with the Prophet Muhammad.

**Combat, the matter resolved, and the curse on the disbelievers.**

He raises the banners of his vigor to step out to combat but when the call comes to line up and advance boldly into battle he breaks down at the rallying of the ranks and cuts himself off from the group afraid of dangerous attacks. God most high said Then when the matter has been resolved upon if they are loyal to God it will be better for them [47:21]. (The curse of Allah) His wrath and torment (is on disbelievers) the Jews. Allah curses those who disbelieve Him and His Prophet. Hence, Mu'adh bin Jabal and Bishr bin Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur, from Bani Salamah, said to them, 'O Jews!

90.text:
The verse puts a value on what a people did and then gives the bill for it, and it does the two in one breath: "Miserable is the price they have sold their souls for—denying Allah's revelation and resenting Allah for granting His grace to whoever He wills of His servants!" The word used for the price is one of wretchedness rather than of size, so the verse is not measuring the price but calling it bad, and the thing sold is named as the soul, which makes the transaction one in which the seller is himself the goods. The two things the price was paid for are of different kinds: the first is an act towards a book, a denial of what Allah revealed, and the second is a feeling towards a giver, a resentment that the giving was His to make. The second half is the heavier of the two, since the denial of a revelation can be a mistake about the revelation, while resentment at a grace given to whom Allah wills is a quarrel with the one who gives it, and the verse puts the quarrel in terms of the will: whoever He wills of His servants, which leaves no room for a claim on the grace by anyone. "They have earned wrath upon wrath" is the earning that answers the selling, and the doubling in it is not an intensifying of one wrath but two of them, so the verse accounts for the two halves of the price with two halves of the wrath. "And such disbelievers will suffer a humiliating punishment" closes the verse with the form the punishment takes, and the humiliation named in it answers the resentment, since what was resented was a grace given to another and what comes back is a punishment that puts the one who resented it down. The price is named first because the verse is about a value, and the value is what the rest of it goes on to settle.

**The price, and the selling of the soul.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the transaction its plain shape: how bad is that for which they have sold their own selves, that they should disbelieve in that which Allah has revealed. He then reads the selling as a selling of one thing for another, that the Jews sold the truth for falsehood and hid the truth, and in a second place he draws out the reflexive form of the verse, that they sold themselves, so what is worst is what they did to themselves rather than what they got by it. Tanwīr al-Miqbās keeps the same construction and names the thing disbelieved in as the Book, and al-Qushayrī keeps it too, with the grudging that follows. Al-Mukhtaṣar states what was given up in the exchange: how miserable is what they accepted in exchange for their portion of faith in Allah and His messengers, so the price is not a thing bought but a portion of faith handed over, and the wretchedness of it is in the rate. The soul in the verse is therefore not a figure for a life or a self in the abstract, since the readings agree that what changed hands was a standing in relation to Allah, and what was taken in return was a position kept in this world. What the verse leaves out is the buyer, and the readings supply one only in the general form of a standing lost, so the sale is described from the side of the seller alone, and the wretchedness of the price is stated rather than compared, since nothing is named that was got in return for it.

**Resenting the grace given to whom Allah wills.**

Maʿārif al-Qurʾān puts the second half of the price as a question about the giving itself. Prophethood cannot be earned by one's own efforts or by one's own merit; it is a special grace which Allah bestows on whomsoever He wills, and the Jews were so envious and malicious that they denied the Prophet and the Qurʾān out of sheer spite, so in denying him they were questioning the will of Allah Himself. That is the shape of the resentment the verse names: not a disagreement about a book but an objection to a choice. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same reading with the reason attached, that they disbelieved what Allah revealed and rejected His prophets unjustly and enviously, because He gave prophethood and the Qurʾān to one who was not of them. Ibn Kathīr renders the clause as a grudging that Allah should reveal of His grace unto whom He wills of His servants, which keeps the will where the verse keeps it. Al-Qushayrī gives the consequence of the grudging in two images: envy caused them to descend from the abode of nobility to the lowland of ignominy, and when they were not satisfied with what the decree brought they were reduced to a state of abasement, so the resentment does not leave the resenting person where he was, and the descent is the price working itself out.

**Wrath upon wrath, and the two ways it was earned.**

The doubling of the wrath is read as an accounting rather than as an emphasis. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān sets out the two ways it was earned: firstly for denying a true prophet, and secondly for the envy and malice behind the denial, so each half of the price carries a wrath of its own. Ibn Kathīr gives the same doubling the form of an acquisition, that they drew on themselves wrath, and that they deserved and acquired multiplied anger, which puts the earning in the verse's own language of a thing gained. Beside that he carries two readings of what the two angers were anger at: Ibn ʿAbbās took it as anger because they ignored some of the Tawrah and disbelieved in what followed, and Abū al-ʿĀliyah took it as anger for their disbelief in the Injīl and in ʿĪsā and then anger for their disbelief in Muḥammad and the Qurʾān, so on the second reading the two wraths belong to two revelations rather than to two faults in one refusal. Tanwīr al-Miqbās renders it as anger upon anger and as curse upon curse, and al-Qushayrī puts the earning as an inviting, that they invited upon themselves that which brings wrath upon wrath, which returns the act to the people doing it. Al-Mukhtaṣar names both of the deeds the anger answers, disbelieving in Muḥammad and distorting the Tawrah beforehand, so the wrath is not a response to a single refusal but to a refusal with a history in it.

**A humiliating punishment, and the disgrace in it.**

The last clause of the verse is read as an addition to pain and not as a description of it. Maʿārif al-Qurʾān takes the punishment named here as one involving not only pain but disgrace, and draws out why the humiliation is added: the condition is peculiar to the infidels and is not meant for a believer punished for his sins, so the disgrace marks a difference of kind between two punishments and not a difference of degree. Ibn Kathīr ties the humiliation to what produced it, that since their disbelief came of transgression and envy, and the envy came of arrogance, they were punished with disgrace, which makes the form of the punishment answer the form of the fault. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the shameful doom as one through which they are humiliated, and carries a second reading of it as a severe punishment, so the clause is taken both for its shame and for its weight. Al-Mukhtaṣar fixes the time and the occasion of it, a humiliating torment on the Day of Judgement for those who disbelieved in the prophethood of Muḥammad, which is the same occasion the last verse's reckoning was kept for. The two readings of the clause are not in competition, since a punishment can be both severe and shameful, and the severity is what makes the shame a punishment rather than a slight: the humiliation is public, it is measured, and it comes at a gathering where the ones the grace was given to are present, which is what the clause adds to the reckoning kept in the verse before it.

**Scorning the worship, and the arrogant gathered small.**

Ibn Kathīr closes the passage with the arrogance the humiliation answers, and he brings the verse on those who scorn His worship, who do not call on Him and do not believe in His oneness, and who will enter Hell humiliated, so the scorning is put in the same terms as the resentment of the verse before it, a refusal of what Allah has made His to give. He then carries the report of how the arrogant are gathered on the Day of Resurrection, in the size of ants but in the shape of men, with everything pressing on them, and the image is the reverse of the position the resentment was defending, since what was resented was a grace given to another and what the gathering gives back is a smallness that cannot be argued with. The humiliation named at the end of the verse is therefore not an extra attached to a punishment already complete but the punishment taking the shape of the fault: a people who objected to being passed over are made small in the presence of the ones they objected to being passed over for.

91.text:
The verse gives a request, an answer, a denial and a question, and the four are put in that order. "When it is said to them" is the setting, and the saying is to them rather than about them, so what follows is a reply given to a request made in their presence. The request and the answer to it run together in the verse: "Believe in what Allah has revealed, they reply, We only believe in what was sent down to us". The thing to be believed in is named in the request by its source and not by its title, a thing Allah has revealed, which leaves the identity of the book to be recognised rather than granted; and the only in the answer is the whole of the refusal, since the belief is not denied but limited, and the limit is drawn not by a book but by a people, what was sent down to us. The reply therefore makes the address of a revelation the test of its acceptance, and a revelation sent to another is on that test not a revelation to be believed in. "and they deny what came afterwards" states the consequence of the limit, and the denial is of what came after, so the sequence is the ground of the refusal, and the thing denied is not a rival book but a later one. The rest of the verse runs in one breath, from the answer to the denial to the question put back to them: "though it is the truth confirming their own Scriptures! Ask them, O Prophet, Why then did you kill Allah's prophets before, if you are truly believers?" The clause against the denial is made of two claims: the book that came afterwards is the truth, and it confirms the Scriptures they already have, so the later book does not compete with the earlier one but bears witness to it, which leaves the limit in the reply without a ground, since a book confirming what was sent down to them is on their own test a book to believe in. The asking that follows is commanded and not left to the argument, so the question carries the weight of an instruction, and it takes the reply at its word: if the belief is in what was sent down to them, then the prophets sent to them are the test of it, and the killing of them is the answer their own history gives. The then in the question ties it to the reply, and the if you are truly believers makes the killing a contradiction of the claim rather than a separate crime, so the verse does not add a charge to the refusal but shows the refusal in the light of what the people making it had already done to the ones who brought what they say they believe in.

**When it is said to them: believe in what Allah has revealed.**

And when it was said to them ‘Believe in what God has revealed that is the Qur’ān and other Books they said ‘We believe in what was revealed to us’ that is the Torah; and wā here indicates a circumstantial qualifier they disbelieve in what is beyond that what is other than that or what came afterwards such as the Qur’ān; yet it is the truth wa-huwa’l-haqqu is a circumstantial qualifier confirming musaddiqan a second circumstantial qualifier for emphasis what is with them. When this group of Jews was told to have faith in the truth and guidance that Allah revealed to His Prophet, they said that they believed in what had been revealed to their prophets, and denied anything besides this, and in what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, although the Qur’ān is the truth, confirming what Allah had already revealed to them. (And when it is said to them), meaning, the Jews and the People of the Book,.

**We only believe in what was sent down to us.**

(They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us.") meaning, it is enough for us to believe in what was revealed to us in the Tawrah and the Injil, and this is the path that we choose,. (Believe in that which Allah hath revealed) meaning: the Qur'an, (they say: We believe in that which was revealed unto us) i.e. the Torah. The Jews flatly refused to believe in any Book of Allah -- like the Evangel or the Holy Qur'an - except in the Torah. Moreover, they also used to add that they believe in the Torah, for it had been sent down to them. This comes to mean that they denied the other Books just because they had not been sent down to them. Although The Jews denied the Truth, They claimed to be Believers!

**The truth confirming what is with them.**

(And they disbelieve in that which cometh after it) other than the Torah, (though it is the Truth) i.e. the Qur'an is the Truth (confirming) affirming the Oneness of Allah (that which they possess) of the Book. (while it is the truth confirming what is with them) meaning, while knowing that what was revealed to Muhammad ,. This means that since what was sent to Muhammad conforms to what was revealed to the People of the Book, then this fact constitutes a proof against them. (Those to whom We gave the Scripture (Jews and Christians) recognize him (Muhammad) as they recognize their sons)(2:146). " And they disbelieve in that which came after it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. When the truth and authenticity of the other Books has been established on the basis of irrefutable arguments, what does, then, this denial mean? If they had any doubts as to the arguments on the basis of which authenticity was being claimed for these Books, they could very well have voiced this doubt, and satisfied themselves on this point.

**Why then were you slaying the prophets of Allah.**

Say to them ‘Why then were you slaying the prophets of God formerly if you were believers?’ in the Torah and in it you were forbidden to kill them this address concerning what their forefathers did is directed towards those present at the time of our Prophet on account of their approval of it that is of what the forefathers had done. Why then were you slaying the prophets of God formerly if you were believersḍ Here the allusion is that when it is said to them Recognize the truth of what has been shown to you from the decree of [divine] harmony min ḥukm al-wifāq by recognizing the situation and the establishment of proof their lower selves permit some of what they find ambiguous insofar as it agrees with their self-serving desires but then they disbelieve in what is beyond their worldly concerns. This means, "If your claim that you believe in what was revealed to you is true, then why did you kill the Prophets who came to you affirming the Tawrah's Law, although you knew they were true Prophets? You killed them simply out of transgression, stubbornness and injustice with Allah's Messengers. "Why then have you killed the Prophets of Allah aforetime, if you indeed have been believers? (Why then slew ye the Prophets of Allah before, if ye are (indeed) believers?) if your claims are truthful. (Say (O Muhammad to them): "Why then have you killed the Prophets of Allah aforetime, if you indeed have been believers?")."

**Killers taken as chiefs, and the truth mistaken for a group.**

To slay a prophet is tantamount to infidelity (Kufr), according to all the Divine Books. Moreover, the prophets whom the Jews had killed were themselves Israelites, and their teachings, were based on the injunctions of the Torah. But the Jews not only killed these prophets, but also accepted the killers as their chiefs. This is a direct denial of the Torah, and falsifies their claim that they believe in the Torah. Therefore, you only follow your lusts, opinions and desires. They are distant from the elite and are not considered to be among the masters who have special claim arbāb al-ikhtiṣāṣ. Also, As-Suddi said, "In this Ayah, Allah chastised the People of the Book,. (Is it that whenever there came to you a Messenger with what you yourselves desired not, you grew arrogant? Some you disbelieved and some you killed.) The Jews were not ready to accept the Quran, because they thought they were already rightly guided. They were sure that the very fact that they belonged to the largest group of the followers of truth, that is, the Israelites, that would be enough to earn them salvation. But, in fact, this was a feeling of ethnic superiority which they mistook for love of truth. The communal values of their group came to occupy the position of pure truth. That was why, when the truth appeared in its original form, they failed to accept it. Had their aim been to find pure truth, they would not have found it difficult, since predictions about it had appeared in their own sacred book, (the Torah) to the effect that now it was the Quran that was the Book of Truth to be followed and not the religion of their own group. In short, nothing that the Jews say or do is acceptable and valid from any possible point of view.

92.text:
The verse is short and it is made of two clauses set against each other. "Indeed, Moses came to you with clear proofs" is the first, and the coming is named with its evidence, so the proofs are not something attached to the messenger afterwards but the form in which he came, and the clearness of them is what the verse insists on, since a proof that has to be worked for is not the kind of proof named here. "then you worshipped the calf in his absence, acting wrongfully" is the second, and the then does the work of the verse, putting the worship at a distance from the coming that is measured in time and not in argument: the proofs had been given, and the calf was worshipped after them and not in place of them being absent. The absence named is the absence of Moses, so the worship happened in a gap rather than in a disagreement, and the wrongful acting at the end of the verse is the qualification that takes the gap away as an excuse, since what was done is named as a wrongdoing and not as a mistake made while waiting. The two clauses are put to people who were not at the mountain and not in the gap, and the you in both of them is the same you, so the verse is making one case out of a people and its past. The calf is named without a description, and the describing of it is left to what comes with the verse, which takes up what the proofs were, what the worship of the calf amounted to, and why the sin of it is counted against people who were not at it.

**Moses came to you with clear proofs.**

And Moses came to you with clear proofs miracles such as the staff his hand and the parting of the sea; then you took to yourselves the calf as a god after him after he had gone to the appointment and you were evildoers for taking it in worship. The "clear signs" mentioned in the verse refers to the miracles which- had manifested themselves even before the Torah was given to Sayyidna Musa (Moses) -- for example, his staff that turned into a .snake, the palm of his hand which shone brightly, the splitting of the sea to make a path for the Israelites, etc. These miracles were meant to affirm the Oneness of Allah and His omnipotence, and to provide an evidence for the prophethood of Sayyidna Musa. (And Moses came unto you with clear proofs) with commands, prohibitions and signs (yet while he was away ye chose the calf) you worshipped the calf (and ye were wrong-doers) unbelievers. And also, your prophet Moses ﷺ, brought clear signs to you, proving that what he said was true. (And indeed Musa came to you with clear proofs) meaning, with clear signs and clear proofs that he was the Messenger of Allah and that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. The clear signs - or miracles - mentioned here are the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the staff and the hand. Musa's miracles also include parting the sea, shading the Jews with clouds, the manna and quails, the gushing stone, etc.

**You worshipped the calf in his absence, and were wrongdoers.**

But after that you made the calf into a god and worshipped it, when Moses had gone to meet his Lord. You were wrongdoers for worshipping others alongside Allah, since only He is worthy of worship. (yet you worshipped the calf) meaning, as a deity instead of Allah, during the time of Musa. (after he left) after Musa went to Mount Tur to speak to Allah. (And the people of Musa made in his absence, out of their ornaments, the image of a calf (for worship). It had a sound (as if it was mooing)(7:148). (and you were Zalimun) meaning, you were unjust in this behavior of worshipping the calf, although you knew that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. (And when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they (repented and) said: "If our Lord have not mercy upon us and forgive us, we shall certainly be of the losers")(7:149). But you were not inclined to worship anything except what was attractive to you-the calf you adopted for yourselves and the idol you desired. [The calf] was taken from them but its traces remained in their hearts and in the hearts of those who came after them. Although the Jews who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet did not themselves take part in the worship of the golden calf, yet they respected such of their forefathers as had done so, and took their side. So, for all practical purposes, they too were guilty of the same sin.

**The unity called for, the worship chosen instead, and the claim to faith.**

That is he called you to declare [God's] unity tawḥīd and separate the [proper] object of worship from any other object of worship maʿbūd and limited thing maḥdūd. Because of that most Jews believe in anthropomorphism tashbīh. In refutation of the Jews, the verse points out that although they lay a claim to 'Iman (faith), yet have been falling into the sin of Shirk (association), which involves a denial not only of Sayyidna Musa but even of Allah Himself. The verse also suggests that no wonder if these people, whose forefathers denied Sayyidna Musa should now be denying the Holy Prophet .

93.text:
The verse is made of a scene, a reply, a diagnosis and a question, and the four run into one another without a break. The whole of it is this: "And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you saying, Hold firmly to that Scripture which We have given you and obey, they answered, We hear and disobey. The love of the calf was rooted in their hearts because of their disbelief. Say, O Prophet, How evil is what your so-called belief prompts you to do, if you actually believe in the Torah!" The scene is a covenant taken and a mountain raised, and the two are put in one clause, so the raising of the mountain belongs to the taking of the covenant and is not a separate event added to it; the covenant is taken under a thing held over the people taking it, and the command that comes with it is to hold firmly and to obey, which is a command about a book already given rather than about a book to come. The reply is the shortest thing in the verse and the most complete: we hear and disobey, which accepts the hearing and refuses the obedience in the same breath, so the refusal is not of the address but of what the address asks for. The diagnosis that follows gives the reason the reply took that shape, and the reason is not in the argument but in the heart, a love rooted there, and the love is of the calf, so the thing that answers the command is named as an affection and not as an opinion. The because of their disbelief puts a cause under the affection, and the cause is the disbelief rather than the reverse, which is what makes the diagnosis a diagnosis and not an excuse. The question at the end is put to the same people in the second person, and it takes their belief as the thing that prompts the doing, so the evil named is not beside their belief but produced by it, and the if you actually believe leaves the belief itself in question, since a belief that prompts this is on the verse's own terms not the belief it claims to be.

**We took your covenant, and raised the mountain above you.**

And when We made a covenant with you to act according to what is in the Torah and raised over you the Mount to drop it on you when you had refused to accept it; We said ‘Take forcefully seriously and with effort what We have given you and listen’ to what you have been commanded and be prepared to accept it They said ‘We hear your words and disobey’ your command; and they were made to drink the calf in their hearts that is to say the love of it the golden calf intoxicated their hearts in the way that wine does on account of their unbelief. Allah reminded the Jews of their errors, breaking His covenant, transgression and defiance, when He raised Mount Tur above them so that they would believe and agree to the terms of the covenant. (And when We made with you a covenant) when we took your consent (and caused the Mount to tower above you) extracted it, elevated it and fixed it above your heads: Remember when you made a binding promise with God to follow Moses, peace be upon him, and to accept what he brought from God. God raised the mountain over you so that you were awestruck, and told you to hold tightly and seriously to the scripture He had sent you, and to listen and follow what was revealed to you, if not God would make the mountain fall upon you, you said that you heard with your ears and rebelled in your actions. And when We made a covenant with you and raised over you the mount Take forcefully what We have given you and listen they said We hear and disobey ; and they were made to drink the calf in their hearts on account of their unbelief.

**We hear and disobey, and the consent that was not in the heart.**

This verse reports the Jews as having replied that they had heard the Command of Allah, but they would not obey, or would not be able to obey. It means that out of sheer fright they said (only with their tongues) that they had heard (that is to say, accepted) the Command of Allah. But there was no real consent in their hearts, and their posture and attitude was such as if they were saying that they would not or could not obey. (They said, "We have heard and disobeyed.") We have mentioned the Tafsir of this subject before. 'Abdur-Razzaq said that Ma'mar narrated that Qatadah said that,. (Hold fast by that which We have given you) be diligent and earnest with what We have given you of the Book, (and hear) obey what you have been commanded, (they said: We hear and rebel) it is as if they were saying: if it were not for the mountain we would have heard your saying and disobeyed your command. No counsel was useful to them and no punishment led them to refrain from their disobediences. They paid no mind to censure lā bi-l-dhamm fīhim iḥtafalū and did not act according to what the situation required wa-lā bi-mūjibi al-amr ʿamilū.

**The love of the calf, and the hearts it was rooted in.**

(And (worship of) the calf was made to sink into their hearts) their love of worshipping the calf sank into their hearts (because of their rejection) as a punishment for their disbelief. If love of worshipping the calf is equal in your eyes to love of your Creator, then: (And their hearts absorbed (the worship of) the calf) means, "They absorbed its love, until its love resided in their hearts. He reiterates the tale of their excessive love for the calf their aversion to accepting the Real and [... ] and their being told of the punishment that would overtake them for the evil they did. So, either through the feebleness of their repentance or through a want of proper hatred for infidelity, their hearts became indolent in religious matters, so much so that when Allah asked them to take a pledge to follow the injunctions of the Torah steadfastly, Mount Tur (Sinai) was suspended over their heads to threaten them.

**The cult found by the sea, and the repentance that was not of a high order.**

When the Israelites succeeded, with the help of Allah, in escaping from Egypt and crossing the sea, they came upon a people who used to worship idols. They found this cult so attractive that they requested Sayyidna Musa (Moses) to fabricate a visible and concrete god for them too. When he reprimanded them, they realized their error, and offered' repentance. Since their repentance was not of a very high order, the darkness of their error did not altogether leave their hearts, but continued to grow, and finally manifested itself in the worship of the golden calf. As for those who had not indulged in the worship of the calf, they did not hate the action of the worshippers of the calf as much as they should have.

**How evil is what your belief prompts you to do.**

Say to them ‘Evil is that thing which your belief in the Torah enjoins on you in the way of the worship of the golden calf if you are believers’ in it as you claim; meaning you are not believers for faith does not command that you worship the calf — their forefathers are meant here. Likewise you do not believe in the Torah because you have denied the prophethood of Muhammad whereas faith in it does not command you to reject him. (Say: "Worst indeed is that which your faith enjoins on you if you are believers.") means, "Worse yet is the manner in which you behaved in the past and even now, disbelieving in Allah's Ayat and defying the Prophets. You also disbelieved in Muhammad , which is the worst of your deeds and the harshest sin that you committed. How can you then claim that you believe, while committing the evil of breaking Allah's covenant, disbelieving in Allah's Ayat and worshipping the calf instead of Allah?" "Worst indeed is that which your faith enjoins on you if you are believers. (Evil is that which your belief enjoineth on you) the worship of the calf enjoins on you, (if ye are believers) if you are truthful that your forefathers were believers. O Muhammad, what their faith commands them to do is evil: disbelieving and turning away from what Allah instructs them to do – if they have any faith at all – because if they truly had faith they would not disbelieve and turn away from it. Having referred to such example of their perversity and rebellion, the Holy Qur'an asks the Jews to have a look at themselves and also at their claim to genuine faith. Hence their claim to be true believers is evidently false.

94.text:
The verse is a challenge put in the form of a conditional, and the condition is one the people addressed have already accepted. The whole of it runs: "Say, O Prophet, If the eternal Home of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively for you Israelites out of all humanity, then wish for death if what you say is true!" The first half of the sentence takes the claim as it stands and does not dispute it, and the taking of it is what gives the second half its force, since a wish for death is only a test of the claim if the claim is the one the verse has just repeated. The home named is the home of the Hereafter, and the exclusivity named is an exclusivity out of all humanity, so the claim is not that the people addressed are first in that home but that they are alone in it, and the challenge is measured to that: if the home is theirs alone, then the passage into it is a thing to be wished for rather than avoided. The wish is put as a wish and not as an act, so what is asked for is not death but the wanting of it, and the wanting is the evidence, since a person certain of a home that is his alone does not have to be persuaded to want to enter it. The if what you say is true at the end ties the challenge back to the saying and not to the believing, so the test proposed is of a statement made and not of a state of the soul, and the statement is one the verse has given in its own words, which leaves no room afterwards for a narrower reading of it.

**If the Home of the Hereafter is exclusively for you.**

Say to them ‘If the Abode of the Hereafter that is Paradise with God is purely yours that is exclusively and not for other people as you allege then long for death — if you speak truly’ here both conditionals are connected to the verb tamannū ‘long for’ so that the first is dependent upon the second in other words ‘If you speak truly when you claim that it is yours then you will naturally incline to what is yours and since the path to it is death long for it death’. "If the abode of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful. (Say to (them): "If the home of the Hereafter with Allah is indeed for you especially and not for others, of mankind, then long for death if you are truthful.") meaning, 'Invoke Allah to bring death to the lying camp among the two (Muslims and Jews).' The Jews declined this offer by the Messenger of Allah ." (Say (unto them): If the abode of the Hereafter) i.e. Paradise (in the providence of Allah is indeed for you alone) specifically for you alone (and not for others of mankind) and not for the believers in Muhammad and his Companions ((as you pretend), then long for death (for ye must long for death) ask for death (if ye are truthful) in your claim. Jews, if Paradise in the Afterlife is just for you, and no other people will enter it, then wish for death, and ask for it, so that you reach this place quickly, and can rest from the burdens and worries of the life of this world, if you are truthful about what you claim. If the abode of the hereafter with God is purely yours and not for other people then long for death-if you speak truly.

**The claim, and the trial proposed for it.**

What they meant in making such a claim was that since their own faith was the true one, they must certainly attain salvation in the other world -- the repentant and the forgiven being admitted to Paradise from the very beginning, the sinners finding release from the fires of Hell after undergoing a punishment for a few days, and the obedient receiving a welcome like sons and beloved friends. The use of certain improper expressions like "sons of Allah" not-withstanding, these claims are in themselves quite correct, provided that they pertain to people who follow a true and valid faith. But the Jews (and the Christians as well) were still following a faith which had been abrogated, and was thus no longer valid -- a fact which nullified their claim. So, the Holy Qur'an suggests an abnormal method, which would not call for much knowledge or understanding, but only put a little strain on the tongue. The proposed trial consists in this -- if the Jews are so sure of the blessings of the other world being reserved for themselves, they should declare that they wish to die, and this declaration would establish them as being genuine in their faith; but if they refuse to accept the challenge, it would show that they were liars. So, they refused to go through the trial, for they were struck with awe, and feared that as soon as they had expressed the wish to die, death would come over them, and they would be sent to Hell. Here we must note that the trial was proposed not for all the Jews of all the ages, but specially for those who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet and who used to deny him out of sheer envy and malice, in spite of having recognized that he was a genuine prophet. The Mubahalah (invocation to Allah to destroy the liars) was called a 'wish' here, because every just person wishes that Allah destroy the unjust opponent who is debating with him, especially when the just person has a clear, apparent proof for the truth he is calling to.

**Then wish for death, if you are truthful.**

(Then long for death), means, "Invoke (Allah) for death. (Then long for death if you are truthful), "Had the Jews invoked Allah for death, they would have perished. Also, the Mubahalah involves invoking Allah for death of the unjust group, because to disbelievers, life is the biggest prize, especially when they know the evil destination they will meet after death. Among the signs of ardent longing ishtiyāq is the desire for death while in the best of health and well-being. Whoever is absolutely and without any doubt confident that the garden is his ardently longs for it. In this is good news for the believers who ardently long for death; there is forgiveness for them. He only bestows the ardent longing on them so that it may be actualized [when] they reach the garden. " Secondly, if they could wish for death in their hearts, they must have declared it orally too, for their victory lay in just such a declaration, and this was a very easy way of refuting the Holy Prophet .

**Their own history, the prophets slain, and the death not sought.**

The fact that the Israelites were not really concerned with truth is proved by their own history. It was they who had slain their own prophets, such as Zachariah and John the Baptist, the only reason for these actions being that these prophets had criticized the Israelites’ mode of living, and sought to bring them back to the divine way (Nehemiah, 9:26). They had seen Moses perform undeniable miracles, but when he was not with them in person, having left them to spend forty days on Mount Sinai, they started worshipping the golden calf; it had only been his personal authority which had kept them under control. When the Mount was raised threateningly above their heads, they temporarily agreed to do ‘all that the Lord hath spoken’ (Exodus, 19:5 , 8, 16 , 18), but, after that, most of them returned to their disobedient ways. If they had really been seeking God, their attention would have been entirely focused on the life after death; but, in fact, they, more than all the others, were obsessed with the love of the present world. But they did not long for the garden-and God said that they will never long for it-and this information was a miracle for the Messenger since it was as He had said. Of old it was said For the negligent shame will suffice on the Day of the Meeting. But they knew very well in their heart of hearts that the Holy Prophet a and the Muslims stood for the truth, while they themselves were the champions of falsehood, and were, in actual fact, infidels.

95.text:
The verse answers the challenge of the one before it, and it answers it by taking the answer away. "But they will never wish for that because of what their hands have done" is a statement about what will not happen, and the never in it is not a prediction about a moment but about a people, so the wish asked for in the verse before is here refused in advance, and the refusal is not left as a refusal but given a cause. The cause is what their hands have done, which puts the reason for not wishing in the record rather than in the reasoning: the thing standing between them and the wish is not a doubt about the home but a knowledge of the road to it. "And Allah has perfect knowledge of the wrongdoers" closes the verse with the knowledge that answers theirs, and the perfect in it is what makes the closing a closing, since a knowledge that misses nothing leaves the wrongdoer nothing to appeal to. The wrongdoers named are the same people the first clause is about, so the two clauses are not two statements but one statement and its ground: they will not wish, and the one they would have to wish in the presence of knows what they have done.

**They will never long for it, because of what their hands sent before them.**

But they will never long for it because of that which their own hands have sent before them as a result of their rejection of the Prophet s the consequence of their mendacity. (But they will never long for it) they will never ask for death, (because of that which their own hands have sent before them) because of what they themselves have done in the religion of Judaism. God most high said But they will never long for it because of that which their own hands have sent before them. " Had they wished death that day, no Jew would have remained alive on the face of the earth. (Had the Jews wished for death, they would have died and seen their seats in the Fire. And, those who invoked such curse against Allah's Messenger would have found no families or property had they returned to their homes)."

**Allah knows the wrongdoers, and will requite them.**

God knows the evildoers the disbelievers and He will requite them. (And Allah is Aware of evil-doers) i.e. the Jews. Allah knows the wrongdoers among them and other people: each person will be given what they have earned. So they claimed that they are Allah's sons and loved ones and said, "Only those who are Christian or Jews shall enter Paradise. " Therefore, they were called to invoke Allah to destroy the lying group, be it them or the Muslims. Nor can one suppose that they did make an oral declaration, for the fact has not been reported, and thus has not come down to us. Such a supposition would be wrong, because the opponents of Islam have always outnumbered its adherents, and if such a thing had happened, they must have been trumpeting it aloud to show to the world that the Jews had successfully passed the test proposed by the Holy Qur'an itself.

**The offer declined, and the eagerness to delay the Hereafter.**

When the Jews declined, every one was sure of their wrong, for had they been sure of their claims, then they would have accepted the proposal. Their lies were thus exposed after they declined the offer to invoke the curse. This life is a prison for the believer and Paradise for the disbeliever. Therefore, the People of the Book wish they could delay the Hereafter, as much as possible. However, they shall certainly meet what they are trying to avoid, even if they are more eager to delay the Hereafter than the polytheists who do not have a divine book. The Holy Qur'an also predicts that they would never have the courage to go through the trial. Nor should one raise the doubt here that they had perhaps accepted the challenge, and "wished" for death in their hearts, as the Holy Qur'an seems to ask. For one, the Holy Qur'an itself reports the prediction that they would never "wish for it. But they did not avail themselves of this opportunity.

96.text:
The verse before this one asked for a wish, and this one explains why the wish was never going to be made, and explains it by describing an appetite. "You will surely find them clinging to life more eagerly than any other people, even more than polytheists" puts the description in the form of a finding, a thing that will be met with and not merely asserted, and the comparison in it is not with people in general but with one group named, the polytheists, who are the ones exceeded. That naming is the point of the clause, since a greed for life is not surprising in people who expect nothing after it, and what the verse is marking is that the people addressed do expect something after it and are greedier all the same. "Each one of them wishes to live a thousand years" gives the appetite a number, and the number is not the measure of a lifetime but of a longing, since a thousand years is past what anyone is granted, so the wish is not for a long life but for a life with no end in view. The each one of them is what makes the clause collective: the wish is not put on their leaders or on a party among them but on every one of them, and the appetite described is therefore the shape of the group rather than an exception inside it. "But even if they were to live that long, it would not save them from the punishment" answers the number with a limit of its own, and the answer is not that the wish will be refused but that its granting would not do what the wish is for, since a life of a thousand years and the punishment are not in competition and the one does not delay the other. The even if makes the case hypothetical and then closes it, so the verse grants the wish in order to show that nothing follows from granting it. "And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do" ends the verse with the seeing that stands over the whole of it, and the seeing is of what they do rather than of what they wish, which puts the reckoning on the acts and leaves the appetite as the reason the acts were done in the way they were done. The four clauses run in one direction: an appetite described, an appetite measured, a measurement shown to be of no use, and a seeing that takes account of the doing behind all three. The verse is therefore not a description of a temperament but the completion of an argument, since the challenge two verses back asked for a wish, and this one shows what had to be true of the people addressed for that wish to be impossible, and shows it in the appetite they had rather than in anything they said.

**Clinging to life, and the people exceeded in it.**

The verse puts the clinging to life in the second person and addresses it to the Prophet, so the finding is one he will make and not one he is being told to imagine, and the surely in it removes the possibility of an exception turning up. What is found is a clinging, which is a stronger word than a preference, since a clinging is what a person does when the thing clung to is being taken away, and the verse gives no occasion for the taking away, so the clinging is described as a standing condition rather than a response to a danger. The comparison with the polytheists is what gives the condition its weight. A people who worship others alongside Allah and do not believe that they will be brought back to life have no reason in their belief to want this life more than another, and their greed for it is only a greed for what they have, so it is consistent with what they hold. The people addressed here are not in that position: they acknowledge the other world, they have a scripture that describes it, and they had even persuaded themselves that its joys were reserved for them and for no one else. The greed of a people in that position is not consistent with what they hold, and the verse sets the two side by side precisely because the inconsistency is the evidence. It is the same weakness that kept them from taking up the challenge of the verse before it, since a challenge to wish for death can only be taken up by people whose longing is turned the other way, and the verse is showing that the refusal of the challenge was not a failure of nerve at a moment but the visible edge of an appetite that was already there. The appetite is described without qualification as to the quality of the life wanted: it is life that is clung to, even a life that is miserable and lowly, so what is wanted is continuation rather than content.

**A thousand years, and the wish behind the number.**

The number in the second clause is a thousand years, and the readings take it as a wish and as a hope at once, which is what a number of that size amounts to when it is wished for by a person who will not see a tenth of it. A wish for a thousand years is not a plan but a statement of direction: it says how far the longing would go if nothing stopped it, and the verse uses it for that purpose rather than for the purpose of describing an ambition anyone actually had. This is why the clause is put on each one of them and not on the group, since a longing of that kind is not a policy that could differ between persons but an appetite present in every one of them. The clause is made sharper by what the people addressed already believed. They were People of the Scripture, they believed in the resurrection and in the reckoning that follows it, and the belief in a reckoning is a belief that this life is a passage with an account at the end of it. A person holding that belief and wishing for a thousand years of the passage is wishing for the passage to be long rather than for the account to be good, and the wish therefore discloses which of the two the person is actually attending to. The verse does not argue the point with them, it states the wish and leaves the disclosure in it, which is why the clause is short and the number is round. A longing measured in thousands is a longing that has stopped measuring in terms of what comes after, and the prolonging of a life is of no value to a person certain of death in any case, since death comes unexpectedly and a life is cut short at a point that no amount of wishing moves. **The length that saves nothing, and the life that did its owner no good.**

The third clause takes the wish and grants it, and the granting is what defeats it. Even if they were to live that long, the punishment is not turned aside by the living, so the thing the wish was for is not obtained by the wish being satisfied. The verse is careful about the form of the denial: it does not say the punishment will come sooner, or that the life will be shortened, but that the length itself does not save, which leaves the person wishing with nothing to gain from the wish being granted. The grant of such a life will not save him even a little from the punishment due to him, and the even a little is what closes the clause, since a saving that is partial would still be a reason to wish for length, and the verse removes that reason. The comparison the readings draw is with a long life that is known to have done its owner no good, the life given to Satan, whose respite was granted and whose torment was not lessened by it, so the case is not hypothetical but a granted life already on record with its outcome attached. The clause also answers the comparison in the first one. The polytheists would love to enjoy a long life because they do not believe in a resurrection after death, and for them the length is all there is to have; the people addressed know the humiliation they will meet in the Hereafter for knowingly ignoring the truth, and for them the length is a delay purchased at the price of knowing what is being delayed. The wish for a thousand years in a person who knows what follows it is a wish for the reckoning to be kept at a distance, and the third clause answers that the distance is not obtainable, since the reckoning is not located at a point in the life that a longer life could push away.

**Allah sees what they do, and gives them what they earned.**

The last clause is the shortest in the verse and the one that gathers the others. Allah is All-Seeing of what they do, and the seeing is named as a seeing rather than as a knowledge, which puts it in the register of a witness present at the acts and not of a record kept at a distance. The readings take the clause as a statement that nothing of what they do is hidden from Him, and that they will be given what they earned, so the seeing has its consequence attached to it and the verse does not leave it as a description of an attribute. The acts the seeing covers are named in the readings with a particular sharpness: contravention and rebellion, and what is concealed about the description and the traits of the Prophet, which is to say the acts that this passage has been about from its beginning. The concealment is the one that matters most here, since the whole of the argument from the covenant onward has turned on a recognition that was not acted upon, and a seeing that reaches what is concealed removes the hiding place the concealment was for. There is a reading in which the doing is addressed to the hearers rather than described of the people spoken about, and the sense holds under either, since what is seen is the doing and the requital that follows it. The clause thus does two things at once. It answers the appetite described in the first two clauses with a witness that the appetite was formed under, and it answers the third clause's limit with the reason the limit holds: the punishment is not turned aside by length because the seeing is not located in time and does not wait for the life to run out.

**Heedlessness of God, and the state of the believer as its opposite.**

The readings that go beneath the verse put the love of this life down to heedlessness of God, and they take the case described here as the extreme of it, an excessive love of remaining in this world being the worst form the heedlessness takes. The reason given is not that the heedless do not know what awaits them but that they know of their own failure to be obedient, so the eagerness for life is an eagerness to postpone a meeting the person is not ready for, and the comparison drawn is with a runaway slave who does not want to be returned to his master. The state of the believer is set against this as its opposite. For a believer the transition of death is a passing to One from whom only good is expected, and that expectation is what makes the transition better than remaining among those against whom the case is being made; the length of the life is not the good in that account, and the ending of it is not the loss. The verse is therefore describing two orientations with one vocabulary: the people addressed want length because they expect the meeting to go badly, and the believers do not want length because they expect it to go well, and the difference between the two expectations is a difference in what each has done rather than in what each has been told. This is what the passage has been building to from the challenge two verses back: the wish could not be made, because the appetite for length already occupied the place the wish would have had to come from. The desire itself is the evidence that the claim was baseless, and that the people making it knew they would have to face the fire, since a certainty of a home reserved for them alone would have produced a longing for that home and not a clinging to this one. The verse ends on the seeing for that reason: the appetite was formed under a witness, and the good news in the passage belongs to those whose longing runs the other way.

97.text:
The verse is an answer to an enmity, and it answers by turning the enmity into a statement about the one it is directed at. The whole of it runs: "Say, O Prophet, Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel should know that he revealed this Quran to your heart by Allah's Will, confirming what came before it—a guide and good news for the believers." The answer is put in the mouth of the Prophet and addressed in the second person, so the verse is a saying commanded rather than a saying passed on, and the one commanded to say it is the person the enmity concerns, since the angel named is the one who brought the revelation down to him. The enemy is described conditionally, whoever is an enemy, which does not concede the enmity but takes it as given for the sake of the answer, and the answer is not a rebuttal of the enmity but a statement of what the one hated has done. What he has done is given with three features: he revealed the Quran, he revealed it to your heart, and he did it by Allah's Will. The first feature puts the book in the angel's hand as the one who brought it down, and the bringing down is what the enmity is answered with, since a book brought down by an angel is not the angel's own book. The second feature puts the receiving in a particular place, the heart, and the place belongs to the one addressed, so the revelation is described as an arrival inside the person receiving it and not as a delivery made at a distance. The third feature takes the angel's choice out of the act entirely, since the will named is Allah's and not his, and an angel acting by another's will is not a party anyone can take sides against. The confirming of what came before it is the fourth thing the verse gives, and it answers the particular shape the enmity took, since a book confirming the earlier books is no rival to them, and the angel who brought it is no enemy of the people who were given them. The guide and the good news at the end describe what the book is for, and the believers named in the good news are the ones it reaches, which leaves the enmity with no ground in the book itself: what the angel brought down is a guide, and a guide is not a thing to be an enemy of except by being an enemy of the guidance.

**Whoever is an enemy of Gabriel.**

Say to them ‘Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel let him die in exasperation — he it was that brought it the Qur’ān down upon your heart by the leave by the command of God confirming what was before it of scriptures a guidance from error and good tidings of Paradise for the believers. "Whoever is an enemy to Jibril (Gabriel)(let him die in his fury), for indeed he has brought it (this Qur'an) down to your heart by Allah's permission, confirming what came before it (i.e. the Tawrah and the Injil) and guidance and glad tidings for the believers "Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His Angels, His Messengers, Jibril and Mika'il, then verily, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers. When they learnt that it was Archangel Jibra'il (Gabriel) who brought the Glorious Qur'an to the Holy Prophet they said that the Archangel was their enemy, as it was through him that rigorous commandments or catastrophic punishments had always descended on them,. and that for this reason they would not accept a Book which had been revealed through his agency. Then Allah, Exalted is He, revealed the following verse about the saying of one of the Jews, 'Abdullah Ibn Suriyyah, that Gabriel was the enemy of the Jews, saying: Say, O Muhammad, to those of the Jews who say that Gabriel is their enemy among the angels, that whoever is against Gabriel – who revealed the Qur’ān to your heart, with Allah’s permission, affirming the sacred scripture that came before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel, showing the way to what is good, and bringing the good news to the believers of the bliss Allah has prepared for them – then he is misguided. But, instead of heeding these admonitions, the Israelites came to regard Gabriel as their enemy, because it had always been he who gave prior warning through the prophets about impending doom. Consequently, when the Prophet Muhammad proclaimed that he was receiving his revelation through Gabriel, they said, ‘So, it is our old enemy Gabriel, who always brings commands from heaven against us! That explains why the scriptures, the birthright of the Israelites, are being conveyed to one who belongs to another tribe.

**He brought it down upon your heart, by Allah's leave.**

(For he it is who hath revealed to your heart) sent Gabriel to you with the Qur'an (by Allah's leave) by Allah's command, (confirming) affirming the Oneness of Allah (that which was before it) of the Book, (and a guidance) from error (and glad tiding) good news (to believers) that Paradise will be theirs. This is why God says, "he it is who sent it down upon thy heart. " It is said that when he was inundated by contemplation in this speech, the revelation would first descend to his heart, for He said to him, "who sent it down upon thy heart. " Then it would turn away from his heart to his understanding and his hearing. Specially, in the state of revelation, the external organs of the senses become dormant, and the heart receives even the words directly without the intervention of the ears. The error would lie in drawing from this phrase the conclusion that Allah has not revealed the words of the Holy Qur'an but only the meanings. Such a supposition is quite baseless, because many verses of the Holy Qur'an itself mention the Arabic language as the vehicle of revelation in the case of this particular Book of Allah. This example should make it easy to see that the revelation of meanings to the heart does in no way preclude the revelation of words as well.

**The messenger, the Book, the missions not chosen, and what the Book is for.**

In refuting this argument, the Holy Qur'an points out that Jibra'il is only a messenger, and has, acting only as a messenger, brought down the Holy Qur'an under a divine command to the Holy Prophet . So, why should the Jews be so particular about the messenger, and not look at the Book itself? As for the Book, it confirms the earlier Books of Allah, provides guidance to men, and gives good tidings to the believers. This being what the Divine Books are meant for, the Holy Qur'an is evidently enough a Divine Book, and must, as such be obeyed. Now, as for the attitude of the Jews towards Jibra'il the Holy Qur'an declares that to be hostile to the angels (including Jibra'il and Mika'il or to the prophets is tantamount to being hostile to Allah Himself. Verse 98 puts down the enemies of angels and prophets as infidels (Kafirin) in saying that Allah is the enemy of the infidels. In other words, those who deny or oppose the angels and the prophets will have their due punishment in the other world. This is the same with those who take Jibril as an enemy, because Jibril did not choose missions on his own, but by the command of his Lord,. Some people say that 'il' means worshipper while whatever word that is added to it becomes Allah's Name, because 'il' is a constant in such conjunction.

**The angels do not hold grudges, and the prophets before.**

Owing to their own rebelliousness, the Israelites had severe punishments meted out to them in ancient times. It was God’s way to warn them of these impending punishments beforehand, and such warnings came to them through the prophets, who were acting on the words of the Archangel Gabriel. The moral was that people had to follow God’s commandments; if they persisted in a sinful life, they would be exposing themselves to His wrath. ’ Now angels, being the rarefied creatures that they are, do not hold grudges against ordinary mortals; they descend to earth only by divine command in order to carry out the tasks assigned to them by their Creator—in this case, the revelation of the Scriptures to the prophet whom God Himself had chosen. Given the clear proofs that the Arab Prophet had had the same revelation communicated to him as had been received by Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and that it tallied with the previous divine scriptures, there were no grounds for the Israelites to reject the divine message. Their negative reaction was the result of their having lead insincere, unrestricted lives, which had become dominated by self-interest, empty convention and racial prejudice. Religion had been adhered to only on a superficial level, just to keep up the pretence that the Israelites were, in fact, faithfully treading the path of God.

**The forms the angel came in, and the revelation brought.**

" Magnanimous and beautiful is the Qur'an that Gabriel brought down from the All-Merciful. " Elsewhere He says, "Brought down by the trustworthy spirit upon thy heart" [26:193-94]. When Gabriel conveyed the pure revelation, sometimes he came in the form of a mortal man, sometimes in the form of an angel. Whenever he brought verses about permitted and forbidden and the explication of the shariahs and rulings, he would be in human form, and there was no talk of the heart. Thus He says, "He it is who sent down upon thee the Book" [3:7]; "Does it not suffice them that We sent down upon thee the Book?" [29:51]. Then again, whenever there was talk of love, the attributes of passion, and the intimations of friendship, he would come in the form of an angel, spiritual and subtle, and he would join with MuṣṬafā's heart. When he returned and left behind the realm of his heart, MuṣṬafā would say, "He broke away from me while I was aware of him.

**Three things asked, the meal of Paradise, and the child's resemblance.**

He came to the Prophet and said, 'I am going to ask you about three things which nobody knows except a Prophet. What will be the first meal taken by the people of Paradise? Why does a child resemble its father, and why does it resemble its maternal uncle?' Allah's Messenger said, "Jibril has just told me the answers." 'Abdullah said, 'He (i.e. Jibril), among all the angels, is the enemy of the Jews.' Allah's Messenger recited the Ayah,. Allah's Messenger then said, (The first portent of the Hour will be a fire that will bring together the people from the east to the west; the first meal of the people of Paradise will be the caudate lobe of the liver of fish. As for the child resembling his parents: If a man has sexual intercourse with his wife and his discharge is first, the child will resemble the father. If the woman has a discharge first, the child will resemble her side of the family.)
