173.text:
He has only forbidden you to eat carrion, blood, swine, and what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah. The verse gathers the few things kept back from the wide table of the verse before it, and the sources read the short list as a mercy rather than a burden, since each entry is named and the reason for it is made plain. The carrion is the animal that dies of itself, and the sources carry what follows from that, that what has not been slaughtered in the appointed way is not food, while the dead of the sea and the locust are set apart and kept lawful. Blood is put after it and is understood as the blood that flows, and the swine is named as a whole, and the last of the four is what is offered to any name other than the name of Allah, so the line is drawn at the act of dedication and not only at the animal. But if someone is compelled by necessity, neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need, they will not be sinful. The verse then opens a door for the one who is trapped, and the sources explain the two conditions carefully, that the need must be real and that the eater takes no more than what keeps him alive and does not treat the allowance as a licence. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The closing words are read by the sources as the reason the door was opened at all, and they bring out that the one who is forced is not asked to die in the name of a rule, since the rule itself was given for his good.

**What carrion, blood, swine and the rest cover.**

He has only forbidden you carrion that is the consumption of it since this is the subject of the general address here and similarly the consumption of what follows all of which is what has not been slaughtered in accordance with prescriptions of the Law; to this the Sunna adds as also constituting carrion what has been severed from a living creature. A special status is however accorded fish and locusts; blood poured forth as in sūrat al-An‘ām see Q. 6145 the flesh of swine the meat is singled out for mention because that part is what people mostly seek every other part being implied thereby; what has been hallowed to other than God that is to say what has been slaughtered in other than His Name al-ihlāl is the raising of one’s voice which they used to do when sacrificing for their gods. The dead animal is known in English as 'carrion' or carcass. In Islamic terminology, it means an animal not slaughtered in accordance with the requirements of the Shari'ah. Allah has prohibited eating the meat of swine, whether slaughtered or not, and this includes its fat, either because it is implied, or because the term Lahm includes that, or by analogy. Allah has only forbidden you from consuming that which died without being sacrificed according to the sacred law and having its blood flow, the meat of pigs and what has had other than Allah’s name mentioned over it when it was sacrificed. (He hath forbidden you only carrion) which He has commanded to immolate, (and blood) and shed blood, (and swineflesh, and that which hath been immolated to any other than Allah) that which is offered as sacrifice purposefully in any other thing than the Name of Allah, i.e. to idols.

**What the dead animal is and what is set apart from it.**

The dead animal is known in English as 'carrion' or carcass. In Islamic terminology, it means an animal not slaughtered in accordance with the requirements of the Shari'ah. If it dies its own death without having been slaughtered or is killed by choking or aggressive hitting, it falls under the category of 'dead' and remains haram . It is on this basis that, in authentic ahadith, fish and locust have been determined as exceptions to the category of maitah (unslaughtered) and thus made halal . So, among animals, the fish and the locust are halal without slaughtering, even if they die their own death or get killed by somebody. Dead animals are those that die before being slaughtered; whether they die by strangling, a violent blow, a headlong fall, the goring of horns or by being partly eaten by a wild animal. Dead animals of the sea are excluded from this ruling, as is explained later, Allah willing, as Allah said: (Its water is pure and its dead are permissible.)

**What the blood that flows comes to.**

The second thing forbidden in the verse is blood. The word, dam (pronounced a, 'sum' in English) meaning 'blood' has been used here in the absolute sense, but, in verse (6:145) of Surah al-An am, it has been subjected to a qualification, that is: Therefore, fuqaha' agree that congealed blood such as, the kidney or spleen, are clean and permissible. Since flowing blood is what is forbidden, the blood that remains on the flesh after slaughtering the animal is clean. The Muslim jurists, the blessed Companions and their successors and the Ummah in general agree on this.

**What is offered to a name other than the name of Allah.**

An animal on which the name of anyone other than Allah has been called (Wa ma uhilla bihi lighayrillah ‌). Allah has prohibited eating the meat of swine, whether slaughtered or not, and this includes its fat, either because it is implied, or because the term Lahm includes that, or by analogy. Similarly prohibited are offerings to other than Allah, that is what was slaughtered in a name other than His, be it for monuments, idols, divination, or the other practices of the time of Jahiliyyah. She said, "Do not eat from what has been slaughtered for that day, (or feast) but eat from their vegetables." Allah has only forbidden you from consuming that which died without being sacrificed according to the sacred law and having its blood flow, the meat of pigs and what has had other than Allah’s name mentioned over it when it was sacrificed.

**What the one who is compelled by necessity may take.**

But if one is forced by necessity without willful disobedience nor transgressing due limits, then there is no sin on him. (But if one is forced by necessity without willful disobedience nor transgressing due limits), meaning, without transgression or overstepping the limits,. (...then there is no sin on him.) meaning, if one eats such items, for,. (But he who is driven by necessity) compelled to eat carrion (neither craving) neither rebelling nor declaring it lawful (nor transgressing) nor committing highway robbery nor purposefully eating it without being driven by necessity, (it is no sin for him) then such a person, who is compelled to eat it without having his fill and without taking anything with him, has not transgressed. Yet if someone is forced to eat something of these forbidden types, and does not sin by eating it when they are not in need, nor do they go beyond the limit of what is necessary, then they have done no wrong and will receive no punishment. Yet whoever is constrained not desiring nor transgressing no sin shall be on him. The aggressor and the transgressor are excluded from this dispensation and to these two categories one should also add every person that sets out on a journey in disobedience such as the fugitive or the excise collector for whom it would be unlawful to eat any of the mentioned unless they repent of their disobedience; this is the opinion of al-Shāfi‘ī.

**What the forgiving and merciful close carries.**

God is Forgiving to His friends Merciful to those who are obedient to Him for He has granted them wide berth in this matter. " Sa'id bin Jubayr said, "Allah is pardoning for what has been eaten of the unlawful, and Merciful' in that He allowed the prohibited during times of necessity. (Lo! Allah is Forgiving) that he ate more than he needs to preserve himself, (Merciful) when He gave him legal dispensation to eat carrion. Allah is Forgiving and Compassionate to whomever repents to Him; and it is from His mercy that He overlooks the eating of forbidden things when it is necessary.

174.text:
Indeed, those who hide Allah's revelations, trading them for a fleeting gain, consume nothing but fire into their bellies. The verse turns from the things that are eaten to the deeds that are swallowed, and the sources read the hiding as the work of the learned among the People of the Book, who kept back what they knew because the keeping back brought them gifts and standing among their own people. The fire in the bellies is the price named for that trade, and the sources join it to the warning about those who take the property of orphans and to the saying that what is eaten or drunk from vessels of gold and silver is a fire in the belly, so the gain is carried into the body and becomes the punishment itself. Allah will neither speak to them on the Day of Judgment. The verse then lists what will be withheld in the world to come, and the sources take the silence as the heaviest of the losses, since it is the refusal of the word of welcome and of the account that would clear them, and they bring out that the loss of speech here is the loss of the mercy that speech would carry. nor will He purify them. The second clause carries the loss of cleansing, and the sources read the two together as the loss of standing and of the word at once, after which the verse states plainly that they will suffer a painful punishment. And they will suffer a painful punishment. The sources carry the account of those who hid the marks of the Prophet and traded them away, and they notice that these people were afraid of losing what they had, so the verse names the price they chose and shows it to be fire. The verse sets what is hidden against what is taken for it, and the gain is called fleeting while the fire is what is consumed into the bellies, so those who hide the revelations are shown taking a thing that passes at the price of a thing that will not pass. Allah will not speak to them and will not purify them, and the painful punishment is where that trading ends, so the verse closes the account of that trading on the Day of Judgment.

**What the concealment of the Scripture was.**

Those who conceal what God has revealed of the Scripture comprising all the descriptions of Muhammad meaning the Jews and sell it for a little price in this world taking this little price in its place from the debased ones among them for fear of losing out if they were to manifest it sc. the truth of Muhammad — they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire because that is their journey’s end; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection out of anger with them neither purify them from the filth of sin; and theirs is a painful chastisement that is the Fire. Mentioned in the earlier verses were unlawful things which are tangible. For instance, religious scholars among the Jews were addicted to giving out false verdicts in favour of people who bribed them. They would go to the limit of distorting the verses of the Torah to suit the desire of their client. Verily, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book, and purchase a small gain therewith (of worldly things), they eat into their bellies nothing but fire. Those who hide what Allah revealed in the scriptures and the signs of the truth and prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ – as the Jews and Christians did, getting something small in return for what they hide, such as leadership, status or money – they only fill their stomachs with that which will cause them to suffer in the fire of Hell. Those who conceal what God has revealed of the scripture and sell it for a little price-they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the fire; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection neither purify them; and theirs is a painful chastisement. This was revealed about the leaders and doctors of the Jews. (Lo! Those who hide anything of the Scripture which Allah hath revealed) what Allah has exposited in the Torah regarding the description and traits of Muhammad, (and purchase) by concealing this (a small gain therewith) a small profit, this was revealed about Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab (they eat into their bellies) they put into their bellies (nothing else than fire) except the unlawful; and it is also said that this means: they eat nothing except that which will turn into fire in their bellies on the Day of Judgement.

**What the wealth they kept was for them.**

Some perceptive Ulama' have said that unlawful wealth is, in reality, the very fire of Hell, even though we do not sense it as such during our lifetime in the mortal world, but once one dies, his or her deeds will appear in the form of fire. They may revel in such compromises as bring them wealth and honour, but in the eyes of God, they are the worst offenders. Hiding the truth for worldly considerations is not one of those offences that God will ignore in the Hereafter. They concealed this information so that they would not lose authority and the position that they had with the Arabs, where they would bring them gifts, and honor them. So they hid the truth so that they may retain the little that they were getting, and they sold their souls for this little profit. They used to get gifts and surpluses from ordinary Jews and hoped that the new prophet will be sent from amongst them.

**What the fire in the bellies is.**

(...they eat into their bellies nothing but fire,) meaning, whatever they eat in return for hiding the truth, will turn into a raging fire in their stomachs on the Day of Resurrection. (Verily, those who unjustly eat up the property of orphans, they eat up only fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in the blazing Fire!)(4:10) (Those who eat or drink in golden or silver plates are filling their stomachs with the fire of Jahannam (Hell).) (Lo! Those who hide anything of the Scripture which Allah hath revealed) what Allah has exposited in the Torah regarding the description and traits of Muhammad, (and purchase) by concealing this (a small gain therewith) a small profit, this was revealed about Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab (they eat into their bellies) they put into their bellies (nothing else than fire) except the unlawful; and it is also said that this means: they eat nothing except that which will turn into fire in their bellies on the Day of Judgement. Those who hide what Allah revealed in the scriptures and the signs of the truth and prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ – as the Jews and Christians did, getting something small in return for what they hide, such as leadership, status or money – they only fill their stomachs with that which will cause them to suffer in the fire of Hell. There is no doubt that people who conceal the contents of the Book of Allah and in return for this breach of trust, collect insignificant worldly gains are simply eating fire.

**What it means that Allah will not speak to them.**

Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and theirs will be a painful torment Those are they who have purchased error at the price of guidance, and torment at the price of forgiveness. (And Allah will not speak to them) nicely (on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He make them pure) He will not absolve them of their transgressions; it is also said that this means: Then on the Day of Judgement, Allah will not speak to them with words that make them joyful; but they will only hear that which makes them sad: they will not be praised, and they will have a painful punishment. When comes the Qiyamah (Doomsday), Allah Almighty will not speak to them affectionately, nor will He purify them by forgiving their sins. They thus deserve Allah's anger, so Allah will not look at them or purify them, meaning that He will not praise them but will cause them to taste a severe torment.

**What the painful punishment is for.**

Allah states that they will suffer such severe, painful torment that those who see them will be amazed at how they could bear the tremendous punishment, torture and pain that they will suffer. (Theirs will be a painful doom) a painful torment that will extend to their hearts. Their punishment will be terrible for they are the kind of people who, during their mortal life, chose to abandon guidance and adopt error, and in the Hereafter, they missed forgiveness and became deserving of punishment. All these punishments to them are because they elected to stray away from the Book of Allah, something so clear and true. (...and torment at the price of forgiveness,) meaning, they preferred torment over forgiveness due to the sins they have committed. It is evident that they must be victims of serious intransigence and are far out in schism, as a result of which they can expect to deserve a matching punishment.

**What the concealment earned them.**

Thus, the Jews earned anger on top of the wrath that they already had earned before, and Allah criticized them again many times in His Book. (Verily, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book.) Meaning the Jews who concealed their Book's descriptions of Muhammad , all of which testify to his truth as a Messenger and a Prophet. Therefore, they have profited failure and loss in this life and the Hereafter. Those who conceal what God has revealed of the Scripture comprising all the descriptions of Muhammad meaning the Jews and sell it for a little price in this world taking this little price in its place from the debased ones among them for fear of losing out if they were to manifest it sc. the truth of Muhammad — they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire because that is their journey’s end; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection out of anger with them neither purify them from the filth of sin; and theirs is a painful chastisement that is the Fire. Those who hide what Allah revealed in the scriptures and the signs of the truth and prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ – as the Jews and Christians did, getting something small in return for what they hide, such as leadership, status or money – they only fill their stomachs with that which will cause them to suffer in the fire of Hell. Those who conceal what God has revealed of the scripture and sell it for a little price-they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the fire; God shall not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection neither purify them; and theirs is a painful chastisement. In this, there is a veiled warning given to the ulama', the religious scholars of the community of the Last of the prophets, that they should keep away from such practices and never fall short in disclosing the true injunctions of Allah for any material reason or vested interest of their own.

175.text:
They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment. The two exchanges are named in one sentence, and the sources notice that both are losses, since what is handed over is worth more than what is received, and they take the sentence as an invitation to wonder that anyone would make such a trade at all. The guidance was there to be taken and the misguidance was chosen instead, and the sources explain that a person does not lose the way by accident but turns from what stands in front of him, while the forgiveness that was within reach is set against the punishment that is taken in its place. How persistent are they in pursuit of the Fire. The question at the end is put as amazement, and the sources carry the sense that these people are not only on the road but in a hurry along it, since they press on to what will destroy them and let go of what would have saved them. The verse follows the account of those who concealed the Scripture and sold what they knew, and the sources read the two passages as one picture, so the trading named here is the trading described there, guidance given up for the little that was gained and forgiveness given up for what the gain brought.

Those are they that have bought error at the price of guidance taking the former in place of the latter in this world and chastisement at the price of pardon the pardon that would have been prepared for them in the Hereafter had they not concealed this matter; what makes them so patient for the Fire? that is how great is the extent of their patience? That is because Allah has revealed the Book in truth. The sentence gives the reason for the punishment named in the verse before it, and the sources read the revealing as the ground of the charge, since the Book was sent with the truth and the people concerned were not left without it. The truth is explained by the sources as what exposes the false and shows the way, and they notice that the Books before it were sent in the same manner, so the offence is measured against a clear gift rather than against a hidden demand. **What the fire spoken of in the verse before is.**

That which has been mentioned of their eating of the Fire and what follows it is because God has revealed the Book with the truth but they are at variance regarding it believing in parts of it while disbelieving in others and concealing them; and those that are at variance regarding the Book concerning this matter namely the Jews — although it is said that these are the idolaters some of whom said with regard to the Qur’ān that it was poetry others that it was sorcery and others still that it was divination — are in schism disagreement far removed from the truth. (...they eat into their bellies nothing but fire,) meaning, whatever they eat in return for hiding the truth, will turn into a raging fire in their stomachs on the Day of Resurrection. (Verily, those who unjustly eat up the property of orphans, they eat up only fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in the blazing Fire!)(4:10) (Those who eat or drink in golden or silver plates are filling their stomachs with the fire of Jahannam (Hell).) They are those who have bought error at the price of guidance and chastisement at the price of pardon; what makes them so patient for the fireḍ That is because God has revealed the Book with the truth; and those that are at variance regarding the Book are in schism far removed.

**What those who concealed the Book came to.**

(Verily, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book.) Meaning the Jews who concealed their Book's descriptions of Muhammad , all of which testify to his truth as a Messenger and a Prophet. They concealed this information so that they would not lose authority and the position that they had with the Arabs, where they would bring them gifts, and honor them. The cursed Jews feared that if they announced what they know about Muhammad , then the people would abandon them and follow him. So they hid the truth so that they may retain the little that they were getting, and they sold their souls for this little profit. They preferred the little that they gained over guidance and following the truth, believing in the Messenger and having faith in what Allah was sent him with. Therefore, they have profited failure and loss in this life and the Hereafter. Thus, the Jews earned anger on top of the wrath that they already had earned before, and Allah criticized them again many times in His Book. Hiding the truth for worldly considerations is not one of those offences that God will ignore in the Hereafter.

177.text:
Righteousness is not in turning your faces towards the east or the west, Rather, the righteous are those who believe in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Books, and the prophets. The verse is a summary of the whole religion, and the sources read it as an answer to the dispute over the direction of prayer, since the point of the turning was never the patch of ground but the obedience that the turning expresses. The list then begins with what is held in the heart, and the sources notice the order of it, the Creator first and then what He sent down and whom He sent, so that the deeds which follow stand on a foundation and are not left as a heap of good acts. who give charity out of their cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, needy travellers, beggars, and for freeing captives. The sources dwell on the words out of their cherished wealth, since the giving is measured by the love the giver has for what he hands over, and they take the long list as a widening of the circle outward from the nearest kin to the stranger on the road, and they notice that the freeing of captives is set among the gifts of money so that wealth is spent on loosening a life and not only on filling a hand. who establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and keep the pledges they make. The verse then joins the worship of the body and the duty of the purse and the keeping of a promise, and the sources bring out that the pledge is named after the prayer and the alms because it is the part of the religion that is tested in ordinary dealings. and who are patient in times of suffering, adversity, and in the heat of battle. The last quality is patience, and the sources explain the three places of it as the trials that come to the body in sickness and want, and the moment when the fighting is at its hottest, so the list ends with what keeps all the rest in place. It is they who are true in faith, and it is they who are mindful of Allah. The sources also read the list as the whole religion gathered in one place, since it keeps the beliefs of the heart and the duties of worship and the dealings with people, and they notice that what follows the verse takes up these matters in detail, so the whole is given first and the parts come after. The sources carry the account of those who took the turning as the whole of the religion and let go of the faith and the dealings, and the verse is given here to set the outward act back in its place under the whole. The verse closes by naming the people it has described, and the sources read the closing words as the sum of everything above, so the reader is shown that righteousness is not a direction a person turns to but a life that he lives.

**What the turning towards the east and the west means.**

This was revealed in response to the claim made by the Jews and the Christians to this effect. Facing the east or the west does not necessitate righteousness or obedience, unless it is legislated by Allah. Abu Al-'Aliyah said, "The Jews used to face the west for their Qiblah, while the Christians used to face the east for their Qiblah. (It is not Birr that you turn your faces towards east and west (in prayers)(2: 177) meaning, "this is faith, and its essence requires implementation. In itself, the East or the West, or any other direction or orientation has no importance or merit. (It is not righteousness) it is not all of righteousness; it is also said that (It is not righteousness) means: it is not faith (that ye merely turn your faces) in prayer (to the East) towards Makkah (and the West) towards Bayt al-Maqdis; (but righteous is) but faith amounts to agreeing with (he who believeth in Allah) and it is also said: the faithful is he who believes in Allah (and the Last Day) in resurrection after death (and the angels) all the angels (and the Scripture) all the revealed Books (and the prophets) and all the prophets; Allah then mentions the obligated duties after mentioning faith, saying: Doing good that pleases Allah does not just mean turning towards the east or the west or disputing about that. There is no doubt that there are certain accepted forms of religious conduct but, in essence, a religious act is aimed at discovering God as the light of the earth and the heavens, One who is closer to man than his jugular vein. What brings man closer to God is not the mere adherence to outward religious forms but such actions as he performs, in total sincerity, for the sake of God alone.

**What belief in Allah, the angels, the Books and the prophets is.**

Believing in God is to trust in God in the full sense of the word. Believing in the Hereafter means giving the utmost importance to the life of the Hereafter instead of to the life of this world. Believing in the angels means believing in God’s emissaries who are running this world at the divine command. Believing in the Book means believing that God has sent His guidance for man, which man must follow. Believing in the prophets is to accept these mortals as God’s chosen messengers. (but Birr is the one who believes in Allah,) and said that what follows are the types of Birr. The 'Books' are the Divinely revealed Books from Allah to the Prophets, which were finalized by the most honorable Book (the Qur'an). The Qur'an supercedes all previous Books, it mentions all types of righteousness, and the way to happiness in this life and the Hereafter. So, when the verse begins, basic principles such as belief in the Book, spending of wealth in charity, fulfillment of promises and patience in distress have been stressed upon which, incidentally, include the basic principles behind all injunctions of the Holy Qur'an. Then, the affirmation of Allah's Oneness was rightfully followed by a refutation of the principles and subsidiaries of Shirk the act of associating others with Allah. Rather, piety is he who has faith in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets; who gives wealth despite lov ing it to kinsfolk, orphans, the indigent, the son of the road, beggars, and slaves; and who per forms the prayer and gives the alms tax; those who are loyal to their covenant when they make a covenant; those who are patient in misfortune, hardship, and moments of peril. Rather, it is having faith in Allah as the only God, the Day of Judgement, all of the angels, all of the revealed scriptures and all of the prophets, without distinguishing between them; charitable spending, despite loving and valuing wealth, to relatives, orphans, the poor, the stranger who is cut off from his family and homeland because of a journey, and whoever has a need that makes it necessary for them to ask people for help; giving money to free slaves from captivity; establishing the prayer as Allah instructed; giving Zakat; being true to promises; and patience in poverty, hardship, illness and in times of conflict without fleeing.

**What the giving of cherished wealth includes.**

(...and gives his wealth, in spite of love for it,) refers to those who give money away while desiring it and loving it. The second possibility is that this pronoun refers to wealth, in which case, it would mean that, while spending in the way of Allah, only that part of one's wealth and possessions which one loves will be deserving of merit. While mentioning these injunctions, the verse has given a number of subtle but eloquent indications, for instance, the spending of wealth has been tied up with: ala hubbihi which has three possible meanings. Firstly, the pronoun in 'hubbihi ' may refer to Allah Almighty, in which case, it would mean that in spending wealth one should not be guided by material motives or the desire to show off. Such spending should rather be done out of love for Allah Almighty, whose exalted majesty requires that this be done with perfectly un-alloyed sincerity (in the sense of the genuine ikhlas of Arabic and not in the sense of some modern casual nicety). Giving out throw-aways in the name of charity is no charity, barring the option of giving it to somebody who can use it, which is better than simply throwing things away. (the kinsfolk) refers to man's relatives, who have more rights than anyone else to one's charity, as the Hadith supports: (to the orphans) The orphans are children who have none to look after them, having lost their fathers while they are still young, weak and unable to find their own sustenance since they have not reached the age of work and adolescence. 'Abdur-Razzaq reported that 'Ali said that the Prophet said: (and to Al-Masakin) The Miskin is the person who does not have enough food, clothing, or he has no dwelling. (and to the wayfarer) is the needy traveler who runs out of money and should, thus, be granted whatever amount that helps him to go back to his land. (and to those who ask) refers to those who beg people and are thus given a part of the Zakah and general charity. (and to set servants free) These are the servants who seek to free themselves, but cannot find enough money to buy their freedom. (By no means shall you attain Birr unless you spend of that which you love.)(3:92) Allah's statement: (and giveth his wealth for love of Him) righteousness after declaring one's faith is that one gives of one's wealth, despite the fact that one loves and desires it and has only a little of it, (to kinsfolk) relatives (and to orphans) orphans of the believers (and the needy) who shy away from asking for assistance (and the wayfarer) the passer-by, the guest (and to those who ask) you to give them from your wealth, (and to set slaves free) those who made a contract to pay for their freedom and those who fight in the way of Allah.

**What the worship and the promise come to.**

Allah's worship is mentioned upto the end of : "And pays the Zakah ", then, dealings with people were covered under : "And those who fulfill their promise'', concluding with the mention of morals under ‌ "The patient". The reason why the keeping of promises has been chosen to represent dealings with people is simple. A little thought would show that staying by a contract entered into or the fulfilling of a promise made, is the essence of all dealings, such as buying and selling, leasing, renting and partnership. (performs As-Salah (Iqamat-As-Salah) means those who pray on time and give the prayer its due right; the bowing, prostration, and the necessary attention and humbleness required by Allah. (and gives the Zakah) means the required charity (Zakah) due on one's money, as Sa'id bin Jubayr and Muqatil bin Hayyan have stated. (and who fulfill their covenant when they make it,) (Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah and break not the Mithaq (bond, treaty, covenant).)(13:20) The opposite of this characteristic is hypocrisy. (and observeth proper worship) He says: righteousness, after fulfilling the obligated duties, is to perfect the performance of the five daily prayers (and payeth the poor-due) give the poor what is due to them as well as similar things. (And those who keep their treaty) those who fulfil the pledges that are between them and their Lord or between them and other people (when they make one, and the patient in tribulation) i.e. fear, affliction and hardship (and adversity) illness, pain and hunger (and time of stress) upon engagement in fighting. They keep it flourishing with service and worship.

**What patience in suffering and battle is.**

Similarly, while referring to the moral principles or the inner deeds, only sabr (patience) is mentioned in the verse, because sabr means to control the human self and guard it against evil. Even a little reflection can lead to the conclusion that sabr is the very essence of all inner deeds; through it, high morals can be achieved and through it, low morals can be eliminated. Yet another change in style made here concerns the use of the word, ‌ and not ‌ on the pattern of which appeared immediately earlier. This means that among the righteous, the sabirin ‌ (the patient) are worthy of special praise since sabr gives one special power to perform righteous deeds. (...and who are patient in extreme poverty and ailment (disease) and at the time of fighting (during the battles).) means, during the time of meekness and ailment. (...and at the time of fighting (during the battles).) means on the battlefield while facing the enemy, as Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Murrah Al-Hamdani, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, As-Suddi, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak and others have stated. And calling them the patient here, is a form of praise, because of the importance of patience in these circumstances, and the suffering and difficulties that accompany them. His trust in God is so great, even in the most dire of circumstances, that he always adheres to the godly path.

**What the true in faith and the mindful are.**

(Such are the people of the truth) means, whoever acquires these qualities, these are truthful in their faith. This is because they have achieved faith in the heart and realized it in deed and upon the tongue. (and they are Al-Muttaqun (the pious).) because they avoided the prohibitions and performed the acts of obedience. The faith in all these matters must so deeply pervade the believer’s psyche that he helps the needy and others in distress by spending his wealth, says his prayers by surrendering himself totally to God, and pays the poor due—his only motivation being to earn God’s pleasure. These are the characteristics of a true believer. One who possesses these qualities will earn God’s blessing in this world as well as in the Hereafter. They are the Mindful who follow what Allah has instructed them to do, and who stay away from what Allah has prohibited. It is they who have been truthful, and it is they who are the godwary. (Such are they who are sincere) who have fulfilled their pledges. (And such are the God fearing) who refrain from breaking their pledges.

178.text:
O believers! The law of retaliation is set for you in cases of murder, a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. The verse opens the long account of dealings by naming the gravest of them first, and the sources explain the law of equality as the limit that ends the feud, since the family of the killed may take the life of the killer and no more than that. They carry the occasion in detail, that two clans had fallen into a quarrel in which the strong demanded the blood of a commoner for a noble and of a woman for a man, and that this verse struck down the claim and set the equal for the equal, so the rule answered a pride that weighed lives by rank. But if the offender is pardoned by the victim's guardian, then blood-money should be decided fairly and payment should be made courteously. The verse then opens the better road, and the sources read the two halves of the sentence as duties laid on both sides, the one who pardons to ask for what is fair and the one who owes to hand it over without delay or harshness, so the mercy is not turned into a new injury. This is a concession and a mercy from your Lord. The sources take these words as the reason the pardon was placed in the law at all, since the family is not forced to kill and the killer is given a way to live. But whoever transgresses after that will suffer a painful punishment. The verse closes with the warning that a settlement is not a licence, and the sources keep the two together, the door opened to pardon and the punishment waiting for the one who crosses the limit once the door has been used. The sources carry the account of the two tribes at length, that the stronger of them would take the life of a man of the weaker for the life of a slave, and the life of a noble for the life of a woman, and that the quarrel had run long before the law came down and closed it. They also explain that the rule of the equal is not a call to kill, since the pardon is left open and the money is named beside it, and they bring out that the pardon may not be turned into a new wrong and that the payment may not be turned into a delay. The sources also notice that the verse places the two rules in one breath so that the family of the killed is given a choice and the killer is given a way out, and they read the closing warning as the guard that keeps the mercy from becoming a trade. The reader is left with a law that keeps the equal and the pardon in one hand, so that justice is kept and revenge is not.

**What the law of retaliation is.**

O you who believe prescribed made obligatory for you is retaliation on equal terms regarding the slain both in the attributes of the one slain and in the action involved; a free man is killed for a free man and not for a slave; and a slave for a slave and a female for a female. In Islamic juristic terminology, Qisas means the equal retaliation of an aggression committed against the body of a person. Therefore, as a term of the Shari'ah, the Qisas is a punishment for killing or wounding in which the principle of equality or likeness is taken into full consideration. Al-Qisas (the Law of equality) is prescribed for you in case of murder: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. The Command and the Wisdom behind the Law of Equality. Islam has laid down the principle of retaliation in like measure (qisas). Retribution for a killer means the forfeiture of his own life. Thus the objective of qisas is the protection of the members of society, and not revenge. (O ye who believe! Retaliation is prescribed for you in the matter of the murdered ones; the freeman for the freeman) a freeman who premeditatedly kills another freeman, (and the slave for the slave) a slave who premeditatedly kills another, (and the female for the female) a female who premeditatedly kills another. O you who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger, it is decreed for you that in cases where someone deliberately attacks and kills someone, the punishment for the murderer should be the same as their crime: the freeman killed for the freeman; the slave for the slave; and the female for the female. Written for you is retaliation in the case of the slain.

**What the occasion of the two tribes carries.**

One of the tribes which was more powerful insisted that they would not agree to anything less than that a free man for their slave and a man for their woman be killed from the other side. On the authority of Ibn Abi Hatim 1, Ibn Kathir has reported that, just before the advent of Islam, war broke out between two tribes. Now that they were Muslims, they started talking about retaliation for those killed on each side. It was to refute this barbaric demand on their part that this verse was revealed. The just law that Islam enforced was that the killer is the one who has to be killed in Qisas . The reason behind this statement is that (the Jewish tribe of) Banu An-Nadir invaded Qurayzah (another Jewish tribe) during the time of Jahiliyyah (before Islam) and defeated them. This verse was revealed regarding two Arab clans but is abrogated by the verse:

**What the free man for a free man means.**

The mention of 'free man for a free man' and 'female for a female' in this verse refers to a specific event in the background of which it was revealed. By saying 'free man for a free man, slave for a slave and female for a female' it is intended to negate their absurd demand that a free man for a slave and man for a woman should be killed in retaliation, even though he may not be the killer. If a woman is the killer why should an innocent man be killed in retaliation? Similarly, if the killer is a slave, there is no sense in retaliating against an innocent free man. It is not permissible to kill an innocent man or someone free for a killer, woman or slave. Let us hasten to clarify that the verse does not mean that Qisas will not be taken from a man who kills a woman or from a free man who kills a slave.

**What the pardon and the blood-money come to.**

If the aggrieved party somewhat relents on its own and forgives the Qisas but does not forgive the offence totally, it will become necessary for the killer to pay diyah or blood-money as fixed, in a fair manner, and promptly. This law of blood-money and pardon is a relief granted by Allah Almighty in His grace, otherwise, there would have been no choice but to face the punishment of death. In case the pardon is not that full, for instance, as illustrated above, one of the two surviving sons does pardon the killer while the other does not, the result will be that the killer will stand released right there from the retaliatory punishment, but the one who has not pardoned the killer will be entitled to half of the blood-money (diyah). The way an incomplete pardon makes payment of blood-money necessary, in the same manner, a mutual settlement between parties concerned on a certain amount makes retaliation inapplicable and payment of the agreed amount becomes necessary. Under the Islamic law, the inheritors of the person killed, whatever their number, will inherit and own the right of retaliation and blood-money in accordance with their share in the inheritance. If blood-money is taken, it will be distributed among the inheritors in accordance with their share in the inheritance. But if anything of the blood is pardoned any one of those who have slain in relation to his brother the one slain so that the retaliation is waived the use of the indefinite shay’un ‘anything’ here implies the waiving of retaliation through a partial pardon by the inheritors of the slain; the mention of akhīh ‘his brother’ is intended as a conciliatory entreaty to pardon and a declaration that killing should not sever the bonds of religious brotherhood; the particle man ‘any one’ is the subject of a conditional or a relative clause of which the predicate is the following fa’ittibā‘un let the pursuing that is the action of the one who has pardoned in pursuing the killer be honourable demanding the blood money without force. And let the payment of the blood money by the slayer to him the pardoner that is the one inheriting from the slain be with kindliness without procrastination or fraud; that stipulation mentioned here about the possibility of retaliation and the forgoing of this in return for blood money is an alleviation a facilitation given to you by your Lord and a mercy for you for He has given you latitude in this matter and has not categorically demanded that one of the said options be followed through in the way that He made it obligatory for Jews to retaliate and for Christians to pardon and accept blood money; and for him who commits aggression by being unjust towards the killer and slaying him after that that is after pardoning — his is a painful chastisement of the Fire in the Hereafter or of being killed in this world. But if the killer is forgiven by the brother (or the relatives) of the killed (against blood money), then it should be sought in a good manner, and paid to him respectfully. (And for him who is forgiven somewhat by his brother) whoever forgives the killing and takes instead blood money, (prosecution according to usage) Allah commands the person who asks for blood money to claim this money according to practised usage: three years if it is a full blood money, two years if it is half of the blood money, or one year if it is a third (and payment unto him) the person who is required to pay blood money is commanded to give the custodians of the murdered person what is due to them (in kindness) without the need to go to court or making it difficult for them. (This) this pardon (is an alleviation) appeasement (and a mercy from your Lord) towards the killer such that he is not killed. If the person killed had forgiven before his death, or his guardian has forgiven in return for the payment of blood money (a sum of money paid by the murderer in return for being pardoned), then the person who forgives should ask for the sum of money fairly, and not follow that up with insult or injury, and the murderer should pay the sum of money in a good way, without hesitation or delay. In allowing this forgiveness and the payment of the blood money your Lord makes things easier for you, and this is a mercy for the Muslim nation. However, qisas in Islam permits a settlement to be arrived at between the killer and the killed. Then the principle of blood-money has the special advantage of giving the bereaved family monetary compensation for the death of one of its members.

**What the limit set by Allah carries.**

If, after all that, anyone crosses the limit set by Allah, such as, the filing of a false or doubtful case of murder, or a post-pardon re-opening of a murder case, he will be severely punished. In the end, the verse points out that wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life, instead, it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing somebody and thus lives will be saved. So after this, whoever transgresses the limits (i.e. kills the killer after taking the blood money), he shall have a painful torment And there is (a saving of) life for you in Al-Qisas (the Law of equality in punishment), O men of understanding, that you may acquire Taqwa. Therefore, do not transgress the set limits, as others before you transgressed them, and thus changed what Allah has ordained for them. (He who transgresseth after this) after taking the blood money and kills the murderer (will have a painful doom) he shall be killed and will not be forgiven or allowed to pay blood money. The main aim of these alternatives is to guarantee the prevalence of brotherly feeling in Islamic society, and to prevent an atmosphere of rivalry taking root.

**What the heirs of the killed may choose.**

And should Qisas (even retaliation) become the choice, the right of Qisas will also be commonly shared by all. Since Qisas is indivisible, the pardon given by any one of the inheritors will hold good and the pardon will become inclusive of the right of retaliation held by other inheritors. It is true that the right of even retaliation is vested in the legal heirs of the persons killed but, in accordance with the consensus of the Muslim community, they do not have the right to settle the score all by themselves, in other words, they cannot kill the killer on their own, instead, they have to seek the help of a Muslim ruler or his deputy to realize their right. Therefore, the legal heirs of the person killed, not knowing the particular circumstances when retaliation does, or does not become necessary, may commit some sort of excess under the heat of their anger. So, by a unanimous agreement of the scholars of the Muslim community, it is necessary that the right of retaliation be secured and made effective through the agency of an Islamic government. The heirs of the deceased person may, of course, opt for the execution of the killer, but they may also, if they so wish, accept blood-money instead, or even forgive him. Whenever someone is killed in the world, retaliation or wergild is mandatory against the killer. In the shariah of friendship, both retaliation and wergild are mandatory for the person killed.

179.text:
There is security of life for you in the law of retaliation, O people of reason, so that you may become mindful of Allah. The verse states the purpose of the law set out in the two verses before it, and the sources read the two words together, that the taking of the killer's life is what keeps the rest alive, since the one who means to take a life knows that his own is answerable for it. They carry the sense that the law is not a licence for revenge but a wall around the lives of the people, and they notice that the verse is addressed to people of reason, since only a mind that weighs ends can see that the restraint of the hand begins in the certainty of the answer. The sources also bring out that the pardon and the money are part of the same order, so the safety of the people is kept both by the equal and by the settlement, and that the one who is mindful of Allah keeps the law because he knows who set it and not because he fears the strength of the family of the killed. They notice too that the verse closes the account of the retaliation and stands at the head of the long passage of dealings that follows, and they take the life named here as the life of the community rather than the life of the killer alone. The reader is left with the measure that a law which preserves life is a mercy, and that being mindful of Allah is the reason a person keeps it when no one is watching.

**What the life in retaliation is.**

In retaliation there is life for you that is great longevity O people of pith possessors of intellect because if the would-be killer knew that he would be killed in retaliation he would refrain from such action and would have thereby given life to himself and to the one whom he had intended to kill; and so it retaliation was stipulated by the Law so that you might fear killing fearing retaliation. This law of blood-money and pardon is a relief granted by Allah Almighty in His grace, otherwise, there would have been no choice but to face the punishment of death. In the end, the verse points out that wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life, instead, it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing somebody and thus lives will be saved. In this way, on the one hand, a capital crime like the taking of life is effectively discouraged, for the fear of losing one’s own life deters one from taking another’s life and, as a result, the life of all the members of a society become protected. Thus the objective of qisas is the protection of the members of society, and not revenge. (And there is a life for you in retaliation) a continuation of existence and a lesson, (O men of understanding) those who possess sound minds among people, (that ye may ward off (evil) that you may ward off killing one another for fear of retaliation. In the law of equivalent punishment decreed by Allah there is life for you, because it spares your blood, stopping further attacks between you. Al-Qisas (the Law of equality) is prescribed for you in case of murder: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female.

**What the people of reason are told.**

In the end, the verse points out that wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life, instead, it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing somebody and thus lives will be saved. (And there is a life for you in retaliation) a continuation of existence and a lesson, (O men of understanding) those who possess sound minds among people, (that ye may ward off (evil) that you may ward off killing one another for fear of retaliation. Those with sense understand this: who are mindful of Allah, keeping to His sacred law and doing as He instructs. Al-Qisas (the Law of equality) is prescribed for you in case of murder: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. Under the first injunction in this connection, the verse prescribes the law of Qisas (even retaliation), that is, the killer will be killed, irrespective of the status of the parties involved.

**What the understanding of the law comes to.**

Those with sense understand this: who are mindful of Allah, keeping to His sacred law and doing as He instructs. In the end, the verse points out that wise people should have no difficulty in seeing that the law of even retaliation does not take life, instead, it gives life, for such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing somebody and thus lives will be saved. Thus the objective of qisas is the protection of the members of society, and not revenge. The main aim of these alternatives is to guarantee the prevalence of brotherly feeling in Islamic society, and to prevent an atmosphere of rivalry taking root. (And there is a life for you in retaliation) a continuation of existence and a lesson, (O men of understanding) those who possess sound minds among people, (that ye may ward off (evil) that you may ward off killing one another for fear of retaliation. So after this, whoever transgresses the limits (i.e. kills the killer after taking the blood money), he shall have a painful torment And there is (a saving of) life for you in Al-Qisas (the Law of equality in punishment), O men of understanding, that you may acquire Taqwa.

**What the life kept by the law is.**

In this way, on the one hand, a capital crime like the taking of life is effectively discouraged, for the fear of losing one’s own life deters one from taking another’s life and, as a result, the life of all the members of a society become protected. The killing of the killer guarantees the saving of lives in a society. Thus the objective of qisas is the protection of the members of society, and not revenge. The main aim of these alternatives is to guarantee the prevalence of brotherly feeling in Islamic society, and to prevent an atmosphere of rivalry taking root. In carrying out the retaliation there is life because when one knows that if he kills he will himself be killed he refrains from killing. In this there is life for the one who kills and the one who is killed.

180.text:
It is prescribed that when death approaches any of you, if they leave something of value, a will should be made in favour of parents and immediate family with fairness. The verse lays a duty on the one who is about to leave the world, and the sources explain the will as the order a person gives about what he leaves behind, so the matter is settled while he can still speak and is not left to those who come after him to quarrel over. The value named in the verse is explained by the sources as wealth, and they take the condition as a sign that the duty falls on the one who has something to leave, so the person who owns nothing is not asked for what he does not have. The will is then directed to parents and to the nearest family, and the sources notice the order, the father and the mother first and then the kin, since the nearer a person is the greater his claim on what the dead man leaves. The fairness named in the verse is read by the sources as a limit as well as a command, and they bring out that no more than a third of the estate may be given away, so that the heirs are not left in want while the giver tries to buy a name for himself. This is an obligation on those who are mindful of Allah. The sources take the closing words as the mark of the people the duty is meant for, and they explain the mindful as the one who orders his affairs before he is asked to, because he knows that the account is real. They also carry what followed the verse, that the shares of the heirs were afterwards fixed by Allah Himself, and that the will in favour of those who already have a share was set aside, while the will for the relatives who have no share and for the causes a person carried in his life remains, and the sources dwell on the change because a duty that once fell on the dying man was taken over by the law he was given. The reader is left with a verse that teaches a person to put his house in order while he still has breath, and that measures the gift by the fairness of it rather than by its size.

**What the will and the making of it come to.**

Literally, al-wasiyyah means an order to do something, either in the lifetime of the maker of wasiyyah or after his death. But, in commonly accepted usage, it refers to what must be done after death. The making of a will made obligatory for one who is leaving behind some wealth has three aspects: Making a will for such relatives is obligatory on the dying person. Now the second injunction regarding the obligation of making a will also stands abrogated in accordance with the consensus of the Muslim ummah. As stated earlier, now making a will is not necessary to cover relatives whose shares have been fixed by the Holy Qur'an. In this verse a particular will was mentioned which was to be made by a dying person about what he left behind. It is recommended that the remaining relatives who do not have a designated fixed share of the inheritance, be willed up to a third, due to the general meaning of the Ayah about the will. The testament of the lords of wealth is one thing, and the testament of the lords of states is some thing else. The testament of the lords of wealth goes out from the wealth, and the testament of the poor men from the states.

**What the wealth left behind is.**

Out of the many meanings the word khayr has in Arabic, 'wealth' happens to be one of them, for instance, in the verse ‌ (Surely he is passionate in his love for good things) where, according to the unanimous agreement of commentators, 'khayr' means 'wealth'. But, in commonly accepted usage, it refers to what must be done after death. (...if he leaves wealth, that he makes a bequest to parents and next of kin.) It has been decreed for you that if one of you is about to die, and they are leaving a large amount of wealth behind, then they should make a will for their parents and close relatives, according to the sacred laws, not exceeding one third of the wealth (the rest of the wealth being distributed according to the laws of inheritance). (It is prescribed for you, when death approacheth one of you, if he leave wealth, that he bequeath unto parents and near relatives) kinsfolk (in kindness) more so and even better to the parents. The testament of the lords of wealth goes out from the wealth, and the testament of the poor men from the states.

**What the parents and the family are given.**

It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you, if he leaves wealth, that he makes a bequest to parents and next of kin, according to reasonable manners. For men there is a share in what the parents and the nearest. of kin have left, and for women there is a share in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left, be it is small or large - a determined share. It should, however, be borne in mind that according to the consensus of the Muslim Ummah it is not obligatory on the dying person to necessarily make a will in favour of relatives who have no fixed shares in the inheritance. Therefore, the obligatory character of a wasiyyah in their favour is also abrogated (Jassas, Qurtubi). It has been decreed for you that if one of you is about to die, and they are leaving a large amount of wealth behind, then they should make a will for their parents and close relatives, according to the sacred laws, not exceeding one third of the wealth (the rest of the wealth being distributed according to the laws of inheritance). (It is prescribed for you, when death approacheth one of you, if he leave wealth, that he bequeath unto parents and near relatives) kinsfolk (in kindness) more so and even better to the parents. This Ayah contains the command to include parents and relatives in the will, which was obligatory, according to the most correct view, before the Ayah about inheritance was revealed.

**What the limit of the third is.**

Making a will for more than one third of the inheritance is not permissible. However, should the inheritors allow the bequest of more than one third, even the whole of what one leaves behind, it shall be permissible. As for the right to make a will covering the one-third of his property, one has the right to make some change in this will or cancel it totally during his life time. " He said, "Yes, one-third, yet even one-third is too much. (One-third, yet even one-third is too much.)" At the end of their lives, the rich give out one-third of their wealth,13 and the poor give out limpidness of states and truthfulness of deeds. It was abrogated by that famous hadith (al-hadith al-mutawatir : the veracity of which stands ensured through an uninterrupted chain of transmitters from many sides who are unlikely to agree on a lie) which was part of the sermon delivered before some one hundred and fifty thousand Companions on the occasion of his last Hajj when he said:

**What the shares that were fixed afterwards were.**

(Allah has given each heir his fixed share. So there is no will for a deserving heir.) Therefore, deserving inheritors take their fixed inheritance without the need to be included in the will or to be reminded of the favor of the inherited person. For men there is a share in what the parents and the nearest. of kin have left, and for women there is a share in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left, be it is small or large - a determined share. When the verses about inheritance were revealed it was made clear who should inherit from the person who has died and how much they should inherit. When the Ayah of inheritance was revealed, this Ayah was abrogated, so fixed shares of the inheritance for deserving recipients were legislated by Allah. Out of these three injunctions, the first one was abrogated by the 'verse of inheritance' as determined by most of the Companions and their immediate successors.

**What the change of a will after it is heard means.**

(Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, whoever changed the will and testament or altered it by addition or deletion, including hiding the will as is obvious, then. (the sin shall be on those who make the change.) But unless this is the objective, the changing of the provisions of a will is unlawful. Islam approves of every lawful device for keeping society free from litigation and quarrels. In fact, this is not permissible without the permission of other inheritors. (Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, Allah knows what the dead person has bequeathed and what the beneficiaries (or others) have changed in the will.

181.text:
But whoever changes the will after hearing it, the blame will only be on those who made the change. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. The verse guards the will that has just been ordered, and the sources explain the change as adding to the bequest or taking from it, so the sin is laid on the hand that alters and not on the one who left the order behind him. The sources notice the words after hearing it, since a person who changes a will he has heard is a witness who turns against what he witnessed, while the one who never heard it is not named. The blame is then fastened to the changer alone, and the sources bring out that the dead man carries nothing of it, since his reward for what he ordered is not cut off by another hand. Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. The two names at the end are read by the sources as the reason the warning is not empty, since the words of the dying and the change made after them are both heard and both known, and the verse closes the account of the will with a warning that fits the offence, since the one who alters an order takes what a family was given and thinks that no one has seen. The reader is left with the duty of care toward what the dead have asked for, and with the knowledge that the hand which changes is the hand the sin rests on.

**What the change of the will is.**

Then if anyone whether a witness or a trustee changes it that is the testament after hearing it and knowing it the sin resulting from the changed testament shall rest upon those who change it here the explicit subject stands in place of the implicit one; surely God is Hearing of the testator’s words Knowing of the deeds of the trustee requiting each accordingly. (Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. (the sin shall be on those who make the change.) Whoever then changes the will, adding to it or taking away from it or stopping something when they know what the will contains, the sin of it will be upon those who changed it, and the person who wrote the will is not held responsible for what they did. Then if anyone changes it after hearing it the sin shall rest upon those who change it; surely God is Hearing Knowing. But unless this is the objective, the changing of the provisions of a will is unlawful.

**What the hearing of the will means.**

(Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, whoever changed the will and testament or altered it by addition or deletion, including hiding the will as is obvious, then. Then if anyone changes it after hearing it the sin shall rest upon those who change it; surely God is Hearing Knowing. (For Allah is Hearer) of the will and words of the deceased, (Knower) if he transgresses or changes it; it is also said that this means: Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower But he who fears from a testator some unjust act or wrongdoing, and thereupon he makes peace between the parties concerned, there shall be no sin on him.

**What those who change the will answer for.**

Whoever then changes the will, adding to it or taking away from it or stopping something when they know what the will contains, the sin of it will be upon those who changed it, and the person who wrote the will is not held responsible for what they did. (And whoso changeth) the will of the deceased person (after he hath heard it-the sin thereof) the onus thereof (is only upon those who change it) and the deceased bears no responsibility. (Then whoever changes it after hearing it, the sin shall be on those who make the change. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, whoever changed the will and testament or altered it by addition or deletion, including hiding the will as is obvious, then. Ibn 'Abbas and others said, "The dead person's reward will be preserved for him by Allah, while the sin is acquired by those who change the will." Then if anyone whether a witness or a trustee changes it that is the testament after hearing it and knowing it the sin resulting from the changed testament shall rest upon those who change it here the explicit subject stands in place of the implicit one; surely God is Hearing of the testator’s words Knowing of the deeds of the trustee requiting each accordingly.

**What Allah hearing and knowing means.**

(For Allah is Hearer) of the will and words of the deceased, (Knower) if he transgresses or changes it; it is also said that this means: (Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.) means, Allah knows what the dead person has bequeathed and what the beneficiaries (or others) have changed in the will. Allah hears all that His creation say, and knows all that they do; and He knows every detail of the situations they are in. Truly, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower But he who fears from a testator some unjust act or wrongdoing, and thereupon he makes peace between the parties concerned, there shall be no sin on him. I heard Allah's Messenger saying in a speech:

182.text:
Whoever suspects an error or an injustice in the will and brings about a fair settlement among the parties will not be sinful. The verse follows the warning given to the one who changes a will, and it opens the way for the person who changes it in order to put a wrong right, so the sources read the two verses together and explain that the change which is forgiven is the one that repairs and not the one that robs. They carry the account of the errors a dying man may fall into, a gift left to a stranger while the family goes without, or a share given to one who has quietly taken more than his due, and they explain that the one who knows of such a thing and brings the parties to agreement has done the work the law asks for. The settlement is named as fair, and the sources take the word as the measure, so the one who stands between them is not free to invent a division but is bound to the share that the law would have given, and the sources notice that the repair is not counted as the alteration which was condemned, since the verse singles out this case by name. Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The closing words are read by the sources as the mercy that covers both the error of the dying man and the work of the one who sets it right, and the verse ends the passage on the will with the door of repair left open. The sources also bring out that the fairness named in the verse is the measure, since the settlement they describe returns the shares to what the law has set, and the one who works it is described as rewarded and not as one who has done wrong. The reader is left with the measure that a wrong in a will is not to be passed over in silence and not to be corrected by taking, but to be settled with the agreement of the people concerned.

**What the error and the injustice in a will are.**

But if any one fears injustice an error in straying from what is right or sin because he has purposely increased the share of a third or specified a rich individual from one making testament read mūsī or muwassī and so makes things right between them the testator and the trustee by commanding that justice be done then no sin shall be upon him with regard to this matter; surely God is Forgiving Merciful. (But he who fears from a testator some unjust act or wrongdoing,) Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and As-Suddi said, "Error. " These errors include such cases as when the inheritor indirectly acquires more than his fair share, such as by being allocated that a certain item mentioned in the legacy be sold to him. Such errors might occur out of the kindness of the heart without thinking about the consequences of these actions, or by sinful intention. Whoever knows that there is an error in judgement from the person who made the will, or that there is some injustice in it, and advises the person and rectifies the wrong, and reconciles between those who are in disagreement about it, then there is no blame on them; rather they are rewarded for putting things right. But if anyone fears injustice or sin from one making a testament and so makes things right between them then no sin shall be upon him; surely God is Forgiving Merciful.

**What putting right the wrong in a will is.**

Whoever knows that there is an error in judgement from the person who made the will, or that there is some injustice in it, and advises the person and rectifies the wrong, and reconciles between those who are in disagreement about it, then there is no blame on them; rather they are rewarded for putting things right. But if any one fears injustice an error in straying from what is right or sin because he has purposely increased the share of a third or specified a rich individual from one making testament read mūsī or muwassī and so makes things right between them the testator and the trustee by commanding that justice be done then no sin shall be upon him with regard to this matter; surely God is Forgiving Merciful. But if anyone fears injustice or sin from one making a testament and so makes things right between them then no sin shall be upon him; surely God is Forgiving Merciful. (But he who feareth from a testator) knows that the testator has committed (some unjust or sinful clause) purposefully committed a mistake or transgression (and maketh peace between the parties) between the inheritors and the testator, i.e. he corrects what is in the will by reducing any bequest to a maximum of a third of the wealth, (no sin for him) he bears no sin in doing so. In such cases, the executive of the will and testament is allowed to correct the errors and to replace the unjust items in the will with a better solution, so that both the Islamic law and what the dead person had wished for are respected and observed.

**What the errors a testator may fall into are.**

" These errors include such cases as when the inheritor indirectly acquires more than his fair share, such as by being allocated that a certain item mentioned in the legacy be sold to him. Or, the testator might include his daughter's son in the legacy to increase his daughter's share in the inheritance, and so forth. Such errors might occur out of the kindness of the heart without thinking about the consequences of these actions, or by sinful intention. (But he who feareth from a testator) knows that the testator has committed (some unjust or sinful clause) purposefully committed a mistake or transgression (and maketh peace between the parties) between the inheritors and the testator, i.e. he corrects what is in the will by reducing any bequest to a maximum of a third of the wealth, (no sin for him) he bears no sin in doing so. Whoever knows that there is an error in judgement from the person who made the will, or that there is some injustice in it, and advises the person and rectifies the wrong, and reconciles between those who are in disagreement about it, then there is no blame on them; rather they are rewarded for putting things right. Where there is a member of a family, like an orphaned grandson, or any other needy member of the family who does not inherit under the Islamic inheritance scheme, the testator may provide for him, as he has been given the power to dispose of up to one third of his property by making a will in his favour. But, making a will is still necessary, specially for a person who owes to others or holds something in trust. However, relatives who do not hold a legal share in the inheritance can be bequeathed upto one third of the total. The third injunction stills holds good with the unanimous approval of the Muslim ummah in which it is not permissible to bequeath more than one-third of what one leaves behind.

**What the correction of the will means.**

In such cases, the executive of the will and testament is allowed to correct the errors and to replace the unjust items in the will with a better solution, so that both the Islamic law and what the dead person had wished for are respected and observed. This act would not constitute an alteration in the will and this is why Allah mentioned it specifically, so that it is excluded from the prohibition (that prohibits altering the will and testament) mentioned in the previous Ayah. (But he who feareth from a testator) knows that the testator has committed (some unjust or sinful clause) purposefully committed a mistake or transgression (and maketh peace between the parties) between the inheritors and the testator, i.e. he corrects what is in the will by reducing any bequest to a maximum of a third of the wealth, (no sin for him) he bears no sin in doing so. He forgives the testator, and He is also merciful because He gave dispensation to reduce bequests to a third and thus commanded that one adhere to fairness. Whoever knows that there is an error in judgement from the person who made the will, or that there is some injustice in it, and advises the person and rectifies the wrong, and reconciles between those who are in disagreement about it, then there is no blame on them; rather they are rewarded for putting things right. But unless this is the objective, the changing of the provisions of a will is unlawful.

**What the forgiving and merciful close carries.**

(Lo! Allah is Forgiving) He forgives the deceased if he transgresses or makes a mistake, (Merciful) in relation to the deed of the testator; it is also said that this means: He forgives the testator, and He is also merciful because He gave dispensation to reduce bequests to a third and thus commanded that one adhere to fairness. Allah is Forgiving towards whomever of His servants repents to Him, and is Compassionate with them. But if anyone fears injustice or sin from one making a testament and so makes things right between them then no sin shall be upon him; surely God is Forgiving Merciful.

183.text:
O believers! Fasting is prescribed for you, as it was for those before you, so perhaps you will become mindful of Allah. The verse opens the long passage on the fast, and the sources explain the word as abstaining from what the body wants for a set time, so the act is a leaving rather than a doing. They notice that the command is given to the believers by name and that it is joined to what was given to the communities before, so the fast is not a new burden invented for this people but an old road, and the sources carry the comfort that a duty shared with those who came earlier is lighter to bear.
