236.text:
The verse takes a marriage that has been contracted and not entered, and gives the ruling on ending it. "There is no blame if you divorce women before the marriage is consummated or the dowry is settled" is the permission, and it is built on two conditions, the touching and the fixing of the dowry, and the verse names both of them so that the case is not left to be guessed at. The blame is lifted rather than the act commanded, so the verse is telling the hearer where a divorce stands clear of sin and not telling him to divorce. "But give them a ˹suitable˺ compensation" is the turn of the verse, and the but in it is what the whole ruling turns on, since the lifting of the blame is followed at once by a duty, and the duty is a gift rather than a payment of what was promised. "the rich according to his means and the poor according to his" fixes the measure of the gift, and the measure is the man's own capacity, so the verse does not name an amount and does not make the same demand of the two. "A reasonable compensation is an obligation on the good-doers" closes the verse by naming who the duty binds, and the naming is by a quality and not by a relation, so the obligation is set down as the mark of a good-doer rather than as a debt that can be counted. The verse stands between the rulings on the waiting period and the ruling on the marriage that has a dowry fixed, and it is the first of the two cases of a divorce before the marriage is entered, so the verse after it takes up the same divorce with the dowry already settled.

**The case the verse takes.**

Keeping the dowry and the consummation in view, a divorce can fall into four situations, and the two that this verse and the verse after it deal with are the two in which the marriage has not been consummated. Where the dowry has not been fixed and the marriage has not been entered, no dowry is due, but the husband is obliged to give something of his own to the woman. Where the dowry has been fixed and the marriage has not been entered, half of the fixed dowry is due, which is the case the next verse takes up. Where the dowry has been fixed and the marriage has been entered, the fixed dowry is paid in full, and that ruling stands elsewhere in the Qurʾān. Where no dowry was fixed but the marriage was entered, the woman is given the dower of her equals, that is, the amount customarily given in her own family circle, and that too is taken up in another verse. The word for touching in this verse is read by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as meaning sexual intercourse, so the condition in the verse is the entering of the marriage and not the meeting of the two. On that reading the two conditions are separate and either of them can be missing on its own, which is why the verse needs both of them in the one phrase.

**Why there is no blame in it.**

The blame is lifted because Allah allowed the divorce after the contract of marriage and before the consummation, and the husband is allowed to divorce his wife before the consummation or before the giving of the dowry where the dowry was deferred. The permission is therefore in the contract itself and not in a failure of it, and the verse is closing a question rather than opening a door. The wording of the condition is worth noticing, because the particle that carries it relates to the verbal action and works as an adverbial as well, so the phrase reads as a state the divorce happens in and not as a second act. One reading of the word for touching is with the mutual form and the other without it, and the two readings give the same sense here, since what the verse is fixing is whether the marriage was entered. What the verse refuses is a divorce that leaves the woman with nothing at all, and that is why the permission is followed in the same breath by the command to provide for her.

**The compensation and what it is.**

The provision asked for is a gift given at the time of the divorce, and it is a gift rather than a dowry, since no dowry was fixed and none is due. Its purpose is given as a compensation for her loss, and it is also given as a thing that makes the parting easier on her feelings, so the gift is measured by what it does for the woman and not by what was promised to her. The verse does not fix an amount for it, and the least of it has been taken as a set of clothes, described elsewhere as a chemise, a head covering and a wrap. The report that stands behind this ruling is the one al-Bukhārī carries in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Sahl bin Saʿd and Abū Usayd, that the Prophet ﷺ married Umaymah bint Sharaḥīl, and when she was brought to him he extended his hand to her and she did not like that, so he ordered Abū Usayd to provide provisions for her along with a gift of two garments. The marriage in that report was ended before it was entered and the gift was given at the ending of it, which is the shape the verse lays down.

**The rich according to his means and the poor according to his.**

The measure the verse gives is the man's own capacity, and it gives it twice, once for the man of ample means and once for the man of restricted income, so the two are held to the same rule and not to the same sum. Because no amount is named anywhere in the verse, the wording carries a persuasion for the man of means, who is not to behave tightly in an act of grace, and the same wording keeps the man of little means inside the ruling rather than outside it. The provision is described as a fair one, and the fairness in it is the fairness of the measure and not of a fixed number, so the two men are answered differently by the same phrase. What the verse leaves open it leaves open on purpose, and the openness is what makes the ruling work in both directions, since a sum named for the rich would fall on the poor and a sum named for the poor would be a small thing from the rich.

**An obligation on the good-doers.**

The last phrase of the verse puts the duty on a described people rather than on all who divorce, and the word for obligation in it is taken either as a second description of the provision itself or as an emphatic verbal noun standing on its own, so the phrase is read either as a quality of the gift or as a statement about it. It is also read as an obligation on those who believe in the oneness of Allah, on the ground that the provision stands in the place of the dowry, and as binding on those who wish to do good in their actions and their dealings. The good-doers named at the end of the verse are therefore the ones the whole ruling is addressed to, and the verse is telling them that a gift given at a parting is part of the doing of good and not a courtesy added to it. The obedient are named with the virtuous in the same phrase, so the duty is set inside obedience and not beside it.

**How the verse stands with the one after it.**

The two verses divide the divorce before consummation by the dowry, and between them they cover both of its cases, so neither of them is read on its own. Where nothing was fixed, the gift of this verse is the whole of what is due, and where something was fixed, half of it is due under the next verse. Over both of them stands the same asking, which is that the two should behave liberally rather than legally, the woman remitting what the law would give her and the man handing over what the law would let him keep. That attitude is asked for in all matters of life and in enmity as well as in friendship, and it is what the good-doers named at the end of this verse are named for. The companionship of human beings with one another is not obligatory but at most permissible, and separation however it comes about is difficult, which is why the compensation is required and why the verse puts it in the hands of the one who is leaving.

237.text:
The verse gives the second of the two cases of a divorce before the marriage is entered. "And if you divorce them before consummating the marriage but after deciding on a dowry" is the case, and the two conditions in it are joined, so the verse deals with a marriage that has a dowry fixed but has not been entered. "pay half of the dowry" is the ruling, and the half is fixed by the verse itself, so the amount is not left to the two. "unless the wife graciously waives it or the husband graciously pays in full" gives the two ways out of the half, and both of them are described with the same word, so the verse asks for a grace on either side and not only on the side that has the right. "Graciousness is closer to righteousness" then states the ground of the asking, and the nearness in it is what the hearer is left with, since the verse does not command the grace but puts it nearer to something. "And do not forget kindness among yourselves" is the command that covers both, and the forgetting named in it is what the verse guards against, since a divorce is a place where kindness is the first thing to go. The verse is short in its ruling and long in its asking, and the asking is the part the two of them have to carry out between themselves, since the half is fixed and the grace over it is not. "Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do" closes the verse with the seeing, and the seeing is what answers the parts of the case the two of them settle between themselves.

**Divorce before consummation after a fixed dowry.**

And if you divorce them before you have touched them and you have already appointed for them an obligation then one-half of what you have appointed must be given to them and the other half returns to you; unless it be that they the women make remission and forgo it or he makes remission by leaving her the entire amount the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage the husband to be or as Ibn ‘Abbās is reported to have said ‘The legal guardian where the female is a minor’; in which case nobody would be at fault; yet that you should remit wa-an ta‘fū is the subject is nearer to piety aqrabu li’l-taqwā is its predicate. If you divorce your wives with whom you have entered into marriage before having sexual intercourse with them and you had fixed the amount of the dowry, you will have to pay half of this amount to them, unless they give up this right of theirs or the husband wishes to pay the full dowry.

**Half of the dowry.**

The Wife gets half of Her Mahr if She is divorced before the Marriage is consummated. This Ayah (2:237) requires the husband to relinquish half of the appointed Mahr if he divorces his wife before the marriage is consummated. In the second situation, when the woman's dower has been fixed before marriage and divorce occurs before actual consummation, the injunction says that the man shall be obligated to pay half of the dower already fixed. Mujahid, An-Nakha'i, Ad-Dahhak, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and Thawri stated that 'liberality' mentioned in the Ayah refers to the woman giving away her half Mahr, or the man giving away the full Mahr. On the other hand, the Wali of the wife is not allowed to give away any of her rightful dues without her permission, especially the dowry. Now, if he yields voluntarily and does not take his half back, this too, would virtually be an act of forgiving.

**The wife waives it or the husband pays in full.**

The use of the word ya fu ('forgives') to cover even the payment of full dower, perhaps, reflects the customary Arab practice of the payment of dower amount simultaneously with the marriage. If so, the husband has become, in the event of a pre-consummation divorce, deserving of taking half of the dower back. Explaining the words of the verse whose hands lies the marriage tie), the Holy Prophet has himself said: , that is, 'the husband is the guardian (wali) of the bond of marriage.' This hadith appears in Darqutni as narrated by Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father on the authority of his grandfather, and also from Sayyidna Aii and Sayyidna ibn Abbas (Qurtubi). " Its beginning is that you recognize what is rightfully due to you from your brother, but then you pardon it and let it go. The Hadith states that the husband is the person who really holds the marriage tie in his hand, as it is up to him to go on with the marriage or end it. (unless they (the women) agree to remit it,) meaning, the wife forfeits the dowry and relieves the husband from further financial responsibility.

**Graciousness and the kindness between the two.**

To give up your right is closer to Mindfulness. "And that you pardon is nearer to godwari ness," and the end is what He says: Allah says here to the husband and wife: it is more conducive to God-fearing if you forgo your right to the other; (And forget not kindness among yourselves) Allah says to both: continue to be kind and generous to each other. But the spirit of goodwill calls for both husband and wife to adopt a liberal rather than a legal attitude. (unless they (the women) agree to remit it,) "Unless the wife forfeits her right."Furthermore, Imam Abu Muhammad bin Abu Hatim said that it was reported that Shurayh, Sa'id bin Musayyib, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ash-Sha'bi, Al-Hasan, Nafi', Qatadah, Jabir bin Zayd, 'Ata' Al-Khurasani, Ad-Dahhak, Az-Zuhri, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Ibn Sirin, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and As-Suddi said similarly. (And to remit it is nearer to At-Taqwa (piety, righteousness).) indicates that the one who forgives, is nearer to At-Taqwa (piety). Forget not kindness between you that is to be bountiful towards one another; surely God sees what you do and will requite you accordingly. Do not forget to show kindness and compassion to one another in matters of rights. The woman should feel that, when the marriage has not been consummated she should, as the law requires, remit half the amount of the bride-gift due to her. While the man should feel, that although he is legally entitled to deduct half of the amount, he should rather hand over all of it as a gesture of goodwill.

**Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.**

(Indeed Allah is Seer of what ye do) of acts of kindness and generosity. Allah sees what you do, so try to do what is best to earn His reward. This honorable Ayah is not a continuation of the Mut'ah (gift) that was mentioned in the previous Ayah (i.e., divorce before the marriage is consummated). Its end is that you recognize what is rightfully due to him from you and you prefer him over yourself. And the act of forgiving has been declared more merit-worthy, and closer to Tagwa (the sense of being responsible to Allah, commonly rendered as piety or fear or righteousness in absence of an exact equivalent); because this forgiveness symbolically indicates that the severance of the bond of marriage was also done with magnanimity and good grace, which is the objective of the Shari'ah and certainly, deserving of great merit -- the forgiveness could come from the woman, or from the man, it does not matter. (Truly, Allah is All-Seer of what you do.) meaning, none of your affairs ever escapes His perfect Watch, and He will reward each according to his deeds.

**The remitting and the liberality.**

And to remit is nearer to At-Taqwa (piety, righteousness). (And to remit it is nearer to At-Taqwa (piety, righteousness).) (And do not forget liberality between yourselves.) meaning, kindness (or generosity), as Sa'id has stated. This attitude of liberality and goodwill is required in all matters of life. Ibn Jarir said, "Some scholars said that this statement is directed at both men and women. You join with him who cuts you off, pardon him who does you wrong, and bestow on him who deprives you." A truly Muslim society is that in which its members are more interested in giving to one another, rather than in taking from one another. Furthermore, this attitude of liberality should be evinced in times of enmity as well as in friendship.

238.text:
The verse turns from the rulings of the household to the prayer, and it gives three things. "Observe the ˹five obligatory˺ prayers" is the command, and the word for observing is a guarding, so the prayers are described as a thing kept and not only as a thing done. "especially the middle prayer" singles out one of them, and the singling out is what the verse is doing here, since the prayers are named together and then one of them is named again. "and stand in true devotion to Allah" gives the manner of the standing, and the devotion in it is the state of the one standing rather than the shape of the act. The verse stands in the middle of the rulings about marriage and divorce, and it is the point where the passage turns from what a person owes to his household to what he owes at fixed hours, and the verse after this gives what becomes of the prayer when its hour comes in a time of danger. The three things in the verse are the prayers, the one among them, and the standing, and they are given in that order, so the guarding comes first and the devotion last.

**Observe the prayers.**

Maintain the five prayers by performing them at their appointed times and the middle prayer either that of the afternoon or the morning or the midday or another prayer there are many opinions on this matter; God has singled it out for mention because of its merit; and stand in prayer submissive to God li Lllāhi qānitīn some have said that this means ‘obedience’ on account of the Prophet s saying ‘Wherever the expression qunūt ‘submission’ appears in the Qur’ān it denotes obedience’ as reported by Ahmad b. Allah then prompted the believers to observe the five daily prayers, saying: Guard your prayers by fulfilling them completely as Allah has instructed. Guard strictly (five obligatory) As-Salawat (the prayers) especially the Middle Salah.And stand before Allah with obedience And if you fear (an enemy), (perform Salah) on foot or riding. Guard over the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God devoutly. Imam Malik reported that Nafi' related that Ibn 'Umar used to describe the Fear prayer when he was asked about it and would then add, "If there is intense fear, pray on foot, riding, facing the Qiblah and otherwise.

**The middle prayer.**

Furthermore, Allah has specifically mentioned the Middle prayer, which is the 'Asr prayer according to the majority of the scholars among the Companions, as At-Tirmidhi and Al-Baghawi have stated. In particular, guard the middle prayer, which is the ‘aṣr (afternoon) prayer; and stand before Allah in submission and devotion. (Be guardians of your prayers) the five daily prayers including the ritual ablution that precede them, their bowings, prostrations, and everything prescribed in them during their appointed times, (and of the midmost prayer) the 'Asr prayer specifically, (and stand up with devotion to Allah) pray to Allah, by performing the bowings and prostrations this prayer includes; it is also said that this means: pray to Him by being obedient to Him in the prayer and not disobedient through engagement in mundane talk. Great care in observing the proper timings of prayer, even in times of the greatest danger, and refraining from all such actions as may mar the spirit of prayer—all this is implied by the ‘guarding’ of prayer. Based on the authority of some ahadith, a very large number of ulama', have said that al-salat al-wusta or the middle salah is the salah of Asr because there are before it, two Salahs during the day, that of Fajr and Zuhr; and after these come two evening Salahs, that of Maghrib and Isha'.

**Stand in devotion to Allah.**

Prayer is the standing of His servants before their Lord. In the tongue of allusion to guard over the prayer is that, when the servant comes into the presence of the prayer, he comes with awe, and when he leaves, he leaves with reverence. Incidentally, the Qur'anic word, Qanitin meaning obedient or submitting, rendered here as 'stand before Allah in total devotion', has been explained in Hadith as denoting sukut or motion-less silence. " Abū Bakr Shiblī said, "If I were given the choice to enter the prayer or to go into paradise, I would not chose that high paradise over the prayer. Muslim, Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir reported that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Allah has ordained the prayer by the words of your Prophet : four (Rak'ah) while residing, two Rak'ah while traveling and one Rak'ah during times of fear. In such a state, one can offer salah (prayer) while standing, with a condition that he can stand in one place without moving, and can make the gesture of sajdah in a lower position than he makes in ruku' .

**Speaking in the prayer.**

Hanbal and others; it is also said to mean ‘in silence’ sākitīn on the basis of a hadīth of Zayd b. Arqam in which he said ‘We used to speak to each other sometimes during prayer but when this was revealed we were commanded to be silent and were forbidden to talk’ as reported by the two Shaykhs Bukhārī and Muslim. The verse 239 has allowed a special way of offering prayers in the state of 'fear' i.e. the state of war. MuṣṬafā gave no station the mark he gave to the prayer when he said, "'The delight of my eyes was placed in the prayer.' Amongst the caresses and beauties, the brightness of my eyes lies in being occupied with Him and whispering secretly with Him. Al-Hafiz Abu Muhammad 'Abdul-Mu'min bin Khalaf Ad-Dumyati stated in his book on the Middle prayer that it is the 'Asr prayer and mentioned that this is the Tafsir of 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Ayyub, 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, Samurah bin Jundub, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id, Hafsah, Umm Habibah, Umm Salamah, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'ishah.

239.text:
The verse gives the prayer in a time of danger and then the prayer after it. "If you are in danger" is the condition, and the danger is not named, so the verse covers the enemy and the water and anything else that makes the standing impossible. "pray on foot or while riding" is the ruling, and the two ways in it are the two ways a person in danger can be, so the verse is not excusing the prayer but changing the manner of it. "But when you are safe" is the turn, and the safety is like the danger in being unnamed, so the verse covers the end of any fear. "˹take time to˺ remember Allah for teaching you what you did not know" gives what the safety is for, and the remembrance is joined to the teaching, so the verse ends by putting the prayer of the safe man inside a gift he did not earn. The verse follows the command to guard the prayers, and it is the exception that keeps that command whole, since a person told to guard the prayers needs to know what the guarding is when he cannot stand. The two halves of the verse are the prayer of the danger and the remembrance of the safety, and the second of them is the longer in what it asks.

**Prayer in danger.**

And if you are in fear of an enemy or a torrent or a predatory animal then standing rijāl plural of rājil praying while walking or mounted rukbān plural of rākib. (And if ye go in fear) of the enemy's sword, (then (pray) standing or on horseback) in whatever direction. If you face danger from an enemy or any other danger, and you are not able to offer the prayer completely, then pray whilst walking or riding, on camels, horses, or in any way you can. And if you are in fear then standing or mounted. Al-Hafiz Abu Muhammad 'Abdul-Mu'min bin Khalaf Ad-Dumyati stated in his book on the Middle prayer that it is the 'Asr prayer and mentioned that this is the Tafsir of 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Ayyub, 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, Samurah bin Jundub, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id, Hafsah, Umm Habibah, Umm Salamah, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'ishah. Imam Malik reported that Nafi' related that Ibn 'Umar used to describe the Fear prayer when he was asked about it and would then add, "If there is intense fear, pray on foot, riding, facing the Qiblah and otherwise.

**On foot or riding.**

In other words in whichever way you can facing the direction of the qibla or otherwise making the gestures of genuflexion and prostration; but when you are secure from any fear then remember God by performing prayer as He taught you what you knew not before He taught you its obligations and its proper ways the particle kāf of ka-mā ‘as’ has the same meaning as mithl ‘like’ while the mā is related to the verbal action or is relative. However, salah cannot be performed while walking. In such a state, one can offer salah (prayer) while standing, with a condition that he can stand in one place without moving, and can make the gesture of sajdah in a lower position than he makes in ruku' . Therefore, it is essential that at times of prayer that state of mind should be induced in the suppliant, which prevails when the most humble stands before the Most High. (And if you fear (an enemy), perform Salah on foot or riding.) meaning, pray in the appropriate manner under these circumstances, whether on foot or riding and whether facing the Qiblah or otherwise. Guard strictly (five obligatory) As-Salawat (the prayers) especially the Middle Salah.And stand before Allah with obedience And if you fear (an enemy), (perform Salah) on foot or riding.

**The safety after the fear.**

(And when ye are again in safety) from the enemy, (remember Allah) pray to Allah performing the bowings and prostrations, (as He hath taught you) in the Qur'an: the traveller prays two units of prayer while the resident prays four units (that which ye knew not) before the revelation of the Qur'an. (And when you are in safety, then remember Allah (pray) meaning, 'Perform the prayer as I have commanded you by completing its bowing, prostration, standing, sitting, and with the required attention (in the heart) and supplication.' Allah said: Then when the fear is gone from you and you are secure return to what you have established [in prayers] and exert your utmost in the times of your devotion in My presence in private or in public. If the danger has gone, remember Allah as He has taught you: remembering Him in the most complete manner within the prayer. If they are unable, then Takbir alone does not suffice, so they should delay the prayer until they are safe. Based on the authority of some ahadith, a very large number of ulama', have said that al-salat al-wusta or the middle salah is the salah of Asr because there are before it, two Salahs during the day, that of Fajr and Zuhr; and after these come two evening Salahs, that of Maghrib and Isha'.

**Remember Allah for what He taught you.**

Also, remember Him for His having taught you guidance and given you light which you were previously unaware of. But when you are secure then remember God as He taught you what you knew not. Incidentally, the Qur'anic word, Qanitin meaning obedient or submitting, rendered here as 'stand before Allah in total devotion', has been explained in Hadith as denoting sukut or motion-less silence. But when you withdraw in your hearts through Me their hands will be unable to reach you since I have appointed victory for you over them. Muslim, Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir reported that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Allah has ordained the prayer by the words of your Prophet : four (Rak'ah) while residing, two Rak'ah while traveling and one Rak'ah during times of fear. (in the manner He has taught you, which you knew not (before).) meaning, just as He has endowed you, guided you and taught you about what benefits you in this life and the Hereafter, so thank and remember Him.

240.text:
The verse returns to the widow and gives what she is left with. "Those of you who die leaving widows should bequeath for them a year's maintenance without forcing them out" is the ruling, and it is put in the form of a bequest, so the verse speaks to a man about what he leaves behind him and not to the family after he is gone. The year is the measure of the maintenance, and the maintenance is joined in the same phrase to the not forcing out, so the two are given together, the provision for her and the keeping of her in the house. "But if they choose to leave" is the turn, and the choosing is described as theirs, so the verse puts the decision in her hand once the provision stands. "you are not accountable for what they reasonably decide for themselves" gives what follows the choosing, and the accountability is taken off the family while the reasonableness is kept as the condition on her decision, so the verse is not leaving the matter open but moving it to her. "And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" closes the verse with the two descriptions, and they stand over both halves of it, the bequest laid on the dead man and the choice left to the widow. The verse stands after the verse that fixed the widow's waiting at four months and ten days, and the two are read together, since the waiting is a period and this verse is the provision that covers it, and the passage closes the rulings of the household with the making clear that comes next. The verse is put in the second person plural, and the plural is what makes it a ruling on a community rather than on one man, since the bequest is written by one and kept by many. The maintenance named in it is of the same kind as the provision the earlier verses named for the divorced women, and here it is given a measure, a year, which runs longer than the waiting itself, so the verse provides for the widow past the end of her waiting and not only through it, and the not forcing out is what makes the provision a place to live in rather than a sum handed over.

**The bequest for the widows.**

And those of you who die leaving wives let them make testament wasiyyatan or wasiyyatun for their wives as an obligation and give them provision what they can enjoy of property and clothes for until the completion of a year matā‘an ilā l-hawl ‘provision for a year’ is a circumstantial qualifier that is without expelling them from their habitations; but if they go forth of their own accord you would not be at fault you the guardians of the dead one regarding what they may do with themselves honourably in accordance with the Law such as adorning themselves or abandoning the mourning or that you should cut off their expenditure; God is Mighty in His Kingdom Wise in His actions. Those of you that pass away leaving behind wives must make a bequest for them to be provided with accommodation and maintenance for a period of one year in which your heirs may not remove them. (And those of you who die and leave behind wives should bequeath for their wives a year's maintenance (and residence) without turning them out,) "The widow used to reside, and have her provisions provided for her for a year, in her deceased husband's house.

**A year's maintenance.**

In the Age of Ignorance, the period of waiting for a widow was one year, and in Islam, it came to be four months and ten days rather than one full year as we already know from ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ : 'They keep themselves waiting for four months and ten days,' in Verse 234, explained earlier. This is to make up for the loss they have suffered and in respect for the deceased. The waiting period after the death of the husband in the beginning of Islam was an uninterrupted year according to the words and actions of the Arabs. It was also mandatory under this arrangement that she be given her maintenance during this period out of what has been left behind by her husband. Consequently, if she wants, she could use her right in this will and remain in the residence (for the rest of the year). "If she wants, she spends the 'Iddah with his family and resides there according to the will (meaning the rest of the year). So, Allah made the rest of the year, which is seven months and twenty days, as a will and testament for her.

**Without forcing them out of the house.**

Therefore, it was made obligatory that a woman should be allowed to live in the premises of her late husband's house for one full year if she so desires. Since this was the right of the woman and she had the choice to receive or leave it, therefore, it was not permissible for the inheritors to evict her out of the house, but it was permissible for her not to live in that house at her discretion, and leave her due for the inheritors. As proof, they said that the widow is required to remain in her (deceased) husband's house (for four months and ten days) according to what Malik reported from Zaynab bint Ka'b bin 'Ujrah. Ibn Abu Hatim also related that 'Ali bin Abu Talhah stated that Ibn 'Abbas said, "When a man died and left behind a widow, she used to remain in his house for a year for her 'Iddah, all the while receiving her provisions during this time. (And those of you who die and leave wives behind them, they (the wives) shall wait (as regards their marriage) for four months and ten days.)(2:234) After the completion of this period she could leave the house of her husband and could enter into a new marriage with another person.

**If they choose to leave.**

If they leave before the end of the year by their own choice, there will be no sin on either you or them for what they do with themselves in terms of their beautification. This, i.e. the sustenance due on the deceased towards any wife he leaves behind, was however abrogated by her inheritance. The testament mentioned here was abrogated by the ‘inheritance’ verse Q. 412 and the waiting of one year without expulsion was abrogated by the previous verse four months and ten Q. 2234 which was revealed later. If the Ayah (2:240) remains (in the Qur'an) after the Ayah that abrogated it (2:234), this might imply that its ruling is still valid.' 'Uthman, the Leader of the faithful, answered him by stating that this is a matter of the revelation, which mentioned these Ayat in this order. 'Therefore, I shall leave the Ayah where I found it in the Qur'an.'. ‘When someone passes away and leaves behind a wife who is not pregnant, it is the duty of these women to wait for a period of four months and ten days...’ [ Sūrah Al-Baqarah: 234]. (In that which you leave, their (your wives') share is a fourth if you leave no child; but if you leave a child, they get an eighth of that which you leave.)(4:12)

**Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.**

(Allah is Mighty) for He is vengeful towards any that leaves what He has commanded, (Wise) in that He abrogated apportioning a year of sustenance and habitation to the wife whose husband is deceased and substituted it with what is due to her of inheritance: a quarter or eighth of the deceased's wealth. It should be noted that most commentators are of the view that the law contained in this verse has been abrogated by the verse: The question that Ibn Az-Zubayr asked 'Uthman means: 'If the ruling of the Ayah (2:240) was abrogated to four months (the 'Iddah of the widow, and refer to 2:234), then what is the wisdom behind including it in the Qur'an, although its ruling has been abrogated? She said that Fari'ah bint Malik bin Sinan, the sister of Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri, told her that she came to Allah's Messenger asking him to return to her family's residence with Banu Khudrah. (Thus Allah makes clear His Ayat (Laws) to you,) meaning, what He allows, forbids, requires, His set limits, His commandments and His prohibitions are all explained and made plain and clear for you. This is a duty on Al-Muttaqin (the pious)Thus Allah makes clear His Ayat (Laws) to you, in order that you may understand.

**The waiting of the widow and this provision.**

In the opinion of al-Shāfi‘ī may God have mercy on him the habitation remains hers. The command to take due care of all prayers (verses 238-239) put in between was to remind that the real thing in life is a constant orientation towards Allah, not only in prayers where it is more pronounced, but also in social relationships such as marriage and divorce, rather, in all areas of one's life. Whoever weeps for an entire year has absolved themselves of any guilt. (There is no sin on you, if you divorce women while yet you have not touched (had sexual relation with) them, nor appointed for them their due (dowry). But bestow on them (a suitable gift), the rich according to his means, and the poor according to his means, a gift of reasonable amount is a duty on the doers of good.)(2:236) only mentions some specifics of this general ruling. So Allah specified the share of the widow in the inheritance and there was no need for the will or the Nafaqah (maintenance) which were mentioned in (2:240)." Ata' quoted Ibn 'Abbas, "This Ayah (2:240) has abrogated (the requirement that) the widow spends the 'Iddah with his (i.e., her deceased husband's) family. So, this is the 'Iddah of the widow, unless she was pregnant, for her 'Iddah then ends when she gives birth.

241.text:
The verse states one duty in one sentence. "Reasonable provisions must be made for divorced women" is the whole of the ruling, and the provision is described as reasonable, so the verse fixes the duty and leaves the amount to the measure of the man, and the women named in it are the divorced women, so the duty follows the divorce rather than the marriage. "a duty on those mindful ˹of Allah˺" gives who the duty binds, and the binding is by mindfulness rather than by relation, so the verse puts the provision in the same place as the rest of what the mindful are asked for. The verse is short because it closes a long set of rulings, and it takes up the provision the earlier verses named in one case and states it for all of them, so nothing in the passage is left without a provision for the woman at the end of it. The verse is put in the passive, and the passive is what makes it a duty without naming the one who owes it, so the duty stands on whoever has the marriage and not on a named person, and the women it covers are all of them, the divorced whose dowry was fixed and the divorced whose dowry was never fixed.

**Provision for the divorced women.**

There shall be provision for divorced women which they are given honourably as is feasible — an obligation haqqan ‘obligation’ is in the accusative because it is governed by an implied verb on those who fear God may He be exalted. (For divorced women a provision in kindness) with generosity and kindness: Divorced women should be gifted something of clothing, money etc. There shall be provision for divorced women honorably-an obliga tion on those who fear. (There is no sin on you, if you divorce women while yet you have not touched (had sexual relation with) them, nor appointed for them their due (dowry). But bestow on them (a suitable gift), the rich according to his means, and the poor according to his means, a gift of reasonable amount is a duty on the doers of good.)(2:236) only mentions some specifics of this general ruling. The scholars who ruled that the Mut'ah (reasonable gift) at the time of divorce is required for every divorced woman, whether she had a bridal-money appointed for her or not, and whether the marriage was consummated or not, relied on this Ayah (2:241) when they issued their ruling.

**A duty on those mindful of Allah.**

Providing compensatory benefits ( mata ) for divorced women has also been dealt with in verses earlier than this, but that was restricted to two types of divorced women who were divorced before privacy and consummation. (And for divorced women, maintenance (should be provided) on reasonable (scale). This is a duty on Al-Muttaqin (the pious).) These rights can be seen as such only by those who are God-fearing. Such provision must be in keeping with the financial position of the husband; and it is a duty on those who are mindful of Allah by fulfilling His instructions and avoiding His prohibitions. The statement of 'Ata' and those who held the view that the Ayah (2:240) was abrogated by the Ayah on the inheritance (4: 12), is only valid for more than the four months and ten days (required in 2:234). (And those of you who die and leave wives behind them)(2:234) used to be the 'Iddah, and the widow had to remain with her (deceased) husband's family (during that period, i.e., four months and ten days).

**What the provision is.**

If the word 'benefit' used in this verse is taken to mean 'dower', its payment is obligatory according to these de-tails. However, if we take math' to mean a particular benefit, that is, the giving of a gift or set of clothes, then giving this to a particular type of divorced woman is obligatory which has been pointed out earlier. It is an obligation because it is in surplus to the dowry, and it is done out of generosity. This is to make-up for their emotional suffering because of the divorce. And those of you who die and leave behind wives should bequeath for their wives a year's maintenance (and residence) without turning them out, but if they (wives) leave, there is no sin on you for that which they do of themselves, provided it is honorable (e.g., lawful marriage). Ibn Abu Hatim also related that 'Ali bin Abu Talhah stated that Ibn 'Abbas said, "When a man died and left behind a widow, she used to remain in his house for a year for her 'Iddah, all the while receiving her provisions during this time.

**The rights beyond the fixed shares.**

Setting forth injunctions regarding social matters, the Quran states, ‘This is an obligation binding on the righteous. But there are further mutual rights which go beyond fixed boundaries. He has repeated the phrase in order to include the woman that has been touched sexually since the previous verse addresses a different issue. The allusion is that you [men ]should not combine separation with depriva tion thereby doubling the difficulty for them [women]. For one whose dower has not already been fixed, a post-consummation divorce will make it obligatory to give her mahr almithl or 'equivalent dower' (as customarily given in the immediate family circle of the woman). (In that which you leave, their (your wives') share is a fourth if you leave no child; but if you leave a child, they get an eighth of that which you leave.)(4:12) So Allah specified the share of the widow in the inheritance and there was no need for the will or the Nafaqah (maintenance) which were mentioned in (2:240)."

242.text:
The verse closes the whole passage in one sentence. "This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you" points back at what has just been given, and the pointing is the verse's whole work, since it takes the rulings of the verses before it and names them as a making clear rather than as a list of commands. "so perhaps you will understand" gives the purpose of the making clear, and the understanding asked for is the hearer's, so the verse ends the passage by turning it over to the one who reads it. The verse stands at the end of the rulings on marriage, divorce, the waiting and the provision, and it is the point where the sūrah turns from the household to the story of the people who went out of their homes, so the making clear is what carries the hearer from one to the other. The verse is one sentence and it carries no ruling in it, and that is what makes it the end of the passage, since everything the passage asked for has been given and what is left is the understanding of what was given.

**The revelations made clear.**

So in the same way that He has explained to you what has been mentioned God makes clear His signs for you so that you might understand reflect. (Thus Allah expoundeth unto you His revelations) His commands and prohibitions (so that ye may understand) what you have been commanded to do. As with the previous explanation, Allah explains these verses – containing His limits and laws – to the believers so that they understand and practice them, and so achieve the good of this world and the Afterlife. This is a duty on Al-Muttaqin (the pious)Thus Allah makes clear His Ayat (Laws) to you, in order that you may understand. (Thus Allah makes clear His Ayat (Laws) to you,) meaning, what He allows, forbids, requires, His set limits, His commandments and His prohibitions are all explained and made plain and clear for you.

**So perhaps you will understand.**

If the word 'benefit' used in this verse is taken to mean 'dower', its payment is obligatory according to these de-tails. However, if we take math' to mean a particular benefit, that is, the giving of a gift or set of clothes, then giving this to a particular type of divorced woman is obligatory which has been pointed out earlier. ’ This shows us an important aspect of Islamic law. (...a gift of reasonable amount is a duty on the doers of good)(2:236) was revealed, a man said, "If I want, I will be excellent and if I do not, I will not. So Allah specified the share of the widow in the inheritance and there was no need for the will or the Nafaqah (maintenance) which were mentioned in (2:240)." Consequently, if she wants, she could use her right in this will and remain in the residence (for the rest of the year).

**The end of the rulings on the household.**

Setting forth injunctions regarding social matters, the Quran states, ‘This is an obligation binding on the righteous. Providing compensatory benefits ( mata ) for divorced women has also been dealt with in verses earlier than this, but that was restricted to two types of divorced women who were divorced before privacy and consummation. In mutual matters there are certain rights on which the law has been laid down. (There is no sin on you, if you divorce women while yet you have not touched (had sexual relation with) them, nor appointed for them their due (dowry). But bestow on them (a suitable gift), the rich according to his means, and the poor according to his means, a gift of reasonable amount is a duty on the doers of good.)(2:236) only mentions some specifics of this general ruling. The scholars who ruled that the Mut'ah (reasonable gift) at the time of divorce is required for every divorced woman, whether she had a bridal-money appointed for her or not, and whether the marriage was consummated or not, relied on this Ayah (2:241) when they issued their ruling.

**The provision and the divorce.**

If the Ayah (2:240) remains (in the Qur'an) after the Ayah that abrogated it (2:234), this might imply that its ruling is still valid.' 'Uthman, the Leader of the faithful, answered him by stating that this is a matter of the revelation, which mentioned these Ayat in this order. 'Therefore, I shall leave the Ayah where I found it in the Qur'an.'. For one whose dower has not already been fixed, a post-consummation divorce will make it obligatory to give her mahr almithl or 'equivalent dower' (as customarily given in the immediate family circle of the woman). But there are further mutual rights which go beyond fixed boundaries. The question that Ibn Az-Zubayr asked 'Uthman means: 'If the ruling of the Ayah (2:240) was abrogated to four months (the 'Iddah of the widow, and refer to 2:234), then what is the wisdom behind including it in the Qur'an, although its ruling has been abrogated? And those of you who die and leave behind wives should bequeath for their wives a year's maintenance (and residence) without turning them out, but if they (wives) leave, there is no sin on you for that which they do of themselves, provided it is honorable (e.g., lawful marriage).

243.text:
The verse tells a story in the form of a question and then draws the lesson out of it. "Have you ˹O Prophet˺ not seen those who fled their homes in the thousands for fear of death?" is the question, and the seeing in it is not the seeing of an eye but the knowing of a thing told, so the verse begins by putting a people in front of the hearer. The two parts of the phrase are the number and the reason, the thousands and the fear of death, and the fleeing is from their homes, so the verse describes a people who left what they had to keep their lives. "Allah said to them, Die!" is the answer to the fleeing, and the command is given in one word, so the thing they ran from came to them by the road they ran by. "then He gave them life" is the second half of the act, and the giving of life follows the command of death in the same breath, so the verse describes a people who died and were brought back. "Surely Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity" draws the lesson out of the story, and the bounty is named as a standing description and not as a single act. "but most people are ungrateful" is the turn at the end, and it sets the bounty against the gratitude that is missing, so the verse closes on what people do with a favour rather than on the favour itself. The verse stands at the head of the passage that goes on to the fighting in the cause of Allah, and the story in it is the ground of the command that follows. The question at the head of the verse is not asking for information but putting a scene in front of the hearer, and the scene is a people who ran from a thing that was going to reach them anyway, so the story is told as a lesson about running rather than as an account of a place.

**Those who fled their homes for fear of death.**

These were a people from among the Children of Israel who fled their homeland after it was afflicted with plague. Do you not know, O Prophet, about those who left their homes in huge numbers fearing death due to the plague or something similar? (Bethink thee (O Muhammad) have you not been informed, O Muhammad, (of those of old, who went forth from their habitations) to fight their enemies (in their thousands) eight thousand in total, but they proved too cowardly to fight, (fearing death) out of fear of being killed, (and Allah said unto them: Die) Allah killed them on the spot, (and then He brought them back to life) after eight days. The Israelites were so greatly stricken with fear that they abandoned their homes and ran away. The second aspect of wisdom here relates to the guidance Allah Almighty has given to man that he should not go where there is a danger of being harmed, or an apprehension of being killed; in fact, he should do his best to keep away from everything that could cause harm or death.

**The death and the life that followed it.**

Then He gave them life after eight days or more as a result of the supplication of their prophet Ezekiel Hizqīl and they lived on for a while with the effects of death still upon them such that when they wore garments these turned into shrouds for the deceased; and this phenomenon remained with their descendants. Then Allah brought them back to life to show them that everything is in His Hands and that they have no control over any benefit or harm. These bones received the command of Allah Almighty through the words of the Prophet and obeyed it. When [the children of Israel] deemed God's power to restore [them] unlikely He showed [His power] to them directly in their own selves. (They say: "Our Lord! Why have you ordained for us fighting? Would that you had granted us respite for a short period?" Say: "Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is better for him who fears Allah, and you shall not be dealt with unjustly even equal to the Fatila (a scalish thread in the long slit of a date stone). Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you even if you are in fortresses built up strong and high!")(4:77-78)

**Allah is ever Bountiful to humanity.**

Truly, Allah is full of bounty to mankind, but most men thank not And fight in the way of Allah and know that Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower Who is he that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it to him many times? (Lo! Allah is the Lord of Kindness to mankind) to these people for He brought them back to life, (but most of mankind give not thanks) for life. Truly God is bounteous [dhū faḌl] to people but most people are not thankful. This formidable event was not only a thought-provoker for the wise of the world, its philosophers and thinkers, and certainly, a decisive argument against the deniers of the Last Day, but was also a guidance for mankind pointing out that running because of the fear of death, be it from jihad or from plague or some other epidemic, is just not possible for one who believes in Allah Almighty and in the fate He has determined -- the one who is certain in his belief ('iman) that there is a time for death; it cannot come a second earlier, and it cannot be postponed to a second later.

**Most people are ungrateful.**

(but most men thank not.) as they do not thank Allah for what He has given them with in their worldly life and religious affairs. The outward disclosure of that however did not benefit those who had not sharpened their insight regarding divine unity tawḥīd. It means that Allah Almighty created everything and then gave it (built-in) guidance in proportion to its state of being. Allah Almighty, in order to impress upon other peoples of the world that no living being can escape death by running away from it, sent two angels who stood on the two ends of the plain and sent forth some sort of shrill cry which caused all of them to drop dead instantly. This includes the grace He showed to that particular group of people from the Bani Israel by bringing them back to life, as well as the grace He has shown to the community of Muhammad by telling them about this incident and by making it a model lesson for them. Imam al-Bukhari has reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mur that Sayyidah A'ishah al-Siddiqah told him that she had asked the Holy Prophet about plague when he informed her that this disease was a punishment sent to a people who were to be punished by Allah's will.

**The story and why it is told.**

Have you not seen an interrogative to provoke amazement and a longing to hear what will follow that is ‘Has your knowledge not attained’ those thousands four eight ten thirty forty or seventy thousand who went forth from their habitations fearful of death? hadhara’l-mawt an object denoting reason. What then, is the purpose of saying ‌ Have you not seen?' Commentators have said that, in all situations where the Holy Prophet has been addressed with the words: ‌ (Have you not seen?) -- although the incident belongs to a time earlier than him, and it cannot be 'seen' by any stretch of imagination -- the act of seeing (ra yah) stands for seeing through the heart (ruyah al-qalb), which means seeing through knowledge and insight. On this occasion God reminded them of an event in the history of the Israelites, where in the trials of life, fear of defeat was defeat itself. Then Allah mentioned the story of the fighters among the Children of Israel, saying: In accordance with the hadith stated above, we have been told that it is prohibited for outsiders to enter an area affected by plague or its likes; while it is equally prohibited for those who live there to run for their lives from that area. Anyone whose insight has been strengthened will not be harmed by a lack of these direct forms of evidence for they have already realized through their faith in the unseen the truth of what they have been told.

**The thousands who went out.**

This refers to a group of people from the Israelites. In the end, to awaken the negligence-prone man, it was said: ‌ ‌ 'But most of the people are ungrateful.' It means that human beings do behold thousands of demonstrations of Divine grace and mercy, yet most of them show no gratitude. Then they all gave serious thought as to why they had been defeated by the Philistines. There is an authentic Hadith that Imam Ahmad reported that 'Abdullah bin 'Abbas said that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab once went to Ash-Sham (Syria). Leaving the city out of fear of death, all of them went out to camp in an open plain located between two mountains. Did you (O Muhammad) not think of those who went forth from their homes in the thousands, fearing death? (Did you (O Muhammad) not think of those who went forth from their homes in the thousands, fearing death?) It must be noted here that this incident belongs to a time thousands of years before the Holy Prophet .

244.text:
The verse takes the lesson out of the story and turns it into a command. "Fight in the cause of Allah" is the command, and the cause named in it is what makes the fighting what it is, so the verse is not asking for a fight but for a fight in a direction. "and know that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" is joined to the command by an and, and the knowledge is given as a thing to know while the fighting is being done, so the verse puts the two descriptions over the act, the hearing of what is spoken in it and the knowing of what is meant by it. The verse is short and it follows the story of the people who died and were given life, so the command is given to people who have just been told that death is not the end of the matter, and the verse after this goes on to the loan that is asked for before the fighting. The two descriptions at the end are what keep the command from being a demand for numbers, since the hearing and the knowing are of the one who fights and not of the enemy, and the verse asks for the fighting and for the knowing of it in the same breath.

**Fight in the cause of Allah.**

So fight in God’s way in order to elevate His religion and know that God is Hearing of your sayings Knowing of your affairs and He will requite you accordingly. (And fight in the way of Allah) in obedience of Allah against your enemies, (and know that Allah is Hearer) of what you say, (Knower) of your intentions and the punishment that is going to visit you if you disobey what you have been commanded to do. Fight, O believers, the enemies of Allah: in support of His path and to promote His Word. (They say: "Our Lord! Why have you ordained for us fighting? Would that you had granted us respite for a short period?" Say: "Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is better for him who fears Allah, and you shall not be dealt with unjustly even equal to the Fatila (a scalish thread in the long slit of a date stone). Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you even if you are in fortresses built up strong and high!")(4:77-78)

**Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.**

Know that Allah hears your statements and knows your intentions and actions, and that He will reward you for them. This means If pain touches you and a cry rises up from you know that God hears your cry knows your states and sees your affairs. Truly, Allah is full of bounty to mankind, but most men thank not And fight in the way of Allah and know that Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower Who is he that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it to him many times? This formidable event was not only a thought-provoker for the wise of the world, its philosophers and thinkers, and certainly, a decisive argument against the deniers of the Last Day, but was also a guidance for mankind pointing out that running because of the fear of death, be it from jihad or from plague or some other epidemic, is just not possible for one who believes in Allah Almighty and in the fate He has determined -- the one who is certain in his belief ('iman) that there is a time for death; it cannot come a second earlier, and it cannot be postponed to a second later.

**The story before the command.**

Ibn Abu Hatim related that Ibn 'Abbas said that these people mentioned herein, were the residents of a village called Dawardan. 'Ali bin 'Asim said that they were from Dawardan, a village several miles away from Wasit (in Iraq). The story of the dead people (2:244 above) also indicates that no caution can ever avert destiny and that there is no refuge from Allah, but to Allah Himself. Then they all gave serious thought as to why they had been defeated by the Philistines. Allah then said to them after He brought them back to life: It is a marvel of nature that the greatest commander of the Muslim army in the early days of Islam, Sayyidna Khalid ibn Walid who was known as the 'sword of Allah' and who spent his entire Islamic life in jihad, did not meet his death as a shahid on the battlefield! Isn't it that these very bones are considered by the whole world, devoid of reason and consciousness but they too, like every single particle of the world, are oriented to Divine commands and, possess senses and perceptive ability in proportion to their state of being, and are obedient to Allah Almighty.

**The fighting and the pain of it.**

The verse brings about an easing of the pain they endure. In the end, to awaken the negligence-prone man, it was said: ‌ ‌ 'But most of the people are ungrateful.' It means that human beings do behold thousands of demonstrations of Divine grace and mercy, yet most of them show no gratitude. Now the Philistines drew near to battle against Israel, ‘But the Lord thundered on that day, with a great thunder upon the Philistines and discomfited them; and they were smitten before Israel’ (Samuel 7:10). It means that Allah Almighty created everything and then gave it (built-in) guidance in proportion to its state of being. In the next verse appears the injunction relating to jihad and qital (fighting in the way of Allah) which was the real purpose in introducing this story, that is: " He, may Allah be pleased with him, was sorry and in pain because he did not die as martyr in battle.

245.text:
The verse asks for a loan and gives the terms of it. "Who will lend to Allah a good loan which Allah will multiply many times over?" is the asking, and it is put in the form of a question, so the verse is looking for a volunteer and not laying a duty. The loan is described as good, and the multiplication is described as many times over, so the two halves of the phrase give the quality asked for and the return promised. "It is Allah ˹alone˺ who decreases and increases ˹wealth˺" is the second statement, and it answers the thought that stands behind the loan, since a person who gives is afraid of being left with less, and the verse takes the decreasing and the increasing out of his hands and puts them where they already are. "And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned" closes the verse on the return, and the return is what gives the loan its weight, since the multiplication is not promised in this world alone. The verse stands between the command to fight and the story of the chiefs of the Children of Israel, and it asks for the wealth before the story asks for the fighting, so the two are asked in the order a person would find them hard in. The verse is a question and not a command, and that is the shape of the whole asking, since a question waits for an answer and a command does not. The loan is called a loan and not a gift, and the name is what makes the return promised, since a loan is given on the understanding that it comes back to the one who gave it. The decreasing and the increasing are named together and in that order, and the order is what answers the fear of the one who gives, since the decrease is named first and the increase second, so the verse is not hiding the loss but putting it where it already is before the gain is mentioned. The return at the end is to Him and not to a place, and that is where the loan is repaid.

**The loan lent to Allah.**

Who is he that will lend God a loan by expending his property in the way of God that is good by expending it for the sake of God Mighty and Majestic out of pureness of heart and He will multiply yudā‘if also read yuda‘‘if it for him manifold? up to ten or seven hundred times or more as will be mentioned soon. (Who is it that will lend unto Allah a goodly loan) in charity sincerely wanting nothing but the sake of Allah, (so that He may give it increase manifold for him?) every act is rewarded a thousand times (Allah straiteneth) withholds wealth from people (and enlargeth) gives plenty to whomever He wills in this worldly life. Who will act as a lender and spend his wealth in the path of Allah, willingly with a good intention so that this may come back to him multiplied? (And it is Allah that decreases or increases (your provisions),) meaning, 'Spend (in Allah's cause) and do not be anxious.' Certainly, Allah is the Sustainer Who increases or decreases the provisions to whomever He wills among His servants. " They all came back to life, looked around and proclaimed, "All praise is due to You (O Allah!) and there is no deity worthy of worship except You.

**The multiplication of the loan.**

It simply means that whatever you spend will surely be returned to you (in the form of a reward in the Hereafter) just as a loan is surely returned. The promise of increased or multiplied return appears in a hadith which declares that a date spent in the way of Allah is so increased by Allah Almighty that it outgrows the mountain of Uhud. This is that loan you gave to God when you were kind to a poor man after God had said, 'Who is it that will lend to God a beautiful loan?'" As for God's caressing the poor in this verse, it is that, when God wants a loan, He wants it for them. " A sound hadith says, "God descends and says, 'Who will supplicate Me that I may respond to him?' Then He spreads His two hands and says, 'Who will lend to one who is neither lacking nor wrongdoing?'" What do you know of the generosity and largesse found in this asking for a loan? Giving 'loan' to Allah Almighty has also been explained as the giving of actual loan to His slaves i.e. the human beings and thereby helping them in their hour of need.

**Allah decreases and increases.**

God straitens sustenance for whomever He wills in order to try him and enlarges it in abundance for whomever He wills in order to test him; and to Him you shall be returned in the Hereafter through the Resurrection where He will requite you for your deeds. And it is Allah that decreases or increases (your provisions), and unto Him you shall return. Allah restricts and widens provision and health in accordance with His wisdom and justice. 1. ‌ ‌ (who would give Allah a good loan?) the word 'loan' refers to good deeds and to the act of spending in the way of Allah, This was expressed figuratively as qard (literally, 'loan'), otherwise everything belongs to Allah. Abu Sulayman, Khalid bin Al-Walid, the commander of the Muslim armies, the veteran among Muslim soldiers, the protector of Islam and the Sword of Allah that was raised above His enemies, said while dying, "I have participated in so-and-so number of battles. The third group is that of sincere Muslims who lost no time and acted as directed by the verse giving the best of their possessions in the way of Allah, such as is the case of Companion Abu al-Dahdah and others. Long afterwards, one of the Prophets of the Children of Israel, whose name was Hizqil (Ezekiel), passed by them and asked Allah to bring them back to life by his hand.

**To Him you will be returned.**

(Unto Him ye will return) after you die and He will requite each according to his works. In the Afterlife, you will return to Him alone and He will give you a reward for your actions. (They say: "Our Lord! Why have you ordained for us fighting? Would that you had granted us respite for a short period?" Say: "Short is the enjoyment of this world. The Hereafter is better for him who fears Allah, and you shall not be dealt with unjustly even equal to the Fatila (a scalish thread in the long slit of a date stone). Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you even if you are in fortresses built up strong and high!")(4:77-78) I will sell it to you until the time when spoils arrive or a gift comes to you from the House of Wealth." ʿAlī bought the camel for sixty dirhams and set off in front of it. He is saying, "Who is it that will give a loan to Him who is neither a wrongdoer that he might take it away, nor a poor man not able to pay it back? While returning qard (loan), paying a little more than taken is a favourable practice only if any increase on the amount of loan has not been made a pre-condition. " He said, "I will buy it for 120 dirhams." ʿAlī said, "I have sold it to you," and took 120 dirhams from him.

**Who it was revealed about.**

This verse was revealed about a man from the Helpers (al-Ansar) named Abu'l-Dahdah or Abu'l-Dahdahah. When this verse was revealed, Sayyidna Abu al-Dahdah presented himself before the Holy Prophet and asked him: '0 Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be sacrificed to you, does Allah Almighty need loan from us, although He is Ghani the one who needs no loan?' The Holy Prophet said: 'Yes, Allah Almighty does wish to grant you entry in Paradise through it.' Hearing this, Sayyidna Abu al-Dahdah said. 'Let the Messenger of Allah stretch his hand forward.' He stretched his hand forward. Allah then prompted the believer to give in charity, saying:

**The spending in the cause of Allah.**

Spending for the cause of God’s religion is called giving a ‘generous loan. God called for a loan to be given to Him and he called it a ‘generous loan’ because He would return it many times over. " Anyone who rec ognizes the worth of this declaration will put forth the bounteous wealth of spirit and heart and say, "I will exert my heart and spirit with none but You. This is because when you ask for a loan, although most of the time you ask from friends, it does happen in the time of constraint that you ask from someone who is not a friend. Truly, Allah is full of bounty to mankind, but most men thank not And fight in the way of Allah and know that Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower Who is he that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He may multiply it to him many times? (The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, is as the likeness of a grain (of corn); it grows seven ears, and each ear has a hundred grains. Allah gives manifold increase to whom He wills.)(2:261) The Holy Prophet said to him: 'Dedicate one of these as waqf (endowment) in the way of Allah and keep the other to take care of your family needs.' 246.text:
The verse tells the beginning of a story in the form of a question and carries it through four exchanges. "Have you not seen those chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses" is the question, and it names the people by their rank and by the time they stand in, so the hearer is given a council of chiefs and a period after a prophet. "They said to one of their prophets" is the first exchange, and the prophet is named as one of their own, so the asking comes from inside the people and not from outside. "Appoint for us a king, ˹and˺ we will fight in the cause of Allah." He said," joins the asking to a promise, and the promise is the fighting, so the kingship is asked for as the means of a fight already wanted. "Are you not going to cower if ordered to fight?" They replied, "How could we refuse to fight in the cause of Allah, while we were driven out of our homes and ˹separated from˺ our children?" — the doubt of the prophet is put as a question about the future rather than as a refusal, so the verse puts the doubt in the mouth of the one who has to do the appointing, and the answer to it is not a hope but a loss, since the reason they give for fighting is what they have already been driven out of and what they have already been separated from. "But when they were ordered to fight, they fled" is the turn of the verse, and the turn is in the but, so the promise and the flight stand in the same sentence with nothing between them, and the ordering that they answered with a question is the same ordering they answered with their feet. "except for a few of them" is the exception, and the few are what the rest of the story is about, since the army that goes on to the river and to the battle is made of them. "And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the wrongdoers" closes the verse on the knowledge, and the wrongdoers named in it are the ones who fled, so the verse ends not with a punishment but with a knowing. The verse is put as a question at its head because the story is being given as a thing known and not as a thing argued, and every speech in it is given in its own words rather than described, so the hearer is given the words of the council and the words of the prophet and is left to hear the difference between the promise and the flight. The exception at the end of the verse is small in words and large in what it carries, since the few who did not flee are the ones the whole of the story that follows is about, and the verse closes on a knowledge that is not a threat but a record of what the flight was.

**The chiefs after Moses.**

Have you not seen the story and the tale of the council an assembly of the Children of Israel after the death of Moses when they said to a prophet of theirs namely Samuel ‘Send establish for us a king to unite us and to whom we can refer matters and we will fight with him in God’s way’. (Bethink thee) have you not been told (of the leaders of the Children of Israel after Moses, how they said unto a prophet whom they had) the prophet is Samuel (Shamwil): About three hundred years after the death of Moses, the Israelites were again subjugated by the polytheistic neighbouring nations.

**Appoint for us a king.**

For this purpose they needed a leader around whom they could rally in order to fight their enemies. When the infidel Amalekites were made to rule over them, they began thinking about correcting the situation. (Talut is the Qur'anic name of the king known in the Bible as Saul) When the Bani Isra'il saw this sign, they believed in the kingdom of Talut, who then mounted an attack on Jalut while the weather was very hot. (Set up for us a king) show to us the king of this army (and we will fight) under his command against our enemy (in Allah's way) in Allah's obedience. Out of sheer selfishness, each one of them, instead of desiring the good of the people as a whole—as a leader should—wanted to be leader and king himself. Their Prophet said to them, "What if Allah appoints a king over you, would you fulfill your vow to fight under his command?"

**The prophet's fear about the fighting.**

He the prophet said to them ‘Might it be that ‘asaytum or ‘asītum if fighting is prescribed for you you will not fight? allā tuqātilū is the predicate of ‘asā ‘might it be’; the interrogative is intended to confirm the expectation that follows sc. that they will not fight. (He said: Would ye then) do you suppose then that you will (refrain from fighting if fighting) against your enemy (were prescribed for you?) made obligatory upon you. The prophet replied, ‘It may be that if Allah makes fighting obligatory, you will not fight! Earlier, anyone who would fight the Israelites would lose, because they had the Torah and the Tabut, which they inherited generation after generation ever since the time of Moses, who spoke to Allah directly. The prophethood halted among their various tribes and only a pregnant woman remained of the offspring of Lavi (Levi), in whom the prophethood still appeared. When he reached the age of prophethood, Allah revealed to him and commanded him to call (his people) to Him and to His Tawhid (Oneness). They approached the matter as one of free choice ikhtiyār demanding that their prophet ask permission for them to fight.

**Driven out of our homes and our children.**

They said ‘Why should we not fight in God’s way when we have been expelled from our habitations and our children?’ as a result of these latter being taken captive or killed that which they suffered at the hands of Goliath and his men. (They said, "Why should we not fight in Allah's way while we have been driven out of our homes and our children?") meaning, 'After our land had been confiscated and our children had been taken from us?' Allah said: After having remained in that state of subjugation for about a quarter of a century, they felt the urge to bring back their period of glory.

**They fled except for a few.**

God exalted be He says Yet when fighting was prescribed for them they turned their backs from fighting in cowardice except a few of them the ones that crossed the river with Saul Tālūt as will be mentioned; and God has knowledge of the evildoers and will requite them accordingly. (Yet, when fighting was prescribed for them) was made obligatory upon them, (they turned away) they refrained from fighting their enemy, (all save a few of them) 313 men. ’ Yet when Allah made fighting obligatory on them, they all turned away, except a few of them. It is said that outwardly they spoke with toughness and seriousness about fighting to defend their possessions and their dwellings when they said Why should we not fight in God's way when we have been expelled from our habitations and our childrenḍ But they did not achieve their objective because their resolve was not purely for the right of God.

**Allah knows the wrongdoers.**

Yet, there were always Prophets sent among them who would command them to work righteous deeds, refrain from doing evil and who would rule them according to the commands of the Torah. If they had said Why should we not fight in the way of God for He has commanded us and made [this] an obligation on usḍ He is our Chief and Protector and His command is binding on us then perhaps they would have fully achieved what they had set out to do. ’ They denied that this would happen and insisted, ‘What would stop us from fighting in Allah’s path when our enemies have removed us from our homes and have taken our children as prisoners? When Allah Almighty willed the return of the chest, it so happened that the infidels were struck by some epidemic or calamity at places where they carried this chest. (But when fighting was ordered for them, they turned away, all except a few of them. And Allah is All-Aware of the wrongdoers) meaning, only a few of them kept their promise, but the majority abandoned Jihad and Allah has full knowledge of them. Allah heard her pleas and gave her a boy whom she called 'Shamwil' meaning 'Allah has heard my pleas.' Some people said that the boy's name was Sham'un (Simeon), which also has a similar meaning. Her husband had been killed, so the Israelites kept her in a house so that Allah may give her a boy, who would be their Prophet. Allah knows the wrongdoers who broke their promise and turned away from His instruction; and He will repay them for their action.

247.text:
The verse gives the appointment, the objection to it and the answer to the objection. "Their prophet told them" is the frame of the verse, and everything after it is speech, so the verse is made of three speeches and nothing else. "Allah has appointed Saul to be your king." They protested," gives the appointment and the protest in one phrase, and the appointment is put in Allah's hand before the protest is heard. "How can he be our king when some of us are more deserving of kingship than he" is the first ground of the protest, and the ground is a claim about themselves, so the objection is not that the appointment is wrong but that it is not theirs. "and he has not been blessed with vast riches." He replied," is the second ground, and the riches are named as the thing he lacks, so the two grounds are rank and wealth. "Allah has chosen him over you and blessed him with knowledge and stature" is the answer, and it answers the two grounds in order, the choosing over them and the two things he has been given, knowledge and stature, which are set against the rank and the riches they claimed. "Allah grants kingship to whoever He wills" takes the matter out of the argument altogether, and the granting is described as Allah's alone. "And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing." closes the answer with the two descriptions, and the bounty in them is the answer to the riches they asked for and the knowledge the answer to the deserving they claimed. The verse is made of speech on both sides, and the prophet's answer does not argue with the grounds they gave but goes over them, since the answer names what Allah chose and what Allah gave rather than what Saul deserves. The two descriptions at the end are the closing of the answer and not a new statement, and they are turned back onto the two things the objectors asked for.
