As-Suddi said, " 'Uzayr observed the bones of his donkey, which were scattered all around him to his right and left, and Allah sent a wind that collected the bones from all over the area. It is said that Allah made him a lesson for people, for he died when he was 40 years old and was brought back to life when his son was 120 years old, (look at the bones) the bones of your ass, (how We adjust them and then cover them with flesh!) after this. When Allah resurrected 'Uzayr after he died, the first organ that He resurrected were his eyes, so that he could witness what Allah does with him, how He brings life back to his body.

**What was made clear, and what a sign for the people means.**

So when it was made clear to him as a result of witnessing it he said ‘I know a variant reading for a‘lam ‘I know’ has the imperative i‘lam ‘know!’ thus making it a command from God with the knowledge of direct vision that God has power over all things’. (And when (the matter) became clear unto him) how Allah gathers the bones, (he said: I know) I had known (that Allah is Able to do all things) of life and death. We did this so that you would know and so that We would make you a sign of the truth of the Resurrection for the people. (And, that We may make thee a token) a sign (to mankind) regarding the matter of bringing the dead to life, that they will be resurrected in the same state they died in, because 'Uzayr died young and was brought back to life as a young person. Then he said I know that God has power over all things in giving life and causing death that is My knowl edge has been increased by what I saw. (He said, "I know that Allah is able to do all things,") meaning, "I know that, and I did witness it with my own eyes. This can be done with far greater conviction if they have actually witnessed with their own eyes the facts which they attempt to convey to the rest of mankind. Prophets are sent by God in order to inform mankind of realities which, for ordinary people, lie beyond the realm of human vision, being screened by a veil of cause and effect. Having provided practical proof of their truthfulness, the time then came for them to inform mankind of those realities of life which God, in order to test men, has kept hidden from them.

260.text:
The verse is the other half of the pair, and it turns on a request and on the answer that the request is given in the form of a task. "And remember when Abraham said, My Lord" opens with an address, and the wording of the request follows at once. "Show me how you give life to the dead, Allah responded" is the asking and the reply put together, and the question asked is about the how rather than about the whether, which is what the rest of the verse works with. "Do you not believe, Abraham replied" is the question put back to him, and it is about the belief in the power rather than about a refusal to grant the sight. "Yes I do" is the answer, given in two words, and "but just so my heart can be reassured, Allah said" states what was being asked for besides belief, a stillness in the heart, and then the command begins. "Then bring four birds" is the first step, and "train them to come to you" makes them known to him before anything is done to them, so the test cannot be answered by a stranger bird arriving. "then cut them into pieces" and "and scatter them on different hilltops" separate the parts of four bodies across the ground, and "Then call them back" with "they will fly to you in haste" brings what was scattered to the one who called, so the whole request is answered in the order it was asked, the how being shown by the doing. "And so you will know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise" ends on what the man gains from it, a knowledge joined to two descriptions, power that nothing is beyond and wisdom that places what it shows where it belongs. The verse before this was about a man shown the revival of a city and of a donkey, and this one gives the same subject to Abraham in the form of a work he is told to do with his own hands.

**The question about the dead, and why it was not doubt.**

And mention when Abraham said ‘My Lord show me how You give life to the dead’ He God exalted be He said to him ‘Why do you not believe?’ in My power to revive; God asks him this even though He knows of his belief in this power as a response to his request and so that the ones listening will know the purpose of the request; ‘Yes’ I do believe he said ‘but I ask You so that my heart may be re-assured’ so that it may be at peace through direct vision in addition to that certainty which is sought through logical reasoning. The answer is that Sayyidna Ibrahim had meant to say that there is no doubt in the actual happening, but the question can be taken in two senses, the obvious one relates to this very position, that is, he wished to inquire how the dead will be raised. Since anybody could have taken Sayyidna Ibrahim's question in this wrong sense, therefore, Allah Almighty, in order to free Sayyidna Ibrahim from this possibility, addressed him with so that he could say ] (bala : yes, why not) in reply, and thus get past the ambush laid out by liars and accusers. It is generally thought that in the first incident, the prophet in question was Ezra (Uzayr) (5th century BC), while in the second, as the Quran itself makes clear, it was Abraham, who lived between the years 2160 and 1985 BC.

**The heart at ease, and the goal of the recognizers.**

(Abraham said: Yea) I am convinced, (but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease) in order that the heat of my heart abates and so that I know that I am your friend and that my prayers are answered. Now what he is respectfully asking for is that highest degree of Itmi'nan which is bestowed upon the very special prophets -- as it was with our Holy Prophet who was granted special Itmi'nan by means of a visual experience of Paradise and Hell. He knew that as long as a heart is not alive, serenity will not come down into it, and as long as serenity has not come down into it, he would not have reached the final goal of the recognizers.

**The four birds, and how they were made to come.**

((His Lord) said: Take four of the birds) of different kinds: a cockerel, a raven, a duck and a peacock (and cause them to incline unto you) cut them into pieces, (then place a part of them on each hill) four different hills, (then call them) by their names, (they will come to thee) walking (in haste). Said He ‘Take four birds and twist them to you sirhunna or surhunna turn them towards you cut them up and mix together their flesh and feathers then set a part of them on every hill in the land around you then summon them to you and they will come to you in haste. When they grow so domesticated that they come to him at his call and he too starts knowing them well enough so that there remains no doubt about a stranger bird taking their place; then he should kill those four birds, make mince-meat of everything -- bones, feathers all included - dividing it in several portions. (cause them to incline towards you) means, cut them to pieces. Abraham took a peacock an eagle a raven and a cock and did with them as has been mentioned but kept their heads with him.

**What came running, and what the doubt that remained was.**

These particular words mean that the birds will come running, which tells us that they will not come flying because if they came flying across the sky, the doubt -- that they went out of sight and were replaced in the process -- would remain. When he called them, then in no time, bone to bone, feather to feather, flesh to flesh, everything took its original form, the birds became alive and came running to Sayyidna Ibrahim Allah Almighty said: '0 Ibrahim, this is how, on the Day of Resurrection, I shall assemble in no time all parts and bodies, and breathe life into them.'. Ibrahim witnessed the feathers, blood and flesh of these birds fly to each other, and the parts flew each to their bodies, until every bird came back to life and came walking at a fast pace towards Ibrahim, so that the example that Ibrahim was witnessing would become more impressive.

**What is scattered, and the power that gathers it.**

They think man becomes dust after death, then somewhere this dust scatters away with the wind, somewhere it flows away with water, somewhere it reappears in the form of trees and planted fields, so much so that its particles spread out to the far sides of the world. Now to gather these scattered parcels and human parts and to infuse life into them are things short-sighted man finds difficult to understand because he measures everybody on the scale of his own power and status, and does not deliberate in the non-analogous Power above him! So, one can only marvel in how many ways and from how many corners of the world the perfect power and the precise plan of Allah Almighty has accumulated in the body of one man the whole wide world's produce, its grains and fruits and everything else man eats and uses as medicine, and which become part of his body. Through Aziz , the perfect power of Allah was pointed to, and through 'Hakim ' (the All-Wise), it was indicated that it is in Allah's wisdom that visual experience of life after death is not granted to everyone, otherwise it is not at all difficult for Allah to make every man see it for himself. When the water rose up, the fish and the beasts of the sea came forward and ate of it, and whatever fell of the carrion was swept away by water; and when the sea ebbed away, wild animals went forward and ate of it, and whatever fell of the carrion became dust.

**Mighty and Wise, and what the end of the verse states.**

(that Allah is Mighty) for He is vengeful against those who do not believe in bringing the dead back to life, (Wise) He gathers the bones of the dead and bring them back to life, just as He gathered these birds and brought them back to life. And know that God is Mighty that nothing is beyond Him Wise’ in His actions. The final goal of the recognizers is the repose of intimacy, the witnessing of the heart, and the constancy of love; the tongue in remembering, the heart in secret whispering, the spirit in joy; the tongue in remembrance, the heart in reflection, the spirit with love; the tongue as spokesman, the heart with explication, and the spirit in face-to-face vision. It was said, "O Abraham, life is found in death and subsistence in annihilation, so go and kill four birds outwardly as We command in order to show reverence for Our command and to make manifest your servanthood.

261.text:
The verse is a parable, and it is placed here because the three verses before it spoke of spending, of what spoils a gift and of what God does not need. "The example of those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah is that of a grain that sprouts into seven ears" takes a single seed and follows it into the field, so the reward is described by the shape of what grows rather than by a number promised in advance, and the cause of Allah is the ground it is sown in. "each bearing one hundred grains" then multiplies the figure without straining it, since a head of corn carrying a hundred grains is what a farmer hopes for and not what he counts on. "And Allah multiplies the reward even more to whoever He wills" opens the calculation again, so the seven hundred is a floor rather than a ceiling, and the distribution of what is added is left to a willing that is not tied to the arithmetic. "For Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing" gives the two qualities the verse rests on, a bounty wide enough to give more than the figure and a knowledge exact enough to know who is given it, so the parable ends where a transaction would have ended, on what the one who pays is and what he knows. The verses after this take up the spending that spoils its own reward by being announced or by being followed with hurt, which is the other half of the same subject, and the parable here is therefore doing a part of the work that those verses finish, since a reward described as a harvest can be lost by the way it is carried to the field. The address throughout is to the man who gives, and the verse never leaves him with a sum he can calculate in advance, only with a shape taken from a field and a will that is not bound to the shape. What the reader is given, then, is a way of thinking about a gift that has already been made, since the grain is not paid for at the threshing floor but in the sowing, and the verse places the whole reward in the act of spending rather than in a reckoning kept for later.

**The grain, the seven ears and the hundred grains.**

The likeness of the quality of the expenditure of those who expend their wealth in the way of God that is in obedience of Him is as the likeness of a grain of corn that sprouts seven ears in every ear a hundred grains likewise what they expend will be multiplied seven hundred times; so God multiplies even more than this for whom He will; God is Embracing in His bounty Knowing those who deserve such multiplications. (The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way) He says: the likeness of the wealth of those who spend in His way (is as the likeness of a grain which groweths seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains) likewise, Allah multiplies what the believers spend in His way from one to seven hundred fold. This grain then produces seven spikes, each carrying a hundred grains.

**The grain sown, and the labour of the farmer.**

It has rather used the form of a similitude featuring a grain of wheat which has a subtle hint towards the labour of a farmer who can hope to get an yield of seven hundred grains out of one grain sown only when the grain is good, and the farmer sowing it should be fully conversant with the art of farming, and the soil where the grain goes should be good too, because, should even one of these factors remain missing, either this grain will be wasted leaving no grain to come out, or it would just not yield enough to reach the production ratio of one grain to seven hundred grains. In the first verse it is said that people who spend in the way of Allah, that is, in Hajj or in Jihad or on the poor, on widows and orphans, or on relatives and friends to help them out, can be likened to one who sows a good grain of wheat in the field from which grows a plant on which sprout seven ears and each ear yields hundred grains. The outcome is that one who spends in the way of Allah receives in return (reward in the Hereafter) on the scale of one to seven hundred, that is, spending one cent could bring the merit of seven hundred cents.

**Infaq, sadaqah and what the two words cover.**

Before we discuss these subjects, it is necessary to know that the Holy Qur'an has pointed out to spending in the way of Allah at several places with the word, DWI (infaq: spending) "and at several others, with the words, (it am: feeding) or (sadaqah: charity) or ; (ad' az-zakat: paying the obligatory zakah properly). A careful look at these Qur'anic words and the way they have been used shows that the words – infaq it am and sadaqah -- are general and as such incorporate all sorts of charitable spendings that aim to seek the good pleasure of Allah. In this section, the word used more often is infaq while the word, sadaqah has been used less often, which indicates that the statement here covers general charities and deeds of generosity, and the injunctions given here include and incorporate all sorts of charities and spendings in the way of Allah. It may be noted that the Qur'an has used a distinct word for the obligatory Zakah which indicates that there are special requirements in receiving and giving of this particular sadaqah.

**What is accepted, and the conditions on what is spent.**

That which is spent in the way of Allah should be clean, pure and halal (lawful) for it appears in Hadith that Allah Almighty accepts nothing except what is clean, pure and halal . Thus, the similitude unfolds for us the great merit spending in the way of Allah has, along with the three conditions as well, which stipulate that one should spend from halal earnings, and the method of spending should also conform to Sunnah, and that one should literally search for the deserving in order to spend on them. Similar to this, there are the same three conditions for the acceptance and increased return of good deeds generally, and of spending in the way of Allah particularly. It is said that people who spend in the way of Allah and do do not publicise their favour after having spent, nor cause any pain to those on whom they have spent, their reward is secure with their Lord.

**How far a good deed is multiplied, and what the fast is for.**

(Every good deed that the son of Adam performs will be multiplied ten folds, to seven hundred folds, to many other folds, to as much as Allah wills. Allah said, "Except the fast, for it is for Me and I will reward for it. One abandons his food and desire in My sake." The fasting person has two times of happiness: when he breaks his fast and when he meets his Lord. Verily, the odor that comes from the mouth of whoever fasts is more pure to Allah than the scent of musk. Fasting is a shield (against sinning), fasting is a shield.) Muslim recorded this Hadith. It appears in authentic and reliable ahadith that the thawab or merit or reward for one good deed is returned ten-fold, and could reach seven hundred-fold. This Ayah indicates that Allah 'grows' the good deeds for its doers, just as He grows the plant for whoever sows it in fertile land.

**A seed in this world, and what is spent for God.**

Every act committed by man is like a seed planted in the ground. If one does something in order to be admired by others, it is as though one is planting a seed in the earth of this world. If, on the other hand, one acts in order to please God, then one has sown a seed in the everlasting fields of the Hereafter, where it will blossom and bear fruit. In this world, one seed produces a thousand grains of corn. What a difference between the compensation for one who expends his wealth and finds his reward and the [compensation for] one who expends his state and finds nearness! (Allah giveth increase manifold) in surplus of this (to whom He will) to whomever deserves it; it is also said: to whomever Allah accepts his spending.

262.text:
The parable of the spent wealth has just been given, and this verse turns from the reward of the spenders to the manner in which a gift may be spoiled after it has left the hand. "Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah and do not follow their charity with reminders of their generosity or hurtful words" is one long description with two things refused in it, and the order of the two is worth noticing, since the reminder comes first and the hurt after it, which is the way the damage usually happens, a word about what was given and then a word that lands as pain. The wording of the first refusal is about following, so the gift itself is not what is weighed here but what is walked behind it afterwards, and the sources describe a reminder as a hint by tongue or by act that the receiver was helped. "they will get their reward from their Lord" is the answer to that restraint, and the phrase from their Lord is where the verse puts the payment, since a man who expects nothing from the person he helped is paid by the one he did not expect it from. "and there will be no fear for them" then opens the reward past the arithmetic of the transaction, and the negation is general, so whatever a person dreads on his own account and on the account of those behind him is covered by one clause. "nor will they grieve" closes the verse with the second of the two negations, and the pair of them, no fear and no grief, is the shape of safety in this sūrah when it speaks of the life to come. The verse stands between a parable about multiplication and a verse about a kind word, and it does the work of both, since it states what a gift is worth and what undoes it, and the reader is left with the lesson that a reward can be emptied by the conduct of the one who is being rewarded rather than by anything the gift itself lacked. The occasion the sources give for the verse is a matter of real money given at Madīnah, which is the same setting as the verses around it, and the rule it states is not a rule about sums but about the tongue that follows the hand, which is the reason the two refusals are given as things done after a gift rather than as part of the gift itself.

**Reminders of generosity, and what they do to a gift.**

Those who expend their wealth in the way of God then do not follow up their expenditure with reminder of their generosity of the one on whom they expended for example by saying ‘I was good to him and restored his affairs’; and injury to that person by mentioning this to people whom he would prefer not to know about it; their wage the reward for their expenditure is with their Lord and no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve in the Hereafter. Allah praises those who spend from their money in His cause, and then refrain from reminding those who received the charity of that fact, whether these hints take the form of words or actions. (or with injury), indicates that they do not cause harm to those whom they gave the charity to, for this harm will only annul the charity. They do not, for one, taunt their beneficiaries with reminders of the favours they have bestowed. Indeed, having spent from their wealth for the cause of God, they do not consider themselves to have bestowed any favour at all upon anyone. (Three persons whom Allah shall neither speak to on the Day of Resurrection nor look at nor purify, and they shall receive a painful torment: he who reminds (the people) of what he gives away, he who lengthens his clothes below the ankles and he who swears an oath while lying, to sell his merchandise.) It is said How can you give something while seeking to maintain your control416 and rights over itḍ It is said that they do not remind others of what they have done for them but rather bear witness to the favor of God [who] grants them success in that [act of generosity].

**Injury, harm, and the charity rendered vain.**

Do not consider the receiver practically disgraced, and do nothing to cause him insult or pain. In this case, the reward of giving away charity is not sufficient enough to nullify the harm and reminders. (O you who believe! Do not render in vain your Sadaqah (charity) by reminders of your generosity or by injury) stating that the charity will be rendered in vain if it is followed by harm or reminders. Ad-Dahhak commented that the example fits one who follows his acts of charity with reminders or harm.

**The reward with their Lord, the fear, and the grief that does not come.**

This is because their hopes are pinned on being rewarded in full by God, so what do they care if human beings show appreciation or not? (nor shall they grieve) regarding the offspring that they leave behind and the adornment and delights of this world. (On them shall be no fear) regarding the horrors of the Day of Resurrection,. They will not feel sorry for this, because they will acquire what is far better for them. On them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve Kind words and forgiving of faults are better than Sadaqah (charity) followed by injury. Those who expend their wealth in the way of God then do not follow up their expenditure with a reminder of their generosity and injury their wage is with their Lord and no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve.

**The two men the verse was revealed about, and what one of them gave.**

(Those who spend their wealth for the cause of Allah) this was revealed about 'Uthman Ibn 'Affan and 'Abd al-Rahman Ibn 'Awf, (and afterward make not reproach) to Allah (and injury) upon whom they spend it on (to follow that which they have spent) after their spending; (their reward is with their Lord) in Paradise, (and there shall no fear come upon them) regarding any future torment, (neither shall they grieve) about what they have left behind. As for 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, he went and gave the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, four thousand silver coins to distribute in charity. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said to him: 'I have eight thousand silver coins; I have kept four thousand for me and my family and I loan these four thousands to my Lord'. Those who spend for the cause of God, on the other hand, adopt a different approach.

**The boasting person, the show, and the deed that vanishes.**

(like him who spends his wealth to be seen of men) meaning, "Do not nullify your acts of charity by following them with reminders and harm, just like the charity of those who give it to show off to people. " The boasting person pretends to give away charity for Allah's sake, but in reality seeks to gain people's praise and the reputation of being kind or generous, or other material gains of this life. All the while, he does not think about Allah or gaining His pleasure and generous rewards, and this is why Allah said,. Such is the case with Allah's action regarding the work of those who show off, as their deeds are bound to vanish and disappear, even though people think that these deeds are as plentiful as specks of dust.

263.text:
The verse takes the two refusals of the verse before it and replaces them with two things that cost nothing. "Kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury" puts a word and a pardon on one side of a balance and a gift on the other, and the sentence is built as a comparison rather than as a permission, so the reader is not told that giving is wrong but that a cheap kindness outranks an expensive one that arrives with harm in it. The wording of the first half is general in both of its parts, a kind word covering what is spoken to the man who asks and a forgiveness covering what is passed over after he has been refused, and the sources make the second of these the harder of the two, since overlooking a persistence is not the same as saying something pleasant. "And Allah is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing" gives the reason the comparison stands, because the one who is being obeyed here does not need the gift and has capacity to wait, so a man who gives in order to be thanked is trading with someone who cannot be impoverished and will not be hurried. The verse is two lines long and is the reply to a hard rule, since a reader told that a gift can be spoiled by a word may conclude that not giving is safer, and this verse answers that a kind word is itself a gift.

**Kind words, and what a generous reply to a beggar is.**

Honourable words kind talk and a generous reply to the beggar and forgiveness towards him for his persistence are better than a voluntary almsgiving followed by injury through reproach and deriding him for his begging; and God is Independent of the voluntary almsgiving of His servants Forbearing in His delaying the punishment of the reproachful and injurious one. (A kind word) a good word for your brother, in his absence, by praying for him and praising him in front of other people, (with forgiveness) that overlooks any misdeed (is better) for him and you (than almsgiving followed by injury) than reminding him about your favour upon him which will hurt him. This means that words spoken to the one who is poor and deprived responding to his overture without showing censure-are better and more perfect than the alms of one who is proud of what he does and then imposes an obligation for it.

**Forgiveness, and the excuse offered before a refusal.**

This was explained by saying that it is a thousand times better to offer some reasonable and appropriate excuse before the person who asks, if the giver feels he is unable to give under conditions of duress; and should the person asking anger the giver by impolite behaviour, it is also a thousand times better to forgive than to give him a charity which is followed by giving him pain. (and forgiving) meaning, forgiving an injustice that took the form of actions or words,.

**Reminders, injury, and a charity rendered vain.**

Do not render in vain your Sadaqah (charity) by reminders of your generosity or by injury, like him who spends his wealth to be seen of men, and he does not believe in Allah, nor in the Last Day. Allah praises those who spend from their money in His cause, and then refrain from reminding those who received the charity of that fact, whether these hints take the form of words or actions. (like him who spends his wealth to be seen of men) meaning, "Do not nullify your acts of charity by following them with reminders and harm, just like the charity of those who give it to show off to people. Such is the case with Allah's action regarding the work of those who show off, as their deeds are bound to vanish and disappear, even though people think that these deeds are as plentiful as specks of dust. (Three persons whom Allah shall neither speak to on the Day of Resurrection nor look at nor purify, and they shall receive a painful torment: he who reminds (the people) of what he gives away, he who lengthens his clothes below the ankles and he who swears an oath while lying, to sell his merchandise.)

264.text:
The third verse in this row of rulings on spending puts the same two refusals as a command to the believers and then gives a picture of what is left. "O believers, Do not waste your charity with reminders of your generosity or hurtful words" opens with the address the section has been building toward, and the verb of the demand is about loss rather than about sin, so the harm described is to the giver's own account, and the two things named are the same two as in the verse before. "like those who donate their wealth just to show off and do not believe in Allah or the Last Day" fixes the comparison, and the pairing of the two halves is deliberate, since a man who gives for a name is placed with a man who does not believe, and the sources attend to that pairing, because the second half of the clause explains the first rather than adding to it. "Their example is that of a hard barren rock covered with a thin layer of soil hit by a strong rain" is the picture, and it is built out of three things, the stone, the dust on it, and the weather that meets them, so the size of the loss is set by the thinness of what was on the rock rather than by the violence of the rain. "leaving it just a bare stone" is the outcome in three words, with nothing further about the man, since the parable is about what remains and nothing remains. "Such people are unable to preserve the reward of their charity" returns to the givers in their own persons, and the wording is about capacity rather than about refusal, so the loss is described as something they were never able to hold on to. "Allah does not guide such disbelieving people" ends the verse where the section began, with guidance withheld from a man who was given a clear road and walked past it, and the reader is left with the rule that an outward act carried by a wrong inward end leaves nothing to be settled at the end.

**Reproach, injury, and the alms rendered void.**

O you who believe annul not the rewards of your voluntary almsgivings with reproach and injury as in the manner of the annulment of the expenditure of one who expends of his substance to show off to men and believes not in God and the Last Day this is the hypocrite. (O ye who believe! Render not vain your almsgiving) the reward of your almsgiving (by reproach) to Allah, i.e. by being conceited (and injury) to the person receiving alms, (like him who spendeth his wealth only to be seen of men) out of ostentation (and believeth not in Allah and the Last Day) does not believe in resurrection after death. Do not waste your charities: verbally -- by causing your favour to be known; or practically by causing pain. (Three persons whom Allah shall neither speak to on the Day of Resurrection nor look at nor purify, and they shall receive a painful torment: he who reminds (the people) of what he gives away, he who lengthens his clothes below the ankles and he who swears an oath while lying, to sell his merchandise.)

**Showing off, and the belief that is not there.**

In this verse, one more condition governing the acceptance of sadaqah has been added by saying that one who spends for public exposure, for name and fame, and does not believe in Allah Almighty and the Day of Resurrection, can be likened to be acting in a situation where he sows a grain on a clean rock which has collected a layer of soil, then comes the rain and washes the whole thing clean. Moreover, there is a hint here in the use of the additional sentence (And does not believe in Allah); perhaps, it aims to suggest that hypocrisy and name-seeking is not just the sort of thing a person who believes in Allah Almighty and the Day of Resurrection would ever do since hypocrisy is a sign of something being wrong with his faith. " The boasting person pretends to give away charity for Allah's sake, but in reality seeks to gain people's praise and the reputation of being kind or generous, or other material gains of this life.

**The rock, the dust on it, and the rain that strips it.**

The likeness of him is as the likeness of a smooth rock on which is soil and a torrent of intense rain smites it and leaves it barren and smooth with nothing on it. (His likeness) the likeness of the person who reminds others about what he has given them and the alms given by one who associates partners with Allah (is as the likeness of rock whereon is dust of earth; a rainstorm smiteth it, leaving it smooth and bare) without any dust on it. Allah says here: the reward of the person who boasts about what he has spent on alms and of the person who hurts those he gives alms to, is like dust on a rock when rain pours down on it and no dust remains. (which leaves it bare.) This Ayah means that heavy rain left the Safwan completely barren of dust. His likeness is the likeness of a smooth rock on which is a little dust; on it falls heavy rain which leaves it bare. (His likeness is the likeness of Safwan) where Safwan, from is Safwanah, meaning 'the smooth rocks,'. (on which is little dust; on it falls a Wabil) meaning, heavy rain,. Such is the case with Allah's action regarding the work of those who show off, as their deeds are bound to vanish and disappear, even though people think that these deeds are as plentiful as specks of dust.

**Not able to do anything with what they earned, and no guidance for such people.**

They have no power lā yaqdirūna is a resumption of the statement about the likeness of the one that expends for show; the person becomes plural on account of the potential plural implication of alladhī ‘the one who’ over anything that they have earned that they did in other words they find no reward for it in the Hereafter just as one finds nothing of the dust that was on the surface of the smooth rock after the rain has washed it away. (They are not able to do anything with what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.) The meaning of 'Allah Almighty will not show disbelievers the way' towards the end of verse 264 is that the Qur'anic guidance is universal. But, disbelievers do not take notice of this guidance, rather go a step farther and make fun of it. As a result, Allah Almighty lets them be deprived of the very taufiq the ability to accept guidance. Such people will never reap what they have sown and Allah Almighty will not let the disbelievers see the way. (Allah guideth not) rewards not (the disbelieving folk) and also those who show off their spending while still associating partners with Allah, just as He does not reward the alms of those who remind others about what they have spent on them. In the fourth verse, the same subject has been taken up differently with a little more emphasis.

**The condition that governs acceptance, and the charity voided.**

From this we know the condition that governs the acceptance of sadaqah and khayrat - spend only to seek the good pleasure of Allah Almighty and with the intention of getting thawab (reward) in the akhirah (Hereafter). This makes it clear that any form of favour-flashing or needy-bashing, after an act of charity renders such charity null and void. If you are martyred a hundred times a day in God's path you'll still be an idol-worshiper if you see yourself in the midst. [DS 708] It has also been said that do not void your charity by counting it a favor and causing discomfort means to void your charity by laying favors on those who ask. And should a true Muslim, who does believe in the Hereafter, expend something simply for name, fame, and under hypocritical motivation, he too, would not get any thawab (reward) for it. All the while, he does not think about Allah or gaining His pleasure and generous rewards, and this is why Allah said,.

265.text:
The rock has just been stripped bare, and this verse gives the other half of the pair, a growth that yields. "And the example of those who donate their wealth, seeking Allah's pleasure and believing the reward is certain" begins with the same act of spending and then names two inward things, a seeking and a certainty, so the difference between this verse and the one before it is not in the size of the gift but in what the giver is doing with his heart while he gives. The wording of the second of the two is about the person himself being made firm, which is why the sources treat the phrase as a certainty he arrives at rather than a boast he makes. "is that of a garden on a fertile hill" sets the new picture in three parts, a garden, a hill, and ground that is fertile, so the position of the garden is what the parable is working on first. "when heavy rain falls" and "it yields up twice its normal produce" are the two clauses that answer the rock verse, since the rain that strips dust from stone is the same weather that doubles a crop here, and the doubling is stated without a figure attached to it. "If no heavy rain falls" then removes the condition altogether, and "a drizzle is sufficient" is the clause handled with most care here, because the point is that the garden does not depend on the weather that a man can measure. "And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do" closes the verse with a watching that covers the doing rather than the amount, which is the same point the two pictures were made to carry, that what a gift becomes is settled by what it was given for. The order of the parts of the verse is worth following, since the seeking of pleasure comes before the certainty, and the two are given as one description of the same people rather than as two qualifications a man has to satisfy one after the other, which is why the sources treat the certainty as the thing that keeps the seeking honest rather than as a second reward for it. A reader who only took the outward half of the parable would come away with a lesson about a garden, and a reader who only took the inward half would come away with a lesson about intention, while the verse has put a hill under the garden so that the two cannot be separated. The two parables are now a pair, a rock with dust on it and a hill with a garden on it, and in both the weather is what decides, since rain that leaves one bare is rain that makes the other bear twice, and the reader is left with the rule that the ground a gift falls on is the thing being described rather than the gift itself.

**A garden on a fertile hill, and what a torrent does to it.**

But the likeness of the expenditure of those who expend their wealth seeking God’s good pleasure and to confirm themselves that is to realise the reward thereof in contrast to the hypocrites who do not hope for it since they do not believe in it is as the likeness of a garden an orchard upon a hill read rabwa or rubwa a high ground; a torrent smites it and it yields gives forth its produce read ukulahā or uklahā its fruits twofold twice the fruits of another garden; if no torrent smites it then dew tall a light drizzle which falls on it and suffices it on account of its altitude. (And the likeness of those who spend their wealth) the likeness of the wealth of those who spend it (in search of Allah's pleasure) seeking Allah's pleasure, (and for the strengthening of their souls) truly, out of conviction and certitude in their hearts that they will be rewarded, (is as the likeness of a garden on a height) on an elevated plain. The example of believers who spend their wealth seeking Allah’s pleasure, with firm conviction in their hearts of Allah’s promise, is like that of a garden on high fertile ground on which heavy rain falls and causes it to produce double its crop. (is that of a garden on a Rabwah) means, the example of a garden on 'a height above the ground', as the majority of scholars have stated.

**Fruit twofold, and the drizzle that is enough.**

In other words it grows and bears fruit regardless of how much rain falls; likewise are the expenditures of those mentioned they will increase with God regardless of how much they were; and God sees what you do and He will requite you for it. (The rainstorm smiteth it and it bringeth forth its fruit twofold. And if the rainstorm smite it not, then the shower) this is like the spending of the believer, whether small or great, when it is done with sincerity and fearingness, Allah multiplies it as He multiplies the fruits of a garden. And should it be that the rain is not that heavy, a light drizzle would become sufficient for it and Allah Almighty sees and knows what you do. The Ayah indicates that the garden on the Rabwah is always fertile, for if heavy rain does not fall on it, light rain will suffice for it.

**Seeking the pleasure, and the certainty the verse names.**

And the parable of those who spend their wealth seeking Allah's pleasure while they in their own selves are sure and certain that Allah will reward them (for their spending in His cause), is that of a garden on a height; heavy rain falls on it and it doubles its yield of harvest. It is said that those who spend in the way of Allah, solely and sincerely, to seek nothing but His pleasure, and thus fortify their selves with steadfastness, are in a situation where there is a fruit farm located on some mound, then it is hit by heavy rains, then it brings forth double of its usual yield. (while they in their own selves are sure and certain) meaning, they are certain that Allah shall reward them for these righteous acts with the best rewards. But the likeness of those who expend their wealth seeking God's good pleasure and to confirm themselves is as the likeness of a garden upon a hill; a torrent smites it and it yields its produce twofold; if no torrent smites it then soft rain [falls upon it] and God sees what you do.

**The sincerity that makes a little enough, and the example it is illustrated with.**

Here the merits of spending in the way of Allah, surely with sincerity of intention, and obedience to conditions set, has been made clear through this similitude. Spending with good intention and sincerity, even if it be just a little, becomes enough and helps one receive the gains of the Hereafter. In verse 265, the fifth under discussion, the acts of charity which are acceptable in the sight of Allah Almighty as valid spendings, have been illustrated with an example.

**What the watching sees, and the reward for spending in hard circumstances.**

(And Allah is All-Seer of what you do) meaning, none of His servants' deeds ever escapes His perfect watch. (Whoever fasts Ramadan with faith and expectation...) meaning, believing that Allah commanded the fast, all the while awaiting His reward for fasting it. However, when spending for God’s cause is done in adverse circumstances, which call for a special exercise of will-power, the reward which God grants on such occasions will be commensurately greater. However, should it be the will of God that holds pride of place in determining his actions, then it will be God on whom his heart is set. But the more difficult the conditions one encounters, the greater will be the increase in one’s will-power and the stronger one’s connection to that on which one’s heart is set.

266.text:
The parable of the garden is now answered with a second parable, and this one is told as a question about what a man would want. "Would any of you wish to have a garden with palm trees, grapevines" opens with a long ownership, and the two kinds of planting named are the two that carry a household, dates and grapes, so the wish being described is not for ornament but for a livelihood. "and all kinds of fruits with rivers flowing underneath and as they grow very old with dependent children" brings with it the rest of what makes the loss unbearable, first that nothing is missing from the garden, then that the owner is at the age when he can no longer work it, and then that children who cannot work it are standing behind him. "a fiery whirlwind hits the garden" is the blow, and the wording is of a wind with fire in it rather than of a fire, so the thing that arrives is the weather itself turned against what it used to feed. "burning it all up" is the completion, with nothing left to salvage, which is why the question form of the verse matters, since a reader who answers it at once has admitted the weight of the loss before he was told what it stands for. "This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you" then names the method of the whole passage, a picture given so that a meaning can be held, and "so perhaps you will reflect" closes on what the picture is for, a thought a man does after he has been shown the garden, the old age, the children and the wind in one view. The verse before this one had a rock, a dust and a rain in it, and here the parts are a garden, an old age and a wind, so the two parables are built out of weather in both cases, and in one the weather makes the growth while in the other it destroys it. The reader who has just been told that a drizzle is enough for a garden planted for God's pleasure is now shown a garden with every thing in it and nothing left after it, and the difference between the two is not the rain but what the growth was for.

**The garden of palm trees and vines, and the fruit in it.**

Would any of you wish to have a garden with date palms and vines, with rivers flowing underneath, and all kinds of fruits for him therein, while he is striken with old age, and his children are weak (not able to look after themselves), then it is struck with a fiery whirlwind, so that it is burnt? (Would any of you like) wish (to have a garden of palm-trees and vines, with rivers flowing beneath it) under its trees, houses and rooms, (with all kinds of fruit for him therein) in the garden; (and old age hath stricken him and he hath feeble offspring) who cannot fend for themselves; (and a fiery whirlwind) a strong cold or hot wind (striketh it) i.e. the garden (and it is consumed by fire. Thus Allah maketh plain His revelations) His signs through commands and prohibitions (unto you, in order that you may give thought) so that you may reflect on the similes of the Qur'an. Does anyone among you like that he owns a fruit farm, growing dates and grapes with streams flowing underneath, and trees laden with all sorts of fruits -- then comes old age for the owner and he has children and a family that can-not stand on their own. It may be noted that there are a series of qualifications added to this similitude-for instance, 'came his old age, he has children too and the children are young and weak.' These have a purpose. Would any of you wish to have a garden an orchard of date-palms and vines with rivers flowing beneath it for him there is in it all manner of fruit then old age smites him and makes him too weak to profit from it and he has seed but they are weak young children who cannot manage it; then a whirlwind i‘sār are violent winds with fire smites it and it is consumed? so that he loses what he is most in need of and now he and his children have become incapacitated confused without any resources.

**Old age, children who cannot help, and the whirlwind with fire in it.**

When the owner of the garden becomes old and is no longer able to work and earn, and he has weak young children who also cannot work, a strong fiery wind strikes this garden and it burns down completely at a time when he is most in need of it because of his old age and for his weak young children. Then there is the situation of one who has children, who are good and young with the hope that they would help the father out. Under these circumstances, should the farm he groomed burn out, his shock would be severe and the pain caused would be limitless. Similarly, an old man with children and family needs that his previous earnings be safe so that they can be used during old age. If, in this condition, his farm and his belongings burn out, there will be no limit to his pain and distress. Under these conditions comes a whirlwind through the farm with fire in it and which burns the farm out.

**The Day of Resurrection, and the deeds that are not there when a man most needs them.**

This is a similitude of how the expenditure of the one expending for show or the one who reproaches after having expended vanishes and how it is of no avail when he will be most in need of it in the Hereafter the interrogative a-yawaddu ‘would any wish’ is intended as a denial. The condition of a person who spends his wealth to show people is like that of this man: when he comes before Allah on the Day of Resurrection, he will have no good actions at a time when he will be most in need of them. This is the condition of the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection when he returns to Allah, for he will not have any good deeds to provide an excuse - or refuge - for him, just as the man in the parable had no strength to replant the garden. So he will be deprived of his reward when he most needs it, just as the man in the parable was deprived of Allah's garden when he most needed it, when he became old and his offspring weak." Very much like this, the sadaqah and khayrat the spendings in charity, which were made hypocritically or for self-promotion, will not come to help him exactly when he would need them most. According to Ibn ‘Abbās this is the person who performs deeds of obedience but when Satan comes to him he begins to work disobedience until all his good deeds have been consumed.

**Sincerity, the second condition, and how the signs are made clear.**

This sincerity means that one should spend exclusively for the good pleasure of Allah Almighty without any admixture of self-promoting ends. Summarising this whole verse, it could be said that ikhlas or sincerity is one big condition governing the acceptance of sadaqah and khayrat with Allah. The second condition, that is, spending according to Sunnah, means that one should be careful while spending in the way of Allah that rights due to someone may not be usurped. It means that spending in charity against given conditions is like hoping to be investing profusely in the Hereafter, but with Allah Almighty this investment comes to naught. So in the way that He has explained what has been mentioned God makes clear the signs to you so that you might reflect and take heed. But the likeness of those who expend their wealth seeking God's good pleasure and to confirm themselves is as the likeness of a garden upon a hill; a torrent smites it and it yields its produce twofold; if no torrent smites it then soft rain [falls upon it] and God sees what you do.

267.text:
The section now moves from what spoils a gift to what a gift should be made of, and it opens with the same address. "O believers, Donate from the best of what you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth" takes the two sources of a person's wealth and asks for the better of each, since what a man earns and what grows for him are named separately, and the word for the produce is attached to a divine verb, so the harvest is described as something brought out for him rather than something he made. "Do not pick out worthless things for donation" puts the same rule the other way round, and the wording is of aiming at a thing on purpose, so what is being kept from a man is a mistake he might have made without noticing rather than a deliberate reach for the worse while the better was in his hand. "which you yourselves would only accept with closed eyes" is the test the verse gives a man, and it is a test he can run in his own affairs, since the sources describe a debt settled short as something a creditor takes only when he shuts his eyes to it, so the rule is that a man may not hand God what he would not look at. "And know that Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy" closes the verse on two attributes that answer the reluctance behind the command, a richness that has no need of the gift and a praise that does not depend on the giver, so the verse has moved from the quality of what is spent to the question of who is being paid, and the reader is left with the standard that a man's own eyes are the measure of what is good enough to give away. The two clauses therefore ask him to look at what he is holding before he hands it over, and the test given him is his own reluctance, since a thing he would only take with his eyes shut is a thing he should not put forward as his offering. The occasion the verse carries is a matter of dates brought out at the harvest and hung in the mosque, which is why the wording about worthless things is so concrete here.

**The good things earned, and the produce of the earth.**

O you who believe expend of that is to say purify the good things you have earned of property and the good things of what We have produced for you from the earth of grains and fruits and seek not lā tayammamū means lā taqsudū the corrupt the vile of it the above-mentioned for your expending it as alms tunfiqūna ‘you expend’ is a circumstantial qualifier referring to the person of the verb tayammamū ‘seek’; for you would never take it the vile part yourselves if you were given it as something due to you; without closing your eyes to it by being careless and mindless so how do you expect to give what is due to God from this?; and know that God is Independent of your expenditures Laudable praised in every situation. (O ye who believe! spend of the good) of the lawful (things which ye have earned) which you have amassed of gold and silver, (and of that which we bring forth from the earth for you) of what is grown in the earth, i.e. grains and fruits, (and seek not the bad (with intent) do not single out what is base among your wealth (to spend thereof (in charity) when ye would not take) accept (it for yourselves save with disdain) and after forgoing some of your rights; likewise Allah does not accept what is base from you; (and know that Allah is Absolute) and free from the need of your spending, (Owner of Praise) He is praised in His acts; as it is said that this means: Spend of the good things which you have (legally) earned, and of that which We have produced from the earth for you, and do not aim at that which is bad to spend from it, (though) you would not accept it save if you close your eyes and tolerate therein.

**Low quality dates, and the eyes a man closes when he is paid less.**

One man brought low quality dates, as a result of which this Qur'anic verse was revealed (O ye who believe! Spend of the good things which ye have earned, and of that which We bring forth from the earth for you, and seek not the bad (with intent) to spend thereof (in charity) when ye would not take it for yourselves save with disdain) . O you who believe expend of the good things you have earned and of what We have produced for you from the earth and seek not the corrupt of it for your expending; for you would never take it yourselves without closing your eyes to it; and know that God is Independent Laudable. (you would not accept it save if you close your eyes and tolerate therein) means, "If you had a right on someone who would pay you less than what you gave them, you would not agree until you require more from them to make up the difference.

**The bunches hung in the mosque, and the verse revealed about them.**

At the time of the harvest of dates, the Helpers used to bring out of their fields bunches of dates and unripe dates and then hang them on a rope between two pillars in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, so that the poor among the Emigrants could eat of them. (O you who believe! Spend of the good things which you have (legally) earned, and of that which We have produced from the earth for you, and do not aim at that which is bad to spend from it,) that it was revealed about the Ansar.

**The purest of money, and what a man elects to give.**

Ibn 'Abbas said, "Allah commanded them to spend from the purest, finest and best types of their money and prohibited spending from evil and dishonest money, because Allah is pure and good and only accepts that which is pure and good. Let us remember that this is for a person who has something good yet elects to spend something not good as (you have earned) and (We have brought forth) do indicate that good things are available with the person making charity, while the sentence (and do not opt for a bad thing spending only from there) proves the spending of something not good deliberately.

**Self-Sufficient, worthy of all praise, and the men of understanding who remember.**

(And know that Allah is Rich (free of all needs), and worthy of all praise) meaning, "Although Allah commanded you to give away the purest of your money in charity, He is far Richer from needing your charity, but the purpose is that the distance between the rich and the poor becomes less. Therefore, whoever gives away good and pure things in charity, let him know that Allah is the Most Rich, His favor is enormous and He is Most Generous, Most Compassionate; and He shall reward him for his charity and multiply it many times. And know that Allah is Rich (free of all needs), and worthy of all praise Shaytan threatens you with poverty and orders you to commit Fahsha' (evil deeds) whereas Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty, and Allah is All-Sufficient for His creatures' needs, All-Knower He grants Hikmah to whom He wills, and he, to whom Hikmah is granted, is indeed granted abundant good. (But none remember (will receive admonition) except men of understanding.) means, "Those who will benefit from the advice are those who have sound minds and good comprehension with which they understand the words (of advice and reminder) and their implications."

268.text:
The command to give has just been given, and this verse explains the pressure that stops a man from obeying it. "The Devil threatens you with the prospect of poverty and bids you to the shameful deed of stinginess" puts the fear of poverty outside the man, as something brought to him, and the wording is of a threat rather than of an argument, since the promise being described is a prediction of loss and not a piece of reasoning about a household budget. The second half of the clause names what the threat is for, a deed whose shame is that it closes a hand, so the verse links a fear and a niggardliness in one movement, the first making the second look prudent. "while Allah promises you forgiveness and great bounties from Him" sets a second promise against the first, and the two are arranged in the opposite order, since God's promise begins with what is removed and ends with what is given, a forgiveness before a bounty, which is the sequence the commentators draw out here. "And Allah is All-Bountiful, All-Knowing" then closes the verse with the two qualities that make the second promise reliable, an abundance wide enough to supply what a man gives away and a knowledge exact enough to know which man will be given it, so the verse has taken a fear about money and answered it, not with a guarantee of income, but with a description of the one who promises. The verse before it asked for the best of what a man earns, and this one removes the motive for giving the worst of it, which is why the two stand together.

**The threat of poverty, and the niggardliness that follows it.**

Satan promises you poverty by making you fear loss when you make a voluntary almsgiving and so you withhold it and enjoins you to indecency niggardliness and the impeding of almsgiving; but God promises you in return for your expenditure His pardon for your sins and His bounty as sustenance from Him; and God is Embracing in His bounty Knowing the one who expends. When a person is obsessed with the idea that spending in charity will cause him poverty, when he does not pick up the courage to go ahead and spend - even after hearing the warning of Allah Almighty - and continues feeling that he should not spend out of what he has, and when, turning away from the Divine promise, his mind takes him to rely on the promise of Satan, he should better be sure that this apprehension of his is being generated by Satan. (Shaytan has an effect on the son of Adam, and the angel also has an effect. As for the effect of Shaytan, it is by his threatening with evil repercussions and rejecting the truth. As for the effect of the angel, it is by his promise of a good end and believing in the truth. Whoever finds the latter, let him know that it is coming from Allah and let him thank Allah for it. Whoever finds the former, let him seek refuge - with Allah - from Shaytan.) What Satan does is to impress on the minds of human beings the importance of personal requirements, and bring about conviction that all their earnings are best spent on personal comforts and luxuries. Satan makes you afraid of poverty by encouraging you to be stingy, and he invites you to commit sins. (The devil promiseth you destitution) makes you scared of poverty upon spending in charity (and enjoineth on you lewdness) by not giving the poor-due.

**Forgiveness promised, and the increase a man is blessed with.**

Conversely, should he come to think that not only his sins will be forgiven by spending in charities, but also his wealth will be blessed with increase - he should then be sure that this thought has come from Allah for which he should be grateful to Him. (But Allah promiseth you forgiveness) of your sins for giving the poor-due (from Himself with bounty) with something in exchange as well as a reward in the Hereafter. (Allah is All-Embracing) in that He replaces what you spend and also forgives sins, (All-Knowing) of your intentions and spending. Satan promises you poverty because of his poverty, and God promises you forgiveness because of His generosity. And know that Allah is Rich (free of all needs), and worthy of all praise Shaytan threatens you with poverty and orders you to commit Fahsha' (evil deeds) whereas Allah promises you forgiveness from Himself and bounty, and Allah is All-Sufficient for His creatures' needs, All-Knower He grants Hikmah to whom He wills, and he, to whom Hikmah is granted, is indeed granted abundant good.

**The pot pours what it has inside, and the wealth of heart.**

Satan himself is poor toward the Real, so he promises poverty, for that is what he has and that is what his hands reach. Yes, everyone does what is worthy of him, and the pot pours what it has inside. "Wealth of heart is three things: an aspiration greater than this world, an object of desire better than the next world, and a yearning for the vision of the Patron." The respect due to wealth in the religion is greater, for in this world, the person is content and has no need for the creatures, whispering secretly with the Real in his heart.

**Surplus wealth, the weaker servants, and what a man hopes for when he appears empty-handed.**

What is desired of man is that he should not regard his wealth as his personal possession but rather as something that belongs only to God. He should spend as much of his wealth as is necessary for his actual needs and the rest he should spend on achieving higher goals. He should give this surplus wealth to the weaker of God’s servants and also spend for the cause of God’s religion. When he spends for the weaker section of society, he hopes that in the Hereafter, when he appears empty-handed before God, he will not be deprived of God’s blessings. When Satan sees that any individual has more wealth than is necessary for his personal needs, he kindles in him another desire, that of indulging in showy activities. At the instigation of Satan, man spends all his money on ostentatious living and feels happy that he has spent his money in the best possible way.

**A loan to the one who is neither poor nor unjust, and two kinds of envy.**

So who would lend to He Who is neither poor nor unjust, Who is worthy of all praise in all His actions, statements, and decisions, of Whom there is neither a deity worthy of worship except Him, nor a Lord other than Him? (There is no envy except in two instances: a person whom Allah has endowed with wealth and he spends it righteously, and a person whom Allah has given Hikmah and he judges by it and teaches it to others.)

269.text:
The section has been arguing about wealth, and this verse moves to the quality that knows how to use it. "Allah grants wisdom to whoever He wills" is stated as a giving with no cause attached to it, so wisdom is described as something handed out by a will rather than as a rank reached by study, and the phrase whoever He wills is the same wording that closed the parable of the multiplied grain. "And whoever is granted wisdom is certainly blessed with a great privilege" then repeats the giving from the side of the one who received it, and the emphasis of the clause is on the amount rather than on the title, since the gift is called much good rather than honour, which is how the sources read the phrase, a good that covers a great deal. "But none will be mindful of this except people of reason" closes the verse with the limit on how widely it lands, and the wording is about being reminded and taking heed rather than about knowing, so the verse ends where it began, on a gift that is not shared out in the way a reader would expect, and the verse after this returns to the act of giving itself, so the wisdom here is doing the work of a measure rather than of a title. The verse after this returns to the act of giving itself, so wisdom here is doing the work of a measure, a standard by which the spending of the previous verses can be weighed.

**Wisdom, the profitable knowledge, and what the word means for a creature.**

He gives wisdom that is the profitable knowledge that leads to righteous action to whomever He will and he who is given wisdom has been given much good because he will end up in perpetual bliss; yet none remembers the tā’ of yadhdhakkar has been assimilated with the dhāl that is to say none is admonished but the people of pith possessors of intellects. (He giveth wisdom unto whom He will) i.e. prophethood to Muhammad ﷺ; it is also said that wisdom here means the interpretation of the Qur'an; as it is said that it refers to being in the right in speech, action and opinion, (and he unto him wisdom) being in the right in speech, action and opinion (is given, he truly hath received abundant good. But none remember) takes admonitions from the similes of the Qur'an or wisdom (except men of understanding) those who have minds from among people. "When the word, hikmah is used for Allah Almighty, it denotes the comprehensive knowledge and solid creative excellence of all things; and when attributed to the non-Divine, it means the rightly-guided knowledge of what exists, and the action which corresponds to it.

**A lot of good given, and the men of understanding who remember.**

(But none remember (will receive admonition) except men of understanding.) means, "Those who will benefit from the advice are those who have sound minds and good comprehension with which they understand the words (of advice and reminder) and their implications." This is the more evident view; more so, since the words of the Qur'an ‌ ‌ "And whoever is given wisdom is certainly given a lot of good" do hint in that direction as they mean that the hikmah covers a lot of good.

**The wings of wisdom, the gaze kept straight, and the man who judges by the Hikmah.**

May I be a ransom for the men dwelling in the Unseen, their secret cores roaming in all that is there! * Give the strong wings of wisdom to the peacock of the Throne and here in this place of the snare you'll see its nest in joy. And when someone like this acts, he acts with wisdom-coming together with the palisades of the Beloved's approval, sacrificing his desire to God's desire, seeing his intimacy in remembering Him, keeping his gaze in accordance with His gaze, resting in his remembrance no matter what arrives; sometimes burned by passion for Him in the playing field of majesty in the station of need, sometimes at ease with His gentleness in the garden of union on the throne of joy. (There is no envy except in two instances: a person whom Allah has endowed with wealth and he spends it righteously, and a person whom Allah has given Hikmah and he judges by it and teaches it to others.)

270.text:
The section has been describing what a gift must be and whom it must not be spoiled for, and this verse removes the last excuse, which is the belief that a small or a hidden thing goes unnoticed. "Whatever charities you give or vows you make are surely known to Allah" covers two kinds of obligation in one clause, what a man hands over without being asked and what he binds himself to by his own word, and the wording of the promise is not about payment but about knowledge, so the verse assures the giver first that nothing has been lost sight of. The two halves are paired deliberately, since a charity is a thing done and a vow is a thing spoken, and the verse puts them together so that a promise a man made to God is treated as something he has already spent. "And the wrongdoers will have no helpers" is the second half, and it is a warning rather than a comfort, since the wrong described here is a withholding or a spending done outside its limits, and the loss stated is that no one stands between such a man and what he has earned. The verse before it spoke of wisdom as a gift given to whoever is willed, and this one states that whatever is done with it is recorded, which is the same rule arriving from the other side, and the pairing of a thing done with a thing spoken covers the whole of what a man can bind himself to, since a charity is a thing he hands over and a vow is a thing he promises, and the verse sets both of them under one knowledge.

**The spending that is not lost, and the vow a man makes on his own word.**

Whatever you spend, no matter how little, for the pleasure of Allah, or any action that you promise to do for Allah without having been required to do it, Allah knows of it and it will not be lost. And whatever expenditure you expend be it as alms or a voluntary almsgiving and whatever vow you make and fulfil surely God knows it and will requite you for it. Here, "and whatever spending you do" covers all spendings - those in which all related conditions are observed and those too, in which all or some conditions are not observed.

**The unjust, the conditions not observed, and the supporters they will not find.**

For instance, it may not be in the way of Allah but be in the ways of sin; or the act of giving may be mixed up with hypocrisy; or may be followed by making a show of the favour before the receiver; or it may not be halal (lawful) and good. The word (al-zalimin) in the text refers to the unjust, the transgressors, who do not observe the necessary conditions. This was made known so that people are persuaded to observe limits and conditions and be warned of their non-observance. It may be absolute, or dependent on something else; or it may or may not have been fulfilled. The purpose of saying all this is that Allah Almighty knows all these things and He shall recompense for them duly. "And whatever spending you do ... and for the unjust, there are no supporters." For the evildoers who prevent almsgiving and vows or expend other than the way they should in disobedience to God they have no helpers to protect them from His chastisement. (And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.) meaning, who will save them from Allah's anger and torment on the Day of Resurrection.

**What the knowledge covers, and the reward that is not lost sight of.**

Allah states that He has perfect knowledge of the good deeds performed by all of His creation, such as charity and various vows, and He rewards tremendously for these deeds, provided they are performed seeking His Face and His promise. (And Allah is Well-Acquainted with what you do) means, "No good deed that you perform escapes His knowledge, and He shall reward for it." ((Allah) will expiate you some of your sins) means, in return for giving away charity, especially if it was concealed. The biggest folly is to be so enamoured of one’s wealth that one fails to spend for the cause of God, and the greatest wisdom lies in recognizing that monetary interests do not present any obstacle to one’s engaging oneself in God’s work. And whatever you spend for spendings (e.g., in Sadaqah) or whatever vow you make, be sure Allah knows it all.

271.text:
The last verse of the section takes up a question the previous verses have been circling, which is whether a gift should be seen. "To give charity publicly is good" opens with a plain yes, and the wording refuses the idea that an open gift is a spoiled one, so the reader is not pushed into a secrecy that would make public giving a fault. "but to give to the poor privately is better for you" then weighs the two and names the side that is better as the one with the poor in it, so the comparison is not between a good deed and a bad one but between two goods, and the reason for the preference is given in the clause itself, better for you, a wording about the giver's own account rather than about the receiver's need. and "and will absolve you of your sins" gives the second gain, with this half of the clause handled carefully, since the expiation is attached to the concealment without being limited to it, so the verse removes a sin and does not promise that only one road can do it. "And Allah is All-Aware of what you do" closes the section with the same watching that ended the parable of the garden, so the whole passage about spending ends where it began, on a knowledge that covers the act, the intention behind it and the manner in which it was carried out. The section that follows turns to the choice of what is given rather than the manner of giving, and the verse here leaves no doubt about which of the two a man should settle first.

**Publishing the alms, and what is better for the one who gives.**

If you proclaim make manifest your voluntary almsgivings that is your supererogatory deeds it is a fine thing to show them; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor that is even better for you than making them manifest or giving it to the rich. (If ye publish) if you show (your almsgiving) which is obligated upon you, (it is well, but if ye hide it) the supererogatory almsgiving (and give it to the poor) the folk of the Platform (ashab al-Suffah), (it will be better for you) than giving it in the open, but both are accepted from you, (and will atone for some of your ill deeds) in proportion of your almsgiving. (But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you.) this indicates that concealing charity is better than disclosing it, because it protects one from showing off and boasting. (If you disclose your Sadaqat, it is well) meaning, "It is well if you make known the charity that you give away." And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers If you disclose your Sadaqat (almsgiving), it is well; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge of the good deeds performed by all of His creation, such as charity and various vows, and He rewards tremendously for these deeds, provided they are performed seeking His Face and His promise. But if you keep it secret and give it to the poor in private, this is better as it indicates sincerity.

**The obligatory alms, and the accusation that an open giving removes.**

As regards the obligatory almsgiving it is better to make it manifest so that it serves as an example and so that one is not accused falsely of not giving; as regards giving it to the poor this is obligatory; and it will absolve you of some of your evil deeds read yukaffir ‘it will absolve’ or nukaffir ‘We will absolve’ either in apocopated form with no final vowel yukaffir nukaffir being a supplement to the locus of fa-huwa ‘that is’ or with nominative inflection yukaffiru nukaffiru indicating the beginning of a new sentence. There may be situations where it becomes more preferable to perform an act of charity openly for some external reasons, such as removing some accusation (of not paying Zakah, for instance) or to persuade others to follow the example. Obviously, this verse covers all types of charity, whether obligatory or supererogatory, and it is more preferable to perform all of them as secretly as possible.

**The charity that is concealed, the show that spoils it, and the receiver's shyness.**

To observe secrecy in a charitable act has religious merits, because it is far from the possibility of riya' (show off), and more graceful for the receiver who can feel shy about receiving charity in public. However, if there is an apparent wisdom behind disclosing the charity, such as the people imitating this righteous act, then disclosing it becomes better than concealing it. It is also beneficial from an earthly point of view, because it does not disclose the amount of wealth one owns. If you reveal your companionship ṣuḥba with Us and make it public you have behaved generously and well. But if you protect Our secret from the intrusion of intermediaries between us you have kept the conditions of love widād and have raised up the lofty edifice of communion wuṣla.

**A part of your sins written off, and the shade on the Day when there is no shade.**

But the reference to expiation here is in the context that even if someone feels a secret charity as useless in this world, he should not feel depressed, because Allah will forgive his sins, and that is a great gain for him. Immediately after the instruction of concealing the 'Sadaqat ', the holy verse says, ‌ (This will write off part of your sins). ((Allah) will expiate you some of your sins) means, in return for giving away charity, especially if it was concealed. (Allah will give shade to seven on the Day when there will be no shade but His. (They are:) a just ruler, a youth who has been brought up in the worship of Allah, two persons who love each other only for Allah's sake who meet and part in Allah's cause only, a man whose heart is attached to the Masjids from the time he departs the Masjid until he returns to it, a person who remembers Allah in seclusion and his eyes are then flooded with tears, a man who refuses the call of a charming woman of noble birth for illicit intercourse with her and says, 'I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds', and a man who gives charitable gifts so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand has given.)
