God is aware of what you do knowing its inner and outer aspects nothing of it being hidden from Him.

**The folly of a man enamoured of wealth, and the wisdom that sees higher realities.**

The biggest folly is to be so enamoured of one’s wealth that one fails to spend for the cause of God, and the greatest wisdom lies in recognizing that monetary interests do not present any obstacle to one’s engaging oneself in God’s work. One who spends his money for the sake of God in the way that He has commanded him to do, proves that he has been blessed with wisdom. One who lives within the cocoon of personal interests and considerations cannot possess the insight which would enable him to see higher realities and experience higher states of consciousness.

272.text:
The section about spending takes up the question of who a gift is for. "You are not responsible for people's guidance O Prophet" is addressed to the man carrying the message, and it removes one duty from him, since the guidance of a person is not something a messenger is given to produce, and the wording of the verse does not soften the refusal or narrow it to a case. "it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills" then gives the other half, a will that distributes guidance, so the verse has moved the matter from the hand that invites to the one who decides, and the sentence stands before a rule about charity so that the reader connects the two. "Whatever you believers spend in charity, it is for your own good" changes the address from the prophet to the believers and turns the gift around toward the giver, so the profit of a spending is described as something that lands in his own account rather than being a cost he pays. "as long as you do so seeking the pleasure of Allah" puts a condition on that return, and the wording is about seeking a face, so the direction of the gift is what decides whether it is for his own good, not the amount of it. "Whatever you donate will be paid back to you in full" answers the worry that a condition this inward makes the transaction unsafe, and the emphasis of the clause is on the completing of a payment rather than on its size, while "and you will not be wronged" closes the verse with the negation of any short measure in what he is given. The sources treat these two halves as one argument, since the removal of a duty over people's guidance is what makes the rule about whom a man gives to so plain, and the occasion the verse carries is about a refusal that was being asked for. The verse before it had ended with a promise that nothing spent is lost sight of, and this one opens the question of guidance, which is why the two belong together.

**The guidance that is not the prophet's duty, and the will that decides it.**

When the Prophet s was prohibited from giving voluntary alms to idolaters as an incentive for them to embrace Islam the following was revealed You are not responsible for guiding them that is to say for people that they should embrace Islam you are responsible only for conveying the Message to them; but God guides with His guidance whomever He will to embrace Islam. O Prophet, you are not responsible for making them believe in the truth and submitting to it: your duty is to guide them to the truth and explain it to them. (The guiding of them is not thy duty (O Muhammad) it is not your duty to guide to Religion the poor from among the people of the Book, (but Allah guideth whomever He will) to His religion. (Not upon you (Muhammad) is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever you spend in good, it is for yourselves, when you spend not except seeking Allah's Face. And whatever you spend in good, it will be repaid to you in full, and you shall not be wronged.) "It is not for you to put them on the right path ... and you shall not be wronged."

**The reward that is for yourselves, and the good a man spends.**

And whatever good property you expend is for yourselves since the reward is for you; for then you are expending desiring only God’s Face this clause is the predicate denoting a prohibition that is to say His reward and not any other transient object of this world and whatever good you expend its requital shall be repaid to you in full and you will not be wronged you will not suffer any diminishment of it both of the last two sentences emphasise the first one. (And whatsoever good thing) wealth (ye spend) on the poor, (it is for yourselves) its reward is for yourselves, (when ye spend) on the poor do do so (save in search of Allah's Countenance) except in seeking Allah's pleasure; (and whatsoever good thing) wealth (ye spend) on the poor among the folk of the Platform, (it will be repaid to you in full) the reward of it will be saved for you in the Hereafter, (and ye will not be wronged) your reward shall not be diminished and your sins will not be increased. As the basic purpose of a Muslim in making a sadaqah is to get that reward, he should not confine himself to giving it to the Muslims only and to avoid giving it to the poor non-Muslims in the hope that this attitude will persuade them towards Islam, because a Muslim is not charged with bringing non-Muslims to the right path. He should seek his own benefit (the reward in the Hereafter) which can also be achieved through giving sadaqah to a non-Muslim. It has been clarified in this verse that a sadaqah given to a non-Muslim also carries a reward in the life to come.

**Seeking Allah's Face, and what a believer spends it on.**

Al-Hasan Al-Basri commented, "Whenever the believer spends, including what he spends on himself, he seeks Allah's Face with it." 'Ata' Al-Khurasani said that the Ayah means, "You give away charity for the sake of Allah. (You will not spend charity with which you seek Allah's Face, but you will ascend a higher degree and status because of it, including what you put in your wife's mouth.) Let us be clear at this point that sadaqah referred to here is nafl supererogatory or voluntary charity) which can be given to a dhimmi (a non-Muslim citizen of a Muslim state) as well. " This is a sound meaning indicating that when one spends in charity for Allah's sake, then his reward will be with Allah. He will not be asked if the charity unintentionally reached righteous, evil, deserving or undeserving persons, for he will be rewarded for his good intention.

**Giving to polytheist relatives, and the sadaqah a harbi is not given.**

Abu 'Abdur-Rahman An-Nasa'i recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said that they, "Disliked giving charity to their polytheist relatives, but were later on allowed to give it to them when they inquired about this matter, and this Ayah was revealed,. It is not permissible to give any kind of sadaqah to a harbi (a non-Muslim citizen of a non-Muslim state) and, however, it is permissible to give the dhimmis all other types of sadaqat, obligatory or supererogatory. The obligatory Zakah is not meant here since it is not permissible to give that to anyone except a Muslim (Mazhari).

**What is repaid in full, and the knowledge that no charity escapes.**

And whatever you spend in good, it will be repaid to you in full, and you shall not be wronged (Charity is) for Fuqara' (the poor), who in Allah's cause are restricted (from travel), and cannot move about in the land (for trade or work). (And whatever you spend in good, surely Allah knows it well) indicates that no charity escapes Him, and He will reward it fully and perfectly on the Day of Resurrection, when it is most desperately needed. You will receive the full reward for any good you spend, no matter how little, because Allah does not wrong anyone. (shall have their reward with their Lord), on the Day of Resurrection, as reward for what they spent in acts of obedience.

**Spending on family while awaiting the reward, and the man who feels satisfied.**

(When the Muslim spends on his family while awaiting the reward for it from Allah, it will be written as charity for him.) One who spends his money for the sake of God in the way that He has commanded him to do, proves that he has been blessed with wisdom. This Ayah praises those who spend in charity for Allah's sake, seeking His pleasure, day and night, publicly and in secret, including what one spends on his family. (Whoever felt satisfied, then Allah will enrich him. Whoever is modest, Allah will make him decent. Whoever is content, then Allah will suffice for him. Whoever asks people, while having a small amout, he will have begged the people.) Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Sa'id said, "My mother sent me to the Messenger of Allah to ask him for help, but when I came by him I sat down. One who lives within the cocoon of personal interests and considerations cannot possess the insight which would enable him to see higher realities and experience higher states of consciousness.

273.text:
The verse fixes the class of people the spending is turned toward, and it does so by describing them from the inside rather than by listing their needs. "Charity is for the needy who are too engaged in the cause of Allah to move about in the land for work" gives a constraint and an occupation together, since they are kept in the land rather than absent from it, and what keeps them there is a cause they have given themselves to, so the poverty being named here is the by-product of a devotion rather than the failure of a man to work. "Those unfamiliar with their situation will think they are not in need of charity because they do not beg" is the sentence the whole description turns on, and the wording is about a man who does not know them rather than about deception, so the error is a plain one, an outsider reading a silence as a sign of ease. "You can recognize them by their appearance" then gives the believer a way out of that error, and the sources discuss what the mark is, since it is not a token worn for the purpose but something a person of good mind reads in a face and in restraint. "They do not beg people persistently" closes the description by returning to the silence, and the wording is of asking pressed on another, so what is denied of them is the importunity a man usually associates with need. "Whatever you give in charity is certainly well known to Allah" finishes the verse on the one who knows, since the class described here is hard to find and easy to mistake, and the assurance is that nothing given to any part of it goes unrecorded. The occasion attached to the verse belongs to the verse before it, and the two should be read together for that reason, since the rule about whom a man gives to and the rule about guidance are given as one passage. Between the second clause and the third there is a movement worth marking, since the first sentence excuses a man who reads a silence wrongly and the second gives him a way to read it rightly, so the verse does not rebuke the mistake but closes it, and the mark the sources discuss is not a sign set up for the purpose of being seen. The last clause then carries the whole description back to the one who knows, which is the same ending the verse before this one had, so the two verses end alike on a knowledge that covers a spending, and the class of people named here is the reason the ending is needed, since a gift given to them cannot be counted by the ordinary sign of a man asking for it.

**The poor who are confined for the cause, and the travel they cannot make.**

((Alms are) for the poor who are straitened) He says: alms are for those who confine themselves (for the cause of Allah) for the obedience of Allah in the Prophet's Mosque, i.e. the people of the Ledge, (who cannot travel in the land) for trade. ((Charity is) for the poor, who in Allah's cause are restricted (from travel) meaning, the migrants who migrated to Allah and His Messenger, resided in Al-Madīnah and did not have resources that sufficiently provided them with their needs,. Here the word, al-fugara ' (the needy: those who need support for their physical sustenance) covers all those who cannot engage themselves in other jobs because of their religious preoccupation. You should spend on those poor people who, because they are busy striving in Allah’s path, are unable to travel to earn a living. (And cannot Darban (move about) in the land) meaning, "They cannot travel in the land to seek means of livelihood.

**The mark that discovers them, the signs a man recognises, and the soliciting they avoid.**

(You may know them by their mark) means, "Those who have good minds discover their situation," just as Allah said in other instances,. (The one who knows them not, thinks that they are rich because of their modesty) meaning, those who do not know their situation think that they are well-off, because they are modest in their clothes and speech. On the surface, this verse gives the sense that they do not solicit importunately but it does not negate soliciting without importunity, as is the actual interpretation of some commentators. (they do not beg of people at all) means, they do not beg and, thus, do not require people to provide them with more than what they actually need. This verse tells us that a faqir (the one who does not own the nisab of Zakah) wearing expensive dress will not be taken as 'need-free' because of that. However, the person who knows will recognise them by the signs that are apparent on their body and clothing. (The Miskin (needy) is not he who wanders about and whose need is sufficed by a date or two, a bite or two or a meal or two. Rather, the Miskin is he who neither has enough resources to sustain him, all the while people are unaware of his need so they do not give to him, nor does he ask people for anything.)

**Souls constrained to obey, and the wealthy people a stranger counts them as.**

They have constrained their souls to obey Him, their hearts to recognize Him, their spirits to love Him, and their secret cores to see Him.23 They have settled down in God's decree and approved of it, they have welcomed His command, they have kept their souls in obedience, they have occupied their hearts with recognition, their spirits have come to be at ease in love, and their secret cores have remained in anticipation of vision, for the Exalted Lord says about them, " They are unable to travel in the earth. You would say that they are without need and you would number them as wealthy, for, despite the defectiveness of their state and the constraint of poverty, they never ask, whether from creatures or from the Real. Their first attribute is that they are constrained in the path of God, that is, they have halted at God's decree. (The unthinking man) the person who does not know them (accounteth them wealthy due to their restraint) because of their attire. They are the beauty of paradise and the adorn ment of the abode of settledness [40:39]-a few of the Emigrants and a few of the Helpers.

**The knowledge that covers what a man spends, and the dress that is not evidence of ease.**

And whatever you spend in good, surely Allah knows it well Those who spend their wealth (in Allah's cause) by night and day, in secret and in public, they shall have their reward with their Lord. (And whatever you spend in good, surely Allah knows it well) indicates that no charity escapes Him, and He will reward it fully and perfectly on the Day of Resurrection, when it is most desperately needed. For instance, if a dead body is found wearing zunnar (waist-cord which is a symbol of some pagan religions), and is uncircumcised, it will not be buried in the graveyard of Muslims. Allah knows of any good or wealth you spend and He will give you a great reward for it. But, in accordance with the consensus of commentators, it means that they just do not ask; (totally refrain from asking) (Qurtubi).

**Their reward with their Lord, the camel a man loves, and the earnings spent on comfort.**

(shall have their reward with their Lord), on the Day of Resurrection, as reward for what they spent in acts of obedience. Abu Sa'id said, "I said to myself, 'I have a camel, Al-Yaqutah, and indeed, it is worth more than a small amount.' And I went back without asking the Prophet for anything. What Satan does is to impress on the minds of human beings the importance of personal requirements, and bring about conviction that all their earnings are best spent on personal comforts and luxuries. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Sa'id said, "My mother sent me to the Messenger of Allah to ask him for help, but when I came by him I sat down.

274.text:
The verse repeats the description of the spenders with no exception carved out of it. "Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night" takes the two halves of a day, and the wording is of a habit rather than of an event, so the people described here are known by the persistence of the thing rather than by its size. "secretly and openly" then closes the other gap, since a gift hidden from a crowd and a gift given in front of one are both counted, which is why the verse reads as an answer to the verses before it, where secrecy was the better of two roads and an open giving was defended against an accusation. "their reward is with their Lord" places the payment where the section has been placing it, with the one who is not asked about his debtors, and the phrase with their Lord carries the sources into a discussion of what a reward is when it is kept rather than paid out. "and there will be no fear for them" opens the second half of the promise, and the negation is general, so the fear being removed is not measured by what the man gave, while "nor will they grieve" is the second negation, given for what he did not give or lost in the giving. The two negations together are the shape of safety in this sūrah, and they are attached here to a spending that has no qualification on its face, which is why the sources attend to the inward condition, sincerity being the thing that makes a secret gift and an open one equal. The absence of a limit in the first half is worth keeping in view while the second half is read, since a spending that is described without an amount attached to it is a spending whose value has been moved entirely to the manner and the direction of it, and the reward being with their Lord is the same wording the section used two verses earlier for the people who give and then do not spoil what they gave. A reader who takes the two halves of the promise as a payment for what was given will miss that they are stated as a removal, a fear that does not arrive and a grief that does not find him, so the profit named here is the absence of two things rather than the arrival of a sum. The occasion given for the verse is about owners of horses, and the sources give it in more than one form, so the verse is read as general even where its occasion was specific.

**Night and day, secretly and openly, and the wage that awaits them.**

Those who expend their wealth night and day secretly and openly their wage awaits them with their Lord and no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve. (Those who spend their wealth) in charity (by night and day, in secret and openly, surely their reward is with their Lord) in Paradise, (and there shall no fear come upon them) perpetually (neither shall they grieve) when others do. Those who spend their wealth for Allah’s sake at night and during the day, secretly and openly, without showing off or looking for fame, will have their reward from their Lord on the Day of Resurrection. Those who expend their wealth night and day, secretly and openly, shall have their wage with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, neither shall they grieve. (Those who spend their wealth (in Allah's cause) by night and day, in secret and in public, they shall have their reward with their Lord. On them shall be no fear, nor shall they grieve.)

**What the horses were, and the verse revealed about their owners.**

The verse was revealed about those who do not keep horses for pride or as a guarantee for debts which are deemed impossible to pay back . Whoever ties a horse for the sake of Allah, and spends on it seeking nothing but the pleasure of Allah, that horse's satiety and hunger, drink and thirst, urine and dung will all be in his balance of good deeds on the Day of Judgement .

**As long as they have wealth they do not slacken, and the fear that does not come for them.**

As long as they have any wealth, they do not slacken from expending it for an hour, night and day. When the wealth is exhausted, they do not slacken from witnessing Him for a moment, night and day.24 This is as they say: As a favour and blessing from Allah, they will have no fear of what the future holds, nor any sadness over what they missed out on in the world.

**Sincerity as the condition of an act of thawab, and the situation where secrecy is better.**

Similarly, spending in the way of Allah, secretly and openly, is an act of thawab both ways, however, the condition is that it should be done with sincerity (ikhlas), and not to earn name and fame. The excellence of spending secretly is limited to a situation where there be no pressing need to spend out openly; and where such a need does exist, spending there openly is certainly better. Based on the authority of Ibn Asakir, there is a report in Ruh al-Ma ani which says that Sayyidna Abu Bakr spent forty thousand dinars in the way of Allah - making it ten thousand during the day, ten thousand during the night, ten thousand openly and ten thousand secretly.

**The greatest way to spend money, and the free time a successful businessman has.**

The greatest way to spend money for the cause of God is to extend monetary help to those of God’s servants who have devoted themselves wholly to the cause of His religion, thus leaving themselves no time to earn for their personal needs. Just as a successful businessman has little free time for anything except his business, similarly one who serves the cause of religion full time has no time to work to make money for himself. The solution to this problem is for those who possess monetary resources to arrange a share for those who, because of their religious commitments, are unable to provide for their own economic needs. On the other hand, those who are monetarily strong, knowing that they have amassed wealth through not devoting themselves to the cause of religion (which they should have done), think that they should, by way of compensation, give a share of their wealth to their brothers in faith.

275.text:
The section on spending turns to a transaction of the same kind, a loan that brings in more than it lent. "Those who consume interest will stand on Judgment Day like those driven to madness by Satan's touch" opens with a standing, and the comparison is to a man touched, so the verse describes the first state of these people at the end rather than their profit at the start, and the wording of the likeness is handled carefully by the sources, since a fainting or a madness is not a punishment a person chooses. "That is because they say" gives the reason for that state, and what they say follows at once, "Trade is no different than interest", a sentence whose whole weight is in the phrase no different, so the fault being described is not the making of a comparison in the mind but the putting of two things in one class after a distinction has been drawn. "But Allah has permitted trading and forbidden interest. Whoever refrains, after having received warning from their Lord, may keep their previous gains, and their case is left to Allah" is that distinction stated again from the other side and then a road opened out of it, since the permission and the refusal are given together without an argument attached, which is why the sources spend their effort on the difference between a sale and a loan rather than on proving that a command needs no cause. The long clause runs from the making of a distinction to a keeping, so the warning itself is what divides a man's account into what is taken back and what is left with him, and the wording of keeping what came before is dealt with by the sources as a remission rather than a profit, while the case being left to Allah keeps the matter of what a man did before the warning out of anyone else's hands. "As for those who persist, it is they who will be the residents of the Fire" is the second half of the division, and "They will be there forever" closes on a staying with no end attached to it, so the verse has moved from a standing in a crowd to a place a man does not leave.

**The comparison they make, the rising of the dead, and the touch that drives a man mad.**

It appears in hadith that the word, la yaqumuna or 'do not stand' means the rising of the dead from their graves on the day of resurrection in the sense that the dealer in riba when he rises from his grave, will rise like the mad man who has been driven crazy by some satan or jinn. The first thing we find out from this sentence is that a human being can faint or go mad under the influence of jinns and satans and the observations of those who have had such experience prove it. (Trading is only like Riba) meaning, they are similar, so why did Allah allow this, but did not allow that, they asked in defiance of Allah's commandments. This is because they made usury permissible and made no distinction between usury and that which Allah has permitted in terms of profit earned through sales transactions. After that, comes the second sentence, in which, giving the reason for this punishment of the consumers of riba, it has been said that these people have committed two crimes. Allah refutes their comparison and explains that He has permitted sale because of the general and specific benefit it contains, and He has prohibited usury because it is oppressive and abusive of people’s wealth.

**The past gains of a man who desists, and what cannot be reclaimed from him.**

Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists from devouring it he shall have his past gains those made before the prohibition and which cannot be reclaimed from him and his affair with regard to pardoning him is committed to God; but whoever reverts to devouring it treating it like trade in terms of lawfulness — those are the inhabitants of the Fire abiding therein. (He unto whom and admonition from his Lord cometh) a prohibition of usury comes from his Lord, (and refraineth (in obedience thereto) from dealing in usury, (he shall keep (the profit) that which is past) he shall not be blamed for his dealing in usury before it was made unlawful, (and his affair (henceforth) in what remains of his life (is with Allah) if He wishes He will protect him and if He wishes He will let him down. (So whosoever receives an admonition from his Lord and stops eating Riba, shall not be punished for the past; his case is for Allah (to judge),) meaning, those who have knowledge that Allah made usury unlawful, and refrain from indulging in it as soon as they acquire this knowledge, then Allah will forgive their previous dealings in Riba,. (As for him who returneth (to usury) after usury has been made forbidden and says trade is just like usury (-such are rightful owners of the Fire) the dwellers of hell.

**A scribe and witnesses for a contract that is still not lawful, and the means that lead to the unlawful.**

They say they only have witnesses and a scribe to write the Riba contract when they want it to appear to be a legitimate agreement, but it is still invalid because the ruling is applied to the agreement itself, not the form that it appears in. Continuing on the subject of prohibiting the means that lead to the unlawful, there is a Hadith that Ahmad recorded in which 'A'ishah said, "When the Ayat in Surat Al-Baqarah about Riba were revealed, the Messenger of Allah went out to the Masjid and recited them and also prohibited trading in alcohol.

**Increase in exchange for a loan and its time, and the riba that was commonly known in Arabia.**

Lexically, riba means increase, and in the verse, it means the increase against which there is nothing in exchange but a loan and its time. "There is no riba except in nasi'ah { loan}", it simply means that the real and primary riba , the one that is commonly understood and termed as riba, is nothing but taking 'profit' on loans. As regards the main riba, which was commonly known in Arabia and which was abandoned by the noble Companions and was enforced by the Holy Prophet announcing its prohibition publicly during his Address of the Last Hajj, it was not possible at all that Sayyidna Umar would have faced any difficulty or doubt in understanding it. This is because the actual reality of this whole system, and the benefit and harm that lies therein, can only be encompassed by the same Alim (the Knower) and Khabir (the Aware), from Whose reach of knowledge the minutest particle of the world cannot escape.

**The year of Hijrah 8, the verses on riba, and the report that does not come from the nobles.**

This is the reason why, in the year of Hijrah 8, when the verses of Surah al-Baqarah relating to the unlawfulness of riba were revealed, there appears no report from the noble Companions anywhere which may indicate that they had to face any doubt in understanding the real nature of riba, and that they had to go as far as to verify it with the Holy Prophet himself, something they did in other matters. He who claimed that this verse is abstract did not understand the clear and confident affirmation of the Shari ah because Allah Almighty sent His messenger to a people of whom he was one, sent him (speaking) in their language, revealed His Book to him so that they comprehend it easily in their language, and in their language the word riba means 'increase"; and in the verse, it means the increase that has no financial consideration against it, (but simply time). Since riba has become the supporting pillar of the prevailing trading system today, it is commonly noticed that people are usually disposed to balk at the idea of its unlawfulness when confronted with its prohibition under the verses of the Book of Allah and the Traditions of the Holy Prophet . The practical sin does have some sort of outward benefit but this second sin against knowledge and belief, that effort be made to prove interest as halal, is greater than the first one.

**The pivot of a human economy, the cure governments came up with, and the percentage a bank doles out.**

In short, the riba of today which is supposed to be the pivot of human economy and features in discussions on the problem of interest, is nothing but this riba, the unlawfulness of which stands proved on the authority of the seven verses of the Qur'an, of more than forty ahadith and of the consensus of the Muslim community. Generally governments did notice this enormously disturbing phenomena but the cure they came up with was to increase the income tax rate for big capitalists, so much so that the maximum rate was set almost close to hundred per cent, which was all designed to funnel capital from them back into the national treasury. Who does not know that this insignificant percentage of interest doled out by 'saving' banks and post offices to clients cannot, by any means, take care of their living expenses.

276.text:
The verse that follows the threat about interest is two lines and does one thing, a reversal. "Allah has made interest fruitless and charity fruitful" takes the very quality that made the transaction attractive, the extra that came back to a man, and removes it, and the wording of the verb is of wiping and effacing rather than of forbidding, so the harm described here falls on the fruitfulness of the gain and not on the amount a man has. "and charity fruitful" sets the opposite half against it, and the same quality is asked for in the other transaction, an increase that grows, so the reader is shown that the two deals differ at the point where a man thinks they are alike, which is exactly the comparison the verse before it refused. "And Allah does not like any ungrateful evildoer" closes on a liking withheld, and the two words describing the person are a refusal to be thankful for what he was given and a wrong done to another, so the verse ends on the reason the first half is true, since a man who takes the increase and forgets the giver is the one whose gain is blighted. The sources read the pair of clauses as one rule about what a blessing is, a good that stays useful rather than a number that rises, and they take up a dirham received as interest and what happens to wealth collected that way in the same discussion, because the verse has made the outcome, not the sum, its subject. The verse is short, and the verse after it will return to the spenders, so this one is doing the work of a hinge, taking the section away from the arithmetic of a loan and putting it back on what a gift becomes. The two verbs of the verse are done to a man rather than by him, since a blighting and a growing are both described as things Allah does, which is why the sentence reads as a statement about outcomes rather than as a second prohibition, the prohibition having already been given in full in the verse before. A reader left with only the first half would conclude that a blighted gain is a small loss, and the closing clause answers that, since a man who is not liked for his ungratefulness has lost something the amount of his wealth cannot describe.

**The blessing taken away from usury, and the almsgivings that are augmented.**

God effaces usury diminishing it and eliminating any blessing in it but He augments voluntary almsgivings with interest increasing them making them grow and multiplying their reward. If they are sincere (Allah hath blighted usury) He has wiped it out and removed its blessedness in the life of this world and in the Hereafter (and made) the obligatory and supererogatory (almsgiving fruitful) accepted and rewarded many times over, when they are done sincerely for His sake. That the outcome of both is contradictory is made clear by this verse which says that Allah Almighty erases the gains obtained through riba or takes away its barakah (blissful abundance); and increases the wealth, or its barakah for the giver of sadaqah. "To ascribe partners to Allah, to practice sorcery, to unjustly kill one whom Allah has declared inviolable, to take riba (interest or usury), to exploit the property of an orphan, to escape at the time of war and to slander the chaste women who are believers, unwary."

**A date given from honest earnings, the reward multiplied, and the hand that accepts it.**

Yet He increases charity and makes it grow by multiplying its reward by ten times up to seven hundred times or even more, and blesses those that give charity from their wealth. (Whoever gives in charity what equals a date from honest resources, and Allah only accepts that which is good and pure, then Allah accepts it with His right (Hand) and raises it for its giver, just as one of you raises his animal, until it becomes as big as a mountain.)

**The dirham received as riba, and the one who writes it down and gives witness to it.**

The Messenger of Allah cursed the one who accepts riba (interest or usury), the one who pays it, the one who writes it and the persons who gives witness to it, and said, "They are all alike." A dirham a man receives as riba (interest or usury) is, in the sight of Allah, more serious than thirty three acts of fornication or adultery in Islam. The Holy Prophet has forbidden the fruits to be sold or purchased before they are eatable, and said, "When zinc (adultery) and riba (usury or interest) become rampant in the people of a town they themselves invite the punishment of Allah.

**What is not made in a factory, the increase that is a certain knock of death, and the wealth whose blessings go away.**

These can be procured against gold and silver, but that which is known as comfort, peace and bliss, is neither made in any factory nor sold in any market. But no sane person would like to have this sort of increase because he knows that this increase is a certain knock of death. May be, the wealth or property does not go to ruins outwardly, but this much is quite certain that its benefits, utilities, and blessings will go away. There are so many statements of the experienced and the knowledgeable which say that the wealth collected through riba may increase faster and higher, but it generally does not survive long enough to run through children and their successors.

**The disbeliever and the sinner whom Allah does not like, and the contrast between sadaqah and usury.**

(And Allah likes not the disbelievers, sinners) indicates that Allah does not like he who has a disbelieving heart, who is a sinner in tongue and action. At the end of the verse , it is said: ‌ ; which means that Allah Almighty does not like any disbeliever, any sinner. Practicing charity (sadaqah) means giving one’s wealth to the needy for the sake of God, while engaging in usury means giving one’s wealth in order to exploit others.

277.text:
The section about interest closes by turning back to the people who did the opposite. "Indeed, those who believe, do good, establish prayer" sets the first three of four things in one line, an assent, a conduct, a prayer held up and an alms-tax paid, so the verse gathers the whole of a religious life rather than a single act of generosity, and the wording of the third and fourth of them is about a duty owed to God and a duty owed to another person, which is why the pair is named together. "and pay alms-tax will receive their reward from their Lord" gives the fourth of them and the return together, and the phrase from their Lord puts the payment with the one who was obeyed, the same wording the verse two places back used for the people who give and then do not spoil what they gave. "and there will be no fear for them" and "nor will they grieve" then give the two negations again, so the promise is not an addition to the reward but the shape of it, a fear that does not arrive and a grief that does not find a man, and the repetition is doing a work here, since the section has just described a transaction whose whole appeal is the safety of an expected increase, and the verse answers that with the only safety it counts. The sources attend to the order of the four things and to the fact that the verse names the doers rather than the deeds, and one of them takes the pair of negations as peace and comfort arriving together. The verse stands after a line about a liking withheld from an ungrateful evildoer, so the two read as a pair, a person not liked and a people given a wage, and the third in the row, the verse after this, turns from description to address. Between the four things named and the two negations there is nothing else stated, so the verse has the look of a settlement rather than an invitation, and the sources draw the arrangement out in both directions, one pair of clauses about what a man does and the other about what will no longer touch him. A reader who takes the alms-tax as the fourth thing in a list of duties will notice that the two duties named last are the prayer and the giving, which are the two the section has been arguing about since the verses on spending began, and that the reward is attached to the whole of them rather than to either one alone, given as a wage that waits rather than a debt that is settled on the spot.

**The four things named together, and the wage that awaits them.**

Those who believe and perform righteous deeds and establish the prayer and pay the alms — their wage awaits them with their Lord and no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve. Those who have faith in Allah, follow His Messenger, do good actions, fulfil their prayers in a complete manner and give Zakat to those deserving it, they shall receive their reward from their Lord and shall not have any fear for their future nor any grief over anything they missed in the worldly life. Those who have faith and do wholesome deeds, who perform the prayer and give the alms tax, shall have their wage with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, neither shall they grieve. And Allah likes not the disbelievers, sinners Truly, those who believe, and do deeds of righteousness, and perform the Salah and give Zakah, they will have their reward with their Lord.

**The works a man does between himself and his Lord, and the disgrace mentioned in the verse before.**

(Lo! Those who believe) in Allah, His messengers, scriptures as well as in the unlawfulness of usury (and do good works) regarding what is between them and their Lord and avoid usury (and establish worship) complete the five daily prayers with all that which is obligated in them (and pay the poor-due) and give the poor-due of their wealth, (their reward is with their Lord) in Paradise (and there shall no fear come upon them) when death is slain (neither shall they grieve) when the Fire is closed. Since, in the verse previous to this, the punishment of Hell and the disgrace the consumers of riba will be facing was mentioned, so in accordance with the general style of the noble Qur'an, the merit - in Akhirah - of the believing-practising Muslims, those steadfast in Salah and Zakah, was mentioned alongside.

**Those who come to be Ours, the wage that is not left to waste, and the caresses in each breath.**

In other words, "Enough for those who come to be Ours will be what they find with Us, for We leave not to waste the wage of those who do beautiful deeds [18:30]. Only those find the world who have worked hard for it; similarly, only those will find the Hereafter who have sacrificed their wealth in order to receive God’s blessings in the Hereafter. " The Pir of the Tariqah said, "O God, all Your caresses are for our sake, for in each breath ap pears so much burning with the light of Your solicitude. Gabriel, with six hundred peacock wings, could not take one step beyond the Lote Tree along with that paragon of the world.

**The honour prepared, the peace and comfort that await, the caresses a man is given, and the Riba that is destroyed.**

The third verse mentions the great reward of peace and comfort that awaits the truly believing and practising Muslims, who are steadfast in Salah and Zakah. Allah states that He destroys Riba, either by removing this money from those who eat it, or by depriving them of the blessing, and thus the benefit of their money. (Allah will destroy Riba) is similar to the statement reported of 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud, "Riba will end up with less, even if it was substantial. Practicing charity (sadaqah) means giving one’s wealth to the needy for the sake of God, while engaging in usury means giving one’s wealth in order to exploit others. Because of their Riba, Allah will torment them in this life and punish them for it on the Day of Resurrection. (And put the wicked (disbelievers and doers of evil deeds) one over another, heap them together and cast them into Hell)[8:37], and,.

278.text:
The address is given once more and the demand is narrowed to what a man is owed. "O believers, Fear Allah" opens with the word the section has been building toward, and the wording of the fear is general, an accountability for what a person does with what he has been given, so the verse begins with the quality rather than with the transaction. "and give up outstanding interest if you are true believers" then names the thing to be left, and the wording is of what remains, a balance still owing rather than a deal already closed, which is why the sources handle the clause as a limit set on the future rather than as a confiscation of the past. The condition at the end of the sentence is the sharpest part of it, since a man is asked to prove his belief by giving up money that is legally his to collect, and the sources discuss the difficulty of a law of that kind, a command with prefixes and suffixes of accountability attached to it because it costs something. The occasion the verse carries is about named families at Makkah and al-Ṭā'if whose debts were being claimed after the prohibition came, and the accounts preserve the answer they gave, so the rule and the case that produced it are kept together. A reader who has just heard that a blighted gain is worse than no gain at all is now told to hand back the expectation itself, and the verse after this gives what follows if he does not.

**Fearing Allah by fulfilling His instructions, and the injunction that covers the real issue.**

O you who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger, fear Allah by fulfilling His instructions and avoiding His prohibitions, and do not demand any usury owed to you that remains with people, if you truly have faith in Allah and in His prohibitions. As the verse opens addressed to Muslims, they were first given the command of that is, 'fear Allah.' Given after that was the injunction covering the real issue. After that, came the injunction: ‌ ‌ that is, 'leave off riba that remains.' Towards the end of the verse it was said: that is, 'if you are believers.' Here it was indicated that ‘Iman (faith, belief) requires that Divine injunctions should be followed faithfully.

**What still remains of the riba, the law that is difficult to act upon, and the gist given after the revelation.**

The gist of the fourth verse : ‌ ‌ those who believe, fear Allah and give up what still remains of the riba if you are believers" is that, after the revelation that prohibited riba, the giving and taking of the amount of riba that remained due against anyone was also prohibited. When a law, which is somewhat difficult to act upon, is given, it has the prefixes and suffixes of accountability of deeds before Allah Almighty, and the punishment and reward of the Hereafter, so that Muslim minds and hearts become prepared to act upon it; the injunction is announced after that. O you who believe fear God and give up abandon the usury that is outstanding if you are believers true to your faith since it is expected of the believer that he adhere to God’s command this was revealed when some of the Companions after the prohibition wanted to reclaim some of the usury from before.

**The sons of 'Amr ibn Umayr, Thaqif, and the verse revealed about them.**

(O ye who believe!) the reference here is to the sons of 'Amr Ibn 'Umayr Ibn 'Awf al-Thaqafi, [and they were four brothers:] Mas'ud [Ibn 'Amr], Hubayb [Ibn 'Amr], 'Abd Yalayl [Ibn 'Amr] and Rabi'ah [Ibn 'Amr] (observe your duty to Allah) fear Allah regarding usury, (and give up what remaineth (due to you) from usury) leave that which the Banu Makhzum owe you of usury, (if ye are (in truth) believers) if you really believe in the prohibition of usury. We heard, and Allah knows best, that this verse was revealed about the Banu Amr ibn Umayr ibn Awf, from Thaqif, and Banu'l-Mughirah, from Banu Makhzum, because Banu'l-Mughirah used to borrow from Thaqif money with usury. This reached the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, and he warned them against going ahead with it.

**The address at the Last Hajj, the men who were warned, and the peace agreement they had.**

But, in spite of this, when the Holy Prophet announced this law in his famous address of the Last Hajj, he made it a point to say that this law does not carry behind it the financial interest of any individual, or nation, or Muslims themselves. Since these people had become Muslims, but did have a mutual peace agreement, the people of Banu Makhzum told them that they had now entered the fold of Islam and had no intention of spending their Islamic earnings in paying off riba. O you who have faith in Allah and follow His Messenger, fear Allah by fulfilling His instructions and avoiding His prohibitions, and do not demand any usury owed to you that remains with people, if you truly have faith in Allah and in His prohibitions.

279.text:
The verse takes the refusal of the command and gives its consequence, then does the same for the man who obeys. "If you do not" is left unfinished on purpose, and the wording carries the whole weight of the clause before it, so the reader has to supply the giving up that was asked for, and the sources treat the terseness as the first half of a threat rather than as an offer. "then beware of a war with Allah and His Messenger" gives that consequence, and the wording of a war is handled by the sources as something distinct from a punishment in the life to come, since a war names an opposition in this one, a man set against a command he can see. "But if you repent, you may retain your principal" opens the way out at once, and the wording of retaining is about keeping what came to him rather than about being punished for what he took, so the verse erases the gain and leaves the capital, and the sources explain why the past is not reopened. "neither inflicting nor suffering harm" closes on a pair of negations that describe an arithmetic as well as an ethics, since the clause refuses a wrong done to a debtor and a wrong done to the one who lent, which is the same balance the verse before this one built out of two transactions. A reader is left with a division with no third part, a man who gives up what is owed to him and a man who insists on it, and the accounts of the two tribes carry the practical case in which the division was decided.

**The threat of war, and the ones who kept dealing in riba.**

But if you do not do what you have been commanded then be warned have knowledge of war from God and His Messenger against you herein is a grave threat for them. (And if ye do not) if you do not abstain from usury, (then be warned of war (against you) from Allah and His Messenger) then be ready for a torment from God in the Hereafter by means of the Fire and its chastisement and also be ready for the sword from His Messenger in the life of this world. (And if you do not do it, then take a notice of war from Allah and His Messenger,) "Whoever kept dealing with Riba and did not refrain from it, then the Muslim Leader should require him to repent. When it was revealed they said ‘What power can we have in a war against Him! If you do not obey the sacred law, then be aware and certain of war with Allah and His Messenger.

**The principal a man takes back, and the riba of the Jahiliyyah that is annulled.**

’ Yet if you repent and forgo it you shall have your principal sums the original amounts not being unjust by charging interest and no injustice being done to you by way of any diminution. The verse then closes with the words: that is, 'if you repent and resolve to leave off the remaining amount of riba in future, you will get your principal. (Verily, every case of Riba from the Jahiliyyah is completely annulled. You will only take back your capital, without increase or decrease. The first Riba that I annul is the Riba of Al-'Abbas bin 'Abdul-Muttalib, all of it is annulled.) If you repent to Allah and leave usury, then you can keep the initial amount that you had given as a loan from your capital, in a manner that does not wrong anyone by taking more than your initial capital and does not wrong you by making you receive less than it.

**Dealing not unjustly, being dealt with not unjustly, and the harm refused on both sides.**

(Wrong not) anyone by demanding interest, (and ye shall not be wronged) by anyone if they give you back your capitals; it is also said that 'wrong not' means: do not harm others; and 'you shall not be wronged' meaning: you shall not be harmed because of your debts. Deal not unjustly, and you shall not be dealt with unjustly And if the debtor is having a hard time, then grant him time till it is easy for him to repay; but if you remit it by way of charity, that is better for you if you did but know And have Taqwa the Day when you shall be brought back to Allah. Yet if you repent you shall have your principal sums not being unjust and no injustice being done to you. Those who willfully persist have no weight or measure miqdār before Us no standing or degree of dignity akhṬār.

**A verse put in the form of a condition, the oppression a society is reformed from, and the justice its members owe each other.**

Perhaps, it is to point out to such details that it was said in the form of a condition ‌ which implies that, if you do not repent, even your principal will be held back. As a consequence, that which he has earned during the period he was a Muslim, goes to his Muslim inheritors, and that which he earns after involvement with kufr is deposited in the Baytul-Mal ( : the Exchequer of an Islamic State). Usury is a form of open economic oppression, that is why Islam has held it unlawful. The basic principle of the reformation of a society is for its members to treat each other with justice. However, just as a usurer is not allowed to make anyone the target of his economic oppression, others should also refrain from subjecting him to their oppression. We have also been enjoined that if the debtor is insolvent, we should have the courage to write off his debt as charity.

**Thaqif, Bani Al-Mughirah, and the answer they gave when Islam came.**

Zayd bin Aslam, Ibn Jurayj, Muqatil bin Hayyan and As-Suddi said that this Ayah was revealed about Bani 'Amr bin 'Umayr, a sub-tribe of Thaqif, and Bani Al-Mughirah, from the tribe of Bani Makhzum, between whom were outstanding transactions of Riba leftover from time of Jahiliyyah. When Islam came and both tribes became Muslims, Thaqif required Bani Al-Mughirah to pay the Riba of that transaction, but Bani Al-Mughirah said, "We do not pay Riba in Islam." 'Attab bin Usayd, the Prophet's deputy on Makkah, wrote to the Messenger of Allah about this matter. They said, "We repent to Allah and abandon whatever is left of our Riba", and they all abandoned it This Ayah serves as a stern threat to those who continue to deal in Riba after Allah revealed this warning. And if he does not go to the limit of considering riba as halal but, nevertheless, in actual practice, does not stop getting involved with it and, on top of that, gangs up with his kind and stands in confrontation with the Islamic government, he then is a rebel.

280.text:
The verse turns from the creditor's claim to a debtor's difficulty, and it is built as two steps with a third left for the reader. "If it is difficult for someone to repay a debt" names a state rather than a fault, and the wording of being straitened is about means running short, so the rule that follows does not ask whether the man is careless or unlucky, only whether he can pay. "postpone it until a time of ease" is the first step, and the sources discuss the word for the ease, whether it names a wide finding or the arrival of capacity, while the verb of the command is a respite given by a person who could press, so the merit of the act lies in the pressing that was not done. "And if you waive it as an act of charity" is the second step and it goes past the respite to a remission, and the wording attaches the forgiveness of a debt to alms rather than to generosity of temperament, which is how a thing owed becomes a gift given. "it will be better for you" gives the gain to the one who remits, and the sources weigh that better against the loss of the capital with a calculation of what a day of respite earns. "if only you knew" closes the verse on a knowledge the reader does not have, and its effect is to leave the comparison open rather than to settle it by a sum, since what is better here is a thing the verse declines to measure. What is brought to the verse includes a man looking for a debtor and finding his household at the door, and the sources use it to show the rule being acted on rather than merely stated.

**Respite and postponement till things are easier, and the reading of a word as maysara or maysura.**

And if any man in debt should be in difficulties then let him have respite a postponement till things are easier read maysara or maysura meaning ‘a time of ease’; but that you should give tassaddaqū where the second tā’ of the softened form tatasaddaqū has been assimilated with the sād the one in difficulty a voluntary almsgiving by waiving his debt is better for you did you but know if you know that it is better for you then do it. And if any man should be in difficulty then [let there be] respite till things are easier; but that you should give a voluntary almsgiving is better for you did you but know. If the person from whom you demand your debt is in hard times and is unable to repay the debt, then refrain from asking until he is able to obtain money and then pay the debt. (And if the debtor) the Banu Makhzum (is in straitened circumstances, then (let there be) postponement to (the time of) ease; and that ye remit the debt as almsgiving would be better for you) than being paid or postponing the debt (if ye did but know) this. It is said that, if your borrower is too poor to pay back your loan, the provision of Shari'ah is that he be given time until he has the means, and should you forgive him your loan, it is much better for you.

**The insolvent man with no way, the difficulties a Lord takes into account, and the judgment that is not hasty.**

His words till things are easier [relate to] the poor insolvent man [who] has no way to obtain anything for himself except through what God appoints for him as the portion of debtors. In that the Lord does not judge us but with His knowledge of our difficulties and weakness and the sincerity of our need for Him and our dedication to Him He is merciful with us.

**A shade on a day when there is no shade, and the charity earned for each day a man gives time.**

In a hadīth it is said ‘Whoever gives respite to one in difficulty or waives his debt God will place him under His shade on a day when there shall be no shade except God’s’ as reported by Muslim. (He will earn charity of equal proportions for each day (he gives time) before the term of the debt comes to an end, and when the term comes to an end, he will again acquire charity multiplied by two times for each day if he gives more time.)" It is said in a hadith from the Musnad of Ahmad that the person who grants respite to a penniless borrower will get a daily thawab of sadaqah in proportion to the amount due against that borrower.

**The debt a man was owed, the boy who came out to him, and the respite commanded.**

Ahmad recorded that Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi said that Abu Qatadah had a debt on a man, who used to hide from Abu Qatadah when he looked for him to pay what he owed him. One day, Abu Qatadah came looking for the debtor and a young boy came out, and he asked him about the debtor and found out that he was in the house eating. That is why we have been commanded that if a debtor has fallen upon hard times, he must be granted respite till he is able to repay his debt.

**The creditor at the term of a debt in the Jahiliyyah, and what is better for a man who remits.**

During the time of Jahiliyyah, when the debt came to term, the creditor would say to the debtor, "Either pay now or interest will be added to the debt." (But if you remit it by way of charity, that is better for you if you did but know) meaning, if you forfeit your debts and cancel them completely. As for the statement - 'if you forgive, that is better for you' - it can be said that this action was obviously a matter of total loss for them because they were not only being asked to surrender riba but also were going to lose their own principal! And to give charity to him by not demanding the debt or giving up a part of it is better for you, if you knew its worth in the sight of Allah.

**Health that frees a man from spending, the needs a little cannot liquidate, and the deadline for repayment.**

Or, it so happens that such rich people have to spend huge amounts of money on undesirable heads such as medicines, treatment and consultancy fees, which is something the poor do not face. First of all, Allah Almighty blesses them with health which frees them from spending on their treatment and, in case they do fall ill, ordinary treatment gives them their health back. The little they have serves to take care of so many needs which will never be liquidated with large amounts of money spent by those whose money is Haram (unlawful). After that there is the sixth verse which, in comparison to the anti-human claim of riba, has stressed upon pure moral behavior of showing lenience to the poor and the have-nots. And this calculation covers the act of giving respite well before the deadline for repayment arrives; and when the deadline for repayment does arrive and the borrower does not have the means to pay, the respite given at that time will bring forth for the giver of respite a daily thawab of giving twice that amount in sadaqah.

281.text:
The last verse of the section stops speaking about a transaction and speaks about an ending. "Be mindful of the Day when you will all be returned to Allah" takes back the fear the section has been using for a debt and sets it on a day, and the wording of a return is about going toward a place rather than arriving at it, so the verse describes a movement every person is in, with the all of the address doing the work of leaving no one out. "then every soul will be paid in full for what it has done" gives the accounting, and the two things it fixes are the scope and the measure, every soul without exception and a payment completed without shortfall, which is why the sources read the clause as the reason the earlier rules were worth obeying at a cost. "and none will be wronged" closes with the negation the section has now heard three times, once about a spending, once about a principal kept and once here about a settlement, so the whole passage about money ends on a refusal that anyone is dealt with unjustly at the end. The sources handle the placement of this verse carefully, since a reading of it as a prohibition of interest in disguise is discussed and set aside, and the line about not expecting a return for a favour is brought in beside it, because a man who lends in order to be thanked and a man who gives in order to be repaid are being answered by the same clause. What is left for the reader is a payment in full for what he has done, which is a sentence that can be heard as comfort or as fear depending on what he did with what he was given. The section that began with a grain of wheat has ended by putting a weight on every act, and the two are the same argument, since a multiplication promised in the earlier verses is a payment in full stated here, given without a shortfall in either direction. A man who was told that a blighted gain is worse than no gain, and that a respite earns more than a collection, is now told that the settlement of both is ahead of him rather than behind him, which is the reason the verse is placed at the close of the passage and not at its beginning, so that everything before it is read under a settlement.

**Being brought back at the time of death and on the day of rising, and the punishment of a day.**

And fear a day wherein you shall be returned to God namely the Day of Resurrection read the passive turja‘ūna meaning ‘you shall be returned’ or the active tarji‘ūna meaning ‘you shall return’ and every soul on that day shall be paid in full the requital of what it has earned what it has done of good or evil; and they shall not be wronged through any loss of a good deed or the incurring of an extra evil deed. Fear the punishment of a day in which you all will be returned to Allah and you will have to stand before Him. (And guard yourselves against a day) fear the torment of a day (in which ye will be brought back to Allah. Then every soul) whether believing or disbelieving (will be paid full that which it hath earned) of good or evil, (and they will not be wronged) their rewards will not be decreased and their sins shall not be increased. There are two kinds of return: [a return] for the bodily and lower selves in the future at the time of death and [a return] for the innermost selves and hearts at every breath. [The latter is] a reckoning-a payment in ready cash versus a promise [regarding the future].

**Every soul paid in full, and no person dealt with unjustly.**

(And have Taqwa for the Day when you shall be brought back to Allah. Then every person shall be paid what he earned, and they shall not be dealt with unjustly.) (And have Taqwa for the Day when you shall be brought back to Allah. Then every person shall be paid what he earned, and they shall not be dealt with unjustly.")

**The gifts given at marital ceremonies, the favour that is not to be counted on, and the pleasure a giver does not seek.**

The gifts of this type are in vogue in some communities at the time of marital ceremonies Since this type of giving is to seek selfish ends and not to seek the pleasure of Allah Almighty, therefore, it was said in the verse that by doing so your wealth may seem to increase, but actually it does not increase with Allah, while that which is given as Zakah and sadaqat to seek the pleasure of Allah Almighty goes on to double and redouble with Allah. According to this explanation, the sense of the verse will match with what was said addressing the Holy Prophet in another verse (74:6): ‌ that is, do not do favour to anyone with the intention that it may bring to you some added benefit in return. According to some scholars of tafsir, this verse does not refer to the prohibition of usury or interest at all, rather, the word 'riba-' used in that verse refers to a gift presented to someone, not in good faith, but with the intention that it would bring back some better gift in return from the receiver. Then, following that, in the verse under discussion, it was further explained that financial help given to someone with the hope that it will bring back greater return from the receiver of the help is certainly no spending in the way of Allah where the purpose is hardly to seek His pleasure.

**A paltry price, the kingdom of the world taken in exchange, and the purgative a man drinks to cleanse him.**

The expression 'paltry price' was used here to indicate that even if the kingdom of the whole world was taken in exchange for the Divinely revealed verses, the price will still be 'paltry.' It does not mean that taking a paltry price against the verses of the Qur'an is Haram, but taking a higher price would be permissible. It is like someone who takes purgative as system-cleanser or lets blood as a therapeutic measure; he looks weak on the outside and seems to miss something in his body but those who know regard this 'decrease' to be a fore-runner of his 'increase' in health and strength. This does not mean that riba will not be prohibited if it happens not to be multiplied many times, because the absolute prohibition of riba has been very clearly stated in Surah al-Baqarah and Surah al-Nisa', irrespective of its being doubled or multiplied many times. In pre-Islam Arabia, the general pattern of riba transactions was that loans were given on riba for a set period of time; when that period expired and the borrower was unable to pay it back, he was given an extension of time on the condition that the amount of riba was to be increased.

282.text:
The longest verse in the sūrah is a piece of procedure, and it opens with the address the section has been using. "O believers, When you contract a loan for a fixed period of time" names a debt with a term attached to it, which is the case where a man most needs a record, and "commit it to writing" is a command given to the parties rather than to a judge, so the writing is something they arrange between themselves. "Let the scribe maintain justice between the parties" brings in a third person and at once limits his role to standing even with both sides, and "The scribe should not refuse to write as Allah has taught them to write" removes the excuse of a man who would rather not be troubled, with the reason given in the same clause, since the skill he has is itself the thing that makes him available. "They will write what the debtor dictates, bearing Allah in mind and not defrauding the debt" then fixes who the words come from and what the writing must not do, and the dictation is put on the one who owes, which is the arrangement the next clause protects: "If the debtor is incompetent, weak, or unable to dictate, let their guardian dictate for them with justice" covers a man whose understanding or body will not carry the task, and the guardian is bound to the same justice the scribe was. "Call upon two of your men to witness" sets the number, "If two men cannot be found, then one man and two women of your choice will witness" gives the alternative, and "so if one of the women forgets the other may remind her" states the reason inside the ruling itself, a reminder held in reserve. "The witnesses must not refuse when they are summoned" closes that side of it, and "You must not be against writing contracts for a fixed period, whether the sum is small or great" returns to the record and refuses a man's preference for leaving the small thing unwritten. "This is more just for you in the sight of Allah, and more convenient to establish evidence and remove doubts, However, if you conduct an immediate transaction among yourselves, then there is no need for you to record it, but call upon witnesses when a deal is finalized" then gives the exception, a hand-to-hand trade that needs no writing, while witnesses are still asked for when a deal is settled. "Let no harm come to the scribe or witnesses. If you do, then you have gravely exceeded your limits" protects the two who are doing the work from being worn down by it, and "Be mindful of Allah, for Allah is the One Who teaches you. And Allah has perfect knowledge of all things" ends the longest verse in the sūrah on a teaching and a knowledge, so the whole procedure is framed by the two things the verse has been assuming all along.

**Write it down when you contract a debt for a fixed term, and the scribe who does not refuse.**

O you who believe when you contract a debt one upon another for a stated term write it down; and let a writer write it down between you justly; and let not any writer refuse to write it down as God has taught him; so let him write and let the debtor dictate; and let him fear God his Lord and not diminish anything of it. It was said that the agreement, big or small, should invariably be written down: 'And, be not loath to write it down, as payable at its time, no matter how short or long.' Of course, if there is a hand-to-hand transaction, not involving any debt, it could be left unwritten. (No scribe should refuse to write) the contract between the creditor and the debtor (as Allah hath taught him) how to write, (so let him write) the contract without addition or omission, (and let him who incurreth the debt dictate) i.e. the indebted person should explain to the scribe the debt he owes, (and let him observe his duty to Allah his Lord) let the indebted person fear his Lord, (and diminish naught thereof) and not diminish any amount of debt he owes upon dictation. (O you who believe! When you contract a debt for a fixed period, write it down) directs Allah's believing servants to record their business transactions when their term is delayed, to preserve the terms and timing of these transactions, and the memory of witnesses, as mentioned at the end of the Ayah,.

**A debtor of low understanding, and the guardian who dictates with justice.**

And if the debtor be a fool a squanderer or weak not up to dictating on account of old age or immaturity or unable to dictate himself on account of being dumb or not knowing the language and so forth then let his guardian the one in charge of his affairs be it a parent an executor a custodian or an interpreter dictate justly. (But if he who oweth the debt is of low understanding) is ignorant of dictation, (or weak) unable to dictate, (or unable himself to dictate) does not know how to dictate to the scribe, (then let the guardian of his interests dictate) the guardian of his wealth who is the creditor (in (terms of) equity) without any addition.

**One man and two women of such as you approve, the shortcoming in a mind, and the reminder that makes one recall the other.**

And summon to bear witness two witnesses men; or if the two be not men then one man and two women such witnesses as you approve of so that if one of the two women errs; the other will remind her; and let the witnesses not refuse whenever they are summoned; and be not disdainful to write it down small or great with its term; that is more equitable in God's sight more upright for testimony and nearer that you will not be in doubt unless it be trade carried out there and then that you give and take between you then you will not be at fault if you do not write it down. (And if two men be not (at hand) then a man and two women, of such as ye approve as witnesses) from among people who are reliable in their witness, (so that if the one erreth (through forgetfulness) so that if one of the women forgets (the other) who did not forget (will remind her. And the witnesses must not refuse) to give witness (when they are summoned) to court. (As for the shortcoming in her mind, the testimony of two women equals the testimony of one man, and this is the shortcoming in the mind. As for the shortcoming in the religion, woman remains for nights at a time when she does not pray and breaks the fast in Ramadan.)

**Be not averse to writing it down, small or great, and the weariness a man is kept from.**

(Be not averse) disinclined (to writing down) i.e. the debt (whether it be small or great, with (record of) the term thereof. That) i.e. that which I mentioned regarding the writing down of the debt (is more equitable) more correct and fairer (in the sight of Allah and more sure for testimony) clearer for the witness when he gives his testimony if he happens to forget, (and the best way of avoiding doubt between you) concerning the debt and the fixed term of its payment; (save only in the case when it is actual merchandise which you transfer among yourselves from hand to hand. You should not become weary to write it (your contract), whether it be small or big, for its fixed term, that is more just with Allah; more solid as evidence, and more convenient to prevent doubts among yourselves, save when it is a present trade which you carry out on the spot among yourselves, then there is no sin on you if you do not write it down.

**Harm that must not come to a scribe or a witness, and the court a witness is forced to appear in.**

(Let neither scribe nor witness suffer (or cause) any harm) also indicates that the scribe and the witness must not cause any harm, such as, when the scribe writes other than what he is being dictated, or the witness testifies to other than what he heard or conceals his testimony. No doubt, under its system of justice, Islam has forced the witnesses to appear in court, and has made the concealment of evidence a grave sin; but at the same time, the other side of the picture has also been duly taken care of, so that people are not made to stay away from testifying. Or, it could be that having witnesses in such cases is only recommended and not obligatory, as evident from the Hadith that Khuzaymah bin Thabit Al-Ansari narrated which Imam Ahmad collected. 'Umarah bin Khuzaymah Al-Ansari said that his uncle, who was among the Prophet's Companions, told him that the Prophet was making a deal for a horse with a bedouin man.

283.text:
The verse takes the case a man cannot document and gives him a substitute. "If you are on a journey and a scribe cannot be found" is the whole difficulty, a road and no writer, and "then a security can be taken" answers it with something held rather than something written, so the record is replaced by a possession. "If you trust one another, then there is no need for a security, but the debtor should honour this trust by repaying the debt" then goes past the substitute altogether, and the wording is careful, since the verse does not say a trust is a weakness in a transaction but places the obligation on the one who is trusted, so the security is what a man takes when he is not willing to rely on a person. "and let them fear Allah, their Lord" puts a watch over the arrangement, and the phrase their Lord is attached to the fear so that the man who could pay and does not is not merely breaking an agreement. "And do not conceal the testimony, for whoever conceals it, their hearts are indeed sinful" then turns from the two parties to the witness, and the wording of a heart is what makes the clause hard, since the sin is placed inside a person rather than on the courtroom floor, while "And Allah fully knows what you do" ends the verse with the knowledge the whole passage has been resting on. The verse is a short one and it closes the longest verse in the sūrah by handling what happens when its procedure cannot be carried out, and a passage brought to it tells of a shield mortgaged for food, which is the same shape as a security taken on a road. The order of the verse is worth holding on to, since a security is offered only after a scribe has been looked for and not found, so the taking of a pledge is a remedy for a missing writer rather than the ordinary form of a loan, and the verse then moves at once past the remedy to the case where no remedy is needed at all. A reader who stops at the first clause would come away with a rule about objects held in pledge, while the middle of the verse is about a bond between two people that nothing is held under.

**A journey, no scribe to be found, and a pledge held instead of a writing.**

And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe, then let there be a pledge taken (mortgaging), then if one of you entrusts the other, let the one who is entrusted discharge his trust, and let him have Taqwa of Allah, his Lord. (If ye be on a journey and you cannot find a scribe) or the means by which to write, (then a pledge in hand (shall suffice) then let the creditor take from the indebted person a security for his loan. And if you are upon a journey travelling and you contract a debt and you do not find a writer then a pledge ruhun or rihān plural of rahn in hand as a guarantee for you. If you are travelling and do not find anyone who can write down the debt for you, then the debtor can give a property to the creditor as a security for his right until the debt is paid. The Sunna clarifies the permissibility of making pledges in towns where writers may be forthcoming; but the stipulation is made in the event of travel because in this case it is more important to have a guarantee; God’s reference to it being ‘in hand’ maqbūda is a condition for the pledge given to be valid and to satisfy the pledgee or his representative.

**The trusted man pays what he was entrusted with, and the fear of their Lord.**

(And if one of you entrusteth another) to give a loan without security (let him who is trusted) with the debt (deliver up that which is entrusted to him) the right of his creditor (and let him observe his duty to Allah, his Lord.) the debtor should fear Allah regarding repayment of his debt, (Hide not testimony) from the judges in court. But if one of you the creditor trusts another the debtor over the debt and does not require a pledge let him who is trusted the debtor deliver his trust the debt; and let him fear God his Lord when delivering it. We should also keep in mind the recurring style of the Qur'an whereby, before and after giving a particular law, it creates an inner impulse to follow Divine injunctions by introducing the fear of Allah and the fear of the Day of Retribution.
